div.p: NIP
PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

IT is said of one fashionable yonng man that he sever paid anything but a compliment. A SOCIETY journal infornis us that "when a gentleman and lady is walking up the street the lady should walk inside the gentleman. AT a dinner party in Boston, a young man, who was visiting from the West, was asked if he was fond of ethnology. "'Well, ye.es," he replied at a venture; "but I don't think I'll take any to- night." A LADY of charitable disposition asked a tramp if she could not assist him by mending his clothes. "Yes, madam," he replied, •‘ I have a button, and f you would sew a shirt on to it you would greatly oblige me." A DANBURY youth who could not sing or play wanted to serenade his girl, whistled fcr half an he& under the window the other evening, and when he got over the fence found about 75 dogs waiting o see wkat he wanted. A FEW days ago a it very handsome woman en- tered a country draper's and asked for a bow. The polite assistant drew himself up and remarked that he was at her service. "Yes ; but I want a buff, and not a green one," was the reply. AN old bachelor editor thus, in his spite, com- ments on a recent moonlight "We left our sanctum at midnight last night, and on our way home we saw a young lady and gentleman holding a gate on its hinges. They were evidently indignant at being kept out so late, as we saw them bite each other several times." CURRAN was sometimes paid in his own coin, as on one occasion when he pressed Godwin for his opinion of a speech he had just delivered. "Since you will have my opinion, said Godwin, folding his arms and leaning back in his chair with sang- froid, "I never did hear anything so bad as your prose except your poetry, my dear Curran." WHEN the water broke into the Thames Tunnel during the progress of the work Hood. said to Planche, "They've been labouring at that affair for a long time, and now the Thames has filled up their leisure." On Planche repeating this to Charles Nemble, he said, "Well, Planche, I can't see anything so "—laughable he would have added; but he began to laugh before he could finish the sentence. "Iv is a good thing to have a friend in need," said Brass thoughtfully. "Do you think so 1" inquired his chum. "I ought to be happy, then, for all my friends are friends in need, judging from the begging letters I get from them." And he sighed deeply. THE following unique epistle was picked up lately in the street:—" Dear Bill,—The reason I didn't laff when you laft at me in the post- office yesterday, was becos I hey a bile on my face, and I can't laff. If I laff, she'll bust. But I love you Bill, bile or no bile, laff or no laff."

WIFE (to husband)—" Mother wants to come and make us a visit, John ; but I have written her that, just at present, while baby is teething, it wouldn't be convenient. If I give you the letter will you think to post it ?" Husband (with an air of perfect confidence)—" Well, I should say I would !" "MY DEAR," said a K Street father to his daughter, "who is the gentleman who has been so attentive to you of late ?" "Oh, papa, he is such a nice gentleman, and he gets S,OCO dols. a year." "Great Scott, child, he must be a Cabinet Minis- ter !" "Oh, no, he isn't, papa; he is the pitcher in a baseball nine." WHEN Ilacleane, the principal of Brighton College, was at Trinity College, Cambridge, he one day met the Marquis Spoleto, a teacher of Italian, and a refugee, and thus accosted him— " Have you many pupils this term 1" " Vel, I 'ave vone in Hebrew." "Dear me," said Macleane, "I had no idea you knew Hebrew." " Vel, no; not exactly. But then, you see, we do not begin for vone five veek." AIONG the guests at the table of a friend was a clergyman of the old school, who, doubtless enjoy- ing "the feast of reason and the flow of soul," was equally alive to the merits of the turtle and the port, which last was exceptionally fine. "I see," said my clerical neighbour, addressing myself, "You stick to port." "Yes," I said, "and so am safe from being half seas over." ONE day Hook observed a pompous gentleman walking in very grand style along the Strand Instantly leaving his companion, he went up to him and said—" I beg your pardon, sir; but may I ask, are you anyone in particular?" bowiqg respectfully, and passing on before the astonished magnifico could collect himself to give a practical or other answer to the query. Two silly brothers, who were very much about town in Hook's time, took pains by dressing alike to deceive their friends as to their identity. Some one was expatiating upon these modern Dromios, at which Hook grew impatient. "Well," said his friend, "we will admit that they resemble each other wonderfully. They are as like as two peas." "They are," retorted Theodore, "and quite as green." AN intimate friend of W. H. Harrison's told him of a/dinner at John Murray's (the elder), when Sir David Brewster gave some account relating to the prismatic oolours of mother-of-pearl. " Mither of part I" said Hogg, the poet; "Murray, what's mither of parl ?' "On, I don't know, replied Murray; "there's hook; he knows everything; ask him." " Well, Hogg," said the novelist, "I 'don't know, unless it's the Venerable Bede." TAMING, the German author, was, in his old age, subject to extraordinary fits of abstraction. On his return home one evening, after he had knocked at his door, the servant looked out of the window to see who was there. Not recognising his master In the dark, and mistaking him for a stranger, he called out, "The professor is not at home." "Oh, very well," called out Leseing, "no matter; I'll call another time," and walked off. TUEATRICAL MANAGER—" I can't tell whether your sister will suit us or not until I've seen her, and talked with her, and seen what she can do. Is this a recent photograph of her? Young Man— " Just taken. She is a good elocutionist, and has • always wanted to go on the stage. She is a good girl, too, and obeys every one of the ten command- ments--" Manager—" Don't care a darn about the ten commandments. Can she say G'yurll' and Me cheyld l' That's what I want to know." —Chicago Tribune. AN eccentric Justice of the Peace, before whom a citizen had prosecuted his daughter's lover for ejecting him from his own parlour on the Sunday evening previous, solemnly decided as follows :- 4' It appears that this young feller was courtin' the plaintiff's gal in plaintiffs parlour, and that plain- :tiff intruded, and was put out by defendant. , _Courtin' is a public necessity, and must not be in- terrupted. Therefore the law will hold that a parent has no legal right in a room where courtin' is afoot • and so the defendant is discharged, and plaintiff pay costs." The scene of the following was at Avignon in France :—" By my faith, said the President of the Tribunal to an interested auditor, "we have just had a superb turkey, tender as a chicken, fat as an ortolan, aromatic as a thrush. By my faith we left nothing but his bones." "And how many were there of you ?" inquired the curious hearer. "Only two," answered the gourmet, with a self-complacent smile. "Only two 1" ejaculated the simple auditor with amazement. " Precisely so." the lawyer an- swered. "Only two. There was myself, and thore was—the turkey." MooRE relates in his Diary :—During breakfast arrived Count Krasinksi, an intelligent Polish refugee and msn of letters. Remarked that there was a strong similarity between the Poles and the Irish, and mentioned as an instance of this, a countryman of his, who having, on some occasion, knocked a man down for being, ea he thought, insolent to him, was expostulated 'with for having done so by some friend, who remarked that, after all, what the man had said to him was not to very offensive. " No, it was not," answered the other; " but still it was safer to knock him down." "Au! what's this?" exclaimed the intelligent I compositor—"' Sermons in stones, books in the running brooks?' That can't be right. I have it. He means • Sermone in books, storms in the running brooks.' That's sense." Aud that is how the writer foiled it. WALTER BAGEHOT used to say banteringly to his mother, by way of putting her off at a time when she was anxious for him to marry, "A man's mother is his misfortune, but his wife is his fault."

div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

The Queen (a Windsor correspondent learns) will stay a few days longer than anticipated upon the Continent and will not return to England till the beginning of next month. Her Majesty, according to present arrangements,is expected to leave Dariaa- stadt on May 2.

Courtfield, the Herefordshire seat of the ancient family of Vaughan of Courtfield, of which the new Archbishop of Westminster, who has just preached his farewell sermon at Salford, is the head, is his- torically celebrated as the nursery of Harry the Fifth. The house stands on the banks of the pic- turesque Wye, not far from the ruins of Goodrich Castle, and commands fine views over the Forest of Dean. and as far away as the Walsh mountains. The present owner of the estate is Col. Francis Vaughan, who is the fourth son of the late Colonel Vaughan, his three elder brothers all being ecclesiastics in the Romish Church.

It is stated that Mr. Ellis Jones Griffith, the Liberal candidate for West Toxteth, Liverpool, is seriously unwell with congestion of the brain. It was only a few days ago that he married, in Liver- pool, Miss Mary Owen, a Flintshire young lady, whose vocal talent is keenly appreciated in the musical Principality. Ir. Ellis Griffith,who springs from the Anglesea farmer class, was president of the Cambridge Union, and is a Fellow of Downing College, Cambridge. He enjoys a fair amount of practice on the North Wales Circuit, and a few months ago he undertook an important legal en- gagement in Persia.

The King of Siam has just had a pavilion of glass built for himself by a Chinese architect, the mater- ial for which, was furnished by a French company. Walls, flours, and ceiling, are formed of slabs of different sorts and thickness of glass joined by im- permeable cement. By one door only can the King enter, and this closes hermetically when he comes in, and ventilator valves in tall pipes in the roof open, as does also a sluice beside a large reservoir in which the glasshouse stands. The transparent edifice then becomes submerged, and the King thus finds himself in a cool and perfectly dry habitation, where he passes the time singing, smoking, eating, and drinking.

In reference to the production at Weimar next week of M. Massenet's opera " Werther," a rather curious circumstance has come to light. tudents of Goethe are aware that, according to the gener- ally accepted theory, Werner the lover is intended to stand for Goethe himself, Albert the husband for the poet's friend Kestner,' and Lotte for Kestner's wife Charlotte Buff, with whom Goethe was in love, It now, however, seems that the name of Herr Giessen, adopted by the leading tenor who will play the part of iVerther, is a mere nom de tHatre, that his real name is Buff, and that he is a grandnephew of this very Charlotte Buff, otherwise Lotte, the heroine of the novel and of the opera.

The most interesting room in Mrs. Tennant's house at Richmond-terrace, where Mr. H. M. Stanley is resting after his long Australian tour, is the studio of Mrs. Dorothy Tennant Stanley. This is on the top floor, takes in the entire space, and has a glass roof, which, when shifted, gives the fair artist an open-air effect to work in. Mrs. Stanley spends a part of every day she is at home in her studio, and her great delight has always been to place it at the disposal of whatever distinguished artist or painter happens to be a guest at the house. Many of these visitors, who have come from various parts of the world, have " thrown " rough sketches upon the walls, doors, and window-panes, which materially add to the attractiveness of the studio.

The Bank Holiday passed off very quietly. The Volunteers seem to have got on better than was to be expected, and in London, until the evening, when some showers fell, the weather did not give much cause for complaint. The uncertainty, however, as to whether the holiday makers would meet in " thun ler, lightning, ar in rain," undoubtedly had the effect of keeping in town a very large number of people who otherwise would have taken a trip into the country. The condition of the streets on Easter Monday compared with what they were some twenty years ago, when the Bank Holiday was established, is remarkable. The annual drink bill per head may have increased, but drunkenness and disorderly conduct hare certainly declined.

Dr. J. E. Neild, the acting coroner of Melbourne, who has been generally complimented on his con- duct of the inquest on the murdered Mrs. Deeming, is a Yorkshireman bordering on the seventies. lie commenced his medical studies at Sheffield, and concluded them in 1848 at University College, London. Emigrating to Australia in 1853, he soon established himself in Melbourne, and has ever since been a leading figure in the medical and journalistic circles of that city. For nearly forty years he has been the foremost dramatic critic of Australia, and on his recent retirement from that position his long and valuable services to dramatic art were recog- nised with a purse of .£l,OOO subscribed by the play- going public of Melbourne.

Another Manchester barrister, Mr. C. T. Fleming, is seeking admission to the " assembly of great thinkers "at Westminster. He has been adopted as the Radical candidate for Doncaster, and stands an excellent chance of wresting the seat from the Unionists, into whose hands it accidentally fell. Mr. Fleming is a man of commanding presence, re- taining in middle life the straight, stalwart form which an early military training gave him. After I serving a term in the Dragoons he took up the law I with considerable success. His barly figure is fre- quently seen in the courts of Manchester and dis- trict, and while his eloquence is heavy,it is flavoured with such rich common sense and sound law tnat very few juries, disagree with him. Of late years he has done a good deal of journalistic work, and is now perhaps more warmly attached to letters than to law.

Rothley Temple, Lord Macaulay's-birthplaco, is for sale by public auction. It is an old manor house some six miles from Leicester, and there the histor- ian was born at the end of the year 1800. It cannot be said that Rothley Temple derived more than nominal lustre from the association, for Macaulay left Leicestershire before he had left infancy, and Birchin-lane, in the City, was the home of his earli- est childhood. Instead of a manorial park, he had Drapers'-gardens for a playground, until he went to live in the old High-street, at Clapham. The Leicestershire manor, however, has many historical interests besides this one, and a thirteenth century chapel of tbe Knights Templars is attached to the estate. It is a wealthy manor, too, for nine hundred acres. produce £2,000 of annual rent ; and, moreover it is at the headquarters of the famous Quorn Hunt, and in the heart of some famous scenery.

Tha cult of the Primrose is dying out. But for I the perennial stereotyped article in one or two Tory papers and the antics of the Primrose League, the public would not be aware that this was Primrose Day. It is eleven years since Lord Beaconsfield died. For some years after his death his ghost haunted Tory meetings. He was always good for a cheer. But whether it be that Toryism has changed, or that old Dizzy's name has lost its force as a rallying cry, certain it is that references to him are now rare in Tory speeches. Perhaps the discovery is being made that after all Beaconsfield was a poli- tical trickster and not a statesman, and that, com- pared with the memories of Palmerston, Russell, Peel, Pitt, Chatham, and other great Premiers his fame will prove ephemeral. The worship of the primrose—without rhyme or reason—by a section of his followers will not last. Every year shows is decrease—whicls the enthusiasts put down to the I increasing scarcity of the primrose.

Sufficient attention is hardly paid to Mr. Edison's latest invention. If be really can construct cheap aerial machines which can navigate at will for 50 miles and hurl down dynamite on the earth be- neath, war will be revolutionised. I suppose that the machines can be projected from vessels. If so a vessel would only have to approach a town situ- ated near the sea shore in order to destroy it. In- deed, in case of a war between England and France, machines might be launched from each coast to do this. What will be the use of fortresses, if a few machines hovering over them can force them to capitulate, or blow them and their garrisons to atoms? 'With a few of these machines, Paris would have been at the mercy of the Germans in 1870. What would be the use ot an army in battle array if dynamite were showered down on it? My hope is that war will be made so murderous that States will hesitate to engage in it • consequently I ' am by no means sorry for fresh and more terrible instruments of slaughter being invented. Neverthe- less, I regret that Mr. Edison's machines are, as he says, not costly. A few in the hands of Anarchists , would play mischief with a town.

div.head: RAILWAY SERVANTS AND THEIR WANTS.
div.p: RAILWAY SERVANTS AND THEIR WANTS.
CANDIDATES CATECHISED.

The Secretary- of the Widnes branch of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, has sub- mitted the following questions to the members and candidates for the Widnes and Northwich Parlia- mentary Divisions, and asking were they in favour of : _

"(1.) A maximum working day of ten hours, with six days to the week, for all railway employes, such hours to be regulated and endorsed by the Board of Trade, the necessary powers being obtained for that purpose from Parliament. (2.) An effective super- vision over the working of all railways, which shall include periodical inspection by qualified and prac- tical sub-inspectors, who shall act under the exist- ing Board of Trade inspectors. (3.) Board of Trade inquiries to be held in all cases of serious accidents to employes, where such accidents ocour in the movement of vehicles and not as new, to be mainly confined to accidents in which the public safety is directly involved. (4.) Railway Companies to be compelled to provide self-acting coupling appli- ances for shunters and effective protection for platelayers when working on the permanent way during the course of public traffic and wherever possible automatic fog signalling to be substituted for the present system. (5.) Certificates of competency on the lines laid down in the measure commonly known as the Enginemen's Certificate Bill to be held by all engine drivers, without which it should be illegal for any one to take charge of an engine. The Board of Trade to grant the certificates, which shall be alto- gether independent of the Companies. (6.) An Employers' Liability Act, on the lines of the Bill introduced by Mr. T. Burt, M.P., in which the un- just doctrine of common employment, shall have no place and contracting out be made illegal. The amount which may be claimed shall be unlimited as in ordinary common law, while the period of giving notice of intention to proceed under the Act shall be extended to six months. (7.) Payment of members of Parliament and of official election ex- penses by the State. In order to put all candidates on an equal footing the payment must be general and not confined to Labour members."

div.head: MR. T. C .RDWARDS MOSS. M.P.,
div.p: MR. T. C .RDWARDS MOSS. M.P.,

. . Writing from the Ennismore Gardens, S.W., replies, "The questions which you enclose front the Amalga- mated Society of Railway Servants will have my careful consideration, but as many of them deal with matters about which enquiry is now being made by the Rail- way Servants (Hours of Labour) Committee, I will ask your society to allow me to postpone sending my answers until that Committee have reported and their report has been laid before the House of Commons."
_Y. I

div.head: MR. H. WADE DEACON
div.p: MR. H. WADE DEACON

writing from Appleton House, replies as follows : (1) I think that the hours of labour on railways should be subject to regulation by the State, but as there is at this moment a committee sitting on this question, I consider it wiser to await its report before pledging my- self to details. (2) Yes. (3) Yes. (4) I am in favour of compelling railway companies to provide effective appliances, and to take all necessary precau- tions in order to prevent accidents to shunters. plate- layers, and others. (5) I have not yet considered this snbject cerefullv, nor have I seen the Bill referred to, and must for the present reserve my judgment. (8) Yes. (7) Yes.

MR. G. WHITELEY, • Conservative Candidate for Northwich Division, replies as follows :—(1.) lam in favour of a Parliamentary limitation of hours for all employes upon railways per- forming responsible work and upon the satisfactory con- duct of which work depends the public safety. I think FIX days' work of ten hours a day to be a sufficiently long week's labour for any man, but would ruder that such labour qnestions should be settled by direct negotiations between employers and employed, rather than by Parlia- mentary enactment. As one who always looked with favour upon Trades Unionism, I rejoice to think that nowadays working-men by combination can obtain assent to any rightful demand they make. (2.) Certainly, I favour it. (3.) Most certainly, 1 am. (4.) I think a Company's action which does not provide every possible apparatus for minimising danger to their employes would be almost criminal. My answer of course is directly affirmative. (5.) I am often a railway passenger, and would therefore favour this suggestion if desired by railway employes. But I am bound to say I am not acquainted with the provisions of the " Enginemen's Certificate Bill." Should you wish a more categorical answer and will kindly send me the Bill I will read it and develop my reply. (6.) I certainly look with favour unon steps in this direction. The Act should be compulsory. May I add this : In the cotton trade it is customary to insure against the claims of workpeople. A workman there- fore seeking compensation has to fight a powerful Cern- pany, which does not hesitate to contest claims up to the House of Lords. The firm with which I am connected dues not insure, as we desire to meet all fair demands directly rather than shelter ourselves under the wing of a rich insurance company. (7). This question seems to me to be a broadly public and political one, and, as such, I should prefer to deal with it upon a public plat- form when I can more freely explain my sentiments. As a man not too richly endowed with this world's pos- sessions and whose business hardly pays kim cent, per cent, nor yet 50 per cent., you may be sure the question has had, and will have, my most careful and serious at- tention.
MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P.
Following is the reply received from Mr. J. T. Brun-

ner, M.P. : " Dear Sir,—l have taken a long time to answer your letter of the 28th March. The delay, however, is not at all due to neglect on my part, but because the matter is of such vast importance that I have felt bound to give to it my utmost care and attention. My guiding motive-as a politician is this, to endeavour to make all men equal, whether rich @r. poor, as far as the law can accomplish that end, subject to each man's right to complete freedom of action and speech. This motive compels me to answer your sixth and seventh questions unhesitatingly, and with great pleasure in the affirmative. The judge-made law of common employment' I have always considered to be most mischievous and most un- fair. . .

As regards the payment of members of Parliament there is one reservation to make, with which you will no doubt agree—na tnely, that no member who is already in receipt of a Parliamentary salary from the State or the Crown should be entitled to any further payment. With respect to the remaining questions, what I have first to say is that when the aims embodied in the last two questions are attained, all the rest will, to use a Scriptural phrase, ' speedily he added unto you.' When contracting out of law is forbidden, you will no longer be dependent upon your employers' generosity for com- pensation, and you will therefore be able to meet them on a far more equal footing than now. When the com- pensation is unlimited, carelessness of men's lives and limbs will become too costly to be indulged. When working-men are represented in the House of Commons in largely increased proportion, such carelessness will become disgraceful, and year by year more nearly impos- sible. I have further to say in reference to the issues raised by your first five questions, that you have among you many men thoroughly capable of forming a sound opinion upon the questions of the number of hours a than should be on duty, what sort of coupling appliances should be used, and whether or not platelayers are efficiently protected. I am all for strengthening your hands, so that you may deal with all such questions yourselves, powerfully, with full knowledge and with wise discretion. Let Mr. Burt's bill become law, and let members of Parliament be paid by the State, and I believe that you will become strong enough fo settle wisely and effectively many difficulties which now beset you and give you trouble, without the increasing encroachments of the Board of Trade, and the constant intervention of Government inspectors. With regard to question No. 1, I dislike proposals to empower the State to compel a man to stop work against his will, but I am so sensible of the paramount import- ance of promoting the public safety, and of increasing the welfare and protecting the lives of railway workers that on January 23rd, 1891,1 recorded in the House of Commons my vote in favour of the following motion : " That in the opinion of the house, the excessive hours of labour imposed on railway servants by the existing arrangements of 'railway companies of the United King- . dom constitute a great social injustice, and are a con- stant source of danger both to the men themselves and the travelling public, and that it is expedient that the Board of Trade should obtain powers by legislation to issue orders when necessary directing railway companies to limit the hours of work of special classes of their ' servants, or to make such a reasonable increase in any class of their servants as will obviate the necessity of overtime work."

I cannot vote for the enacting of a law compelling an equal restriction of the working day for a signalman at Crewe, or Clapham Junction and for a porter at a road- side country station, but I await the report of the strong select committee which, as a result of the above motion, was appointed to inquire into the hours of work of rail- way servants. You may rely upon it that I shall study it with care and with sympathy, and that I shall be pre- pared to act in the spirit and upon the principles laid down in the above motion.

With regard to the second and third questions you are, f course, more thoroughly and closely acquainted than I with the difficulties and necessities of your position with regard to minute inspection and to inquire into accidents, and I should be very glad of an opportunity to meet you, so as to have these matters fully explained to me. I would remark that under Mr. Burt's bill, unless I am mistaken, you will have a right to demand a public in- quiry in default of adequate compensation at all times, though it would be before a court of law instead of the Board of Trade. With regard to question four, I am in favour of corn-

pelling railway companies in such matters as coupling appliances and fog signalling to adopt at all times the best available appliances. With regard to the fifth, I would make a certificate of competency for railway enginemen as much a matter of necessity as it is fer engineers onboard of ships at sea. I trust you will perceive that I have approached the subject matter of your questions in a spirit and with a seriousness befitting the consideration of issues and prin- ciples which so vitally affect personal freedom and indus- trial well-being.—Yours faithfully, J. T. BIZIINNER.

div.head: TORTURE IN CHINA.
div.p: THE TORTURE IN CHINA.

The paradoxical principle of Chinese justice which refuses to convict a prisoner until he has made a confession of guilt—even though this confession has to be extorted by torture—is curiously exemplified in the case of a trial of a man named Chen Chi-Ilui, in the neighbourhood of Hong Kong, on a charge of being a leading member ef the band or secret society known as the Kolao Hui. It is, as a local authority puts, it, "almost at the doors of the residents in the foreign settlements at Shanghai" that this man has been subjected to a series of tortures under the eyes of a polished Chinese gentleman, and by the direction of an offi- cial specially designated by the Viceroy of Nanking one of the highest dignitaries of the Empire. The strangest part of the matter is that these proceed- ings are justified on the plea of "anxiety to avoid punishing an innocent man." In the first instance, the accused appears to have been subjected to the ancient ordeal of the rack,supplemmted with kneel- ing on toils of chains and the burning of paper un- der the nostrils. These means failing, the Viceroy's deputy, Yu, ordered "some more agonising torture," the revolting details of which we forbear from in- flicting on the reader. Still no confession passed the lips of the unhappy Chen Chi-Hui. At this , point, according to the report, " the hour waxed late, and the Court adjourned," presumptively to renew these cold-blooded barbarities on the mor- row.

div.head: ---'.-7--. A HEROINE OF THE TELEGRAPH.
div.p: ---'.-7--. A HEROINE OF THE TELEGRAPH.

In the Franco-German War of 1870 the Uhlans played havoc with the French telegraph wires. On arriving at a village they would ride up to the tele- graph office, cut out the connections, and carry off the apparatus, or else employ it to deceive the enemy. They were outwitted, however, on one occasion, and by a woman. Mdlle. Juliette Dodu, a girl of 18, was director of the telegraph station at Pithiviers, where she lived with her mother when the Prussians entered the town. They took posses- sion of the station, and, turning out the two women, confined them to their dwelling on a higher floor. It happened that the wires from the office in running to the pole on the roof passed by the door of the girl's room, and she contrived the idea of tap- ping the Prussian messages. She had contrived to keep the telegraph instrument, and by means of a connection with the wire was able to carry out her purpose. Important telegrams of the enemy were thus obtained and secretly communicated to the sub-prefect of the town, who conveyed them across the Prussian lines, to the French commander. Mdlle. Dodu and her mother were both arrested,and proofs of their guilt were soon discovered. They were brought before a court-martial and speedily condemned to death, but the sentence had to be confirmed by the commander of the corps d'armee, Prince Frederick Charles, who, having spoken with Mdlle. Dodu on several occasions, desired her to be produced. Ile inquired her motive in committing so grave a breach of what is called the "laws of war." The girl replied, "Je suis Francaise " (I am a Frenchwoman). The prince confirmed the sen- tence, but, happily, before it was executed, the news of the armistice arrived and saved her life. In 1878 this telegraphic heroine was in charge of the post- office at Montreuil, near Vincennes, and on the 13th of August she was decorated with the Legion of Honour by Marshal MacMahon, President of the Republic.

div.head: HIS NARROW ESCAPE.
div.p: HIS NARROW ESCAPE.

In 1852 the United States began a war with the Navajo Indians of New Mexico, a tribe as cunning and as treacherous as the Apaches. The war lasted several years, and the soldiers were subjected to many hardships and dangers. One of them,Ephraim B. Cobleigh,relates in the "History of Boxborough," his native town, an adventure that recalls Job's words : I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. He says : A detachment of twenty-five soldiers were sent out to find grazing grounds, and Sergeant Major Cobleigh went with them. The Navajos about Fort Defiance were supposed to be " friendlies." After a day's march the detachment went into camp for the night. The next morning, three soldiers, Cabliegh. Myers, and Ryan, rode a mile away from the camp, and came suddenly upon a small band of Indians, who made signs of friendliness. On learn- ing that the troopers were searching for grazing grounds, the Indians said," Good water, good grass I a little way round the mountain—we show you the way." The troopers followed the lead of the Nava- jos, a few of whom fell behind before entering a trail worn in the rocks, with a steep ledge on one side and a precipice on the other side. Cobleigh became suspicious, but as it was now impossible to retreat, he kept his thoughts to himself. Suddenly they entered a beautiful valley, hemmed in by great sandstone walls, and saw before them a camp with hundreds of Indians, men, women, and I children. " We're in for it, boys !" exclaimed Cobleigh, as their escort invited them to dismount. Their horses were turned loose, and their rifles taken away. Three stakes were driven into the ground before the troopers' eyes, who then knew that they were to be roasted. The Indians took off their clothes, and bound them to the stakes with bits of cedar bark. Ryan had red hair, and his scalp was therefore coveted by every warrior. Theygave him most of their attention, dancing and yelling around him, while he howled at them all sorts of Irish epithets. Cobleigh, finding that the Indians took little notice of him, wriggled his hands from the cedar strips and unfastened his limbs. His horse, frightened at the noise, had come near its master. With a bound, Cobleigh, naked as he was, vaulted on its back, and in an instant was speeding over the narrow defile by which he had entered the valley. Fortunately the horse was used to moun- tain travel, and without one false step carried him at full speed to the camp of his comrades. But twenty-three men were too small a band to rescue Ryan and Myers—they were never seen again.

div.head: FATALITY TO A ST. HELENS FOOTBALLER.
div.p: THE FATALITY TO A ST. HELENS FOOTBALLER.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher F01k.," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," &e., tke.
CHAPTER XXXIV. THE WRECK OF THE BONNY BESS.

Clinging to Bell's strong arm, and bending to the blast, Lady Callerley made very good headway; and the two girls were not long in arriving at Frenchman's Bay. The village, as they passed through it, was almost deserted; indeed, it seemed as though every man, woman, and child in the place had flocked to the shore. _ _

Under the influence of a great dread, prudence was comletely laid aside. It was not so much matter now whether the coastguard got scent of the contemplated landing or no, since the danger had waxed greater on the sea than on the shore. Behind a grassy dyke crouched old Carr and a few other ancients of the village. Two of them had rested their long telescopes upon the top, and were anxiously peering over the dark sea, growling out their comments, now and again. Leaning well within sound of their combined wisdom was Jack Breamish, who was on terms of good fellowship with most of the fisher-folk. They never thought of mistrusting Jack, good-for-nothing Jack, who, according to them, was nobody's enemy but his own. He was as much interested in the Sate of the Bonny Bess as though he possessed a share of her. Indeed, it was part of his ill-doings, in his sister- in-law's eyes; that he was all too fond of the com- pany of the smuggling fraternity. Once or twice, when he was quite a lad, he had sneaked off from Breainish Hall, and persuaded them to give him a trip to the continent; making himself both pleasant and useful when aboard, and enjoying the fun of it immensely. Therefore old Carr held him as of no account, and talked quite freely before him. "Them beggars 'll be close on his heels, poor chap, an' he'll ha' te take his chance o' givin' them the slip by runnin' in to land." "Ay, ay, it's Hobson's choice aw'se feared." Jack, who had been listening half absently, started, as two figures fought their way past the little haven of refuge that the old salts had formed unto themselves.

That was Bell Widdrington of a surety, that tall strong figure sheltering the smaller one. But— who was the other? Something familiar yet un- definable in the Walk and figure struck him with wonder. But no! of course it could not be. Bell had pinned up the long skirt of Lady Callerley's riding habit, and wrapped up her head in a shawl after the fisher fashion ; and so the little lady simply looked like a very small edition of Bell. After a moment's consideration, Jack, decided that it must be Ailsie who was Bell's companion. _

Nevertheless, the very suggestion of ii', likeness was sufficient to attract him to follow in the wake of the twb figures ; which he did in a leisurely way—or as much of a leisurely way as was com- patible with an easterly gale. Bell guided and assisted Lady Callerley down a steep narrow path used by the fisher people. The sharp showers of sleet winch kept falling at intervals rendered it extremely slippery, and only by the exercise of great caution was it possible to descend without falling. But the fisher girl was as sure- footed ,as a goat, and so -well used to the path be- sides, that she could have gone down in the dark with perfect safety. To her practical eyes, too, the semi-obscurity of the autumn twilight was quite available for all pradical purposes. When they reached the shore, she steered for a place she knew of, where a big fall of stone from the cliffs formed a sort of slater from the blast sweeping in from seaward—for below as above the cliffs the gale was entirely merciless. Here she anchored her companion,whose strength, by this time, was completely exhausted ; and whom 1 the sight of this pit less shore, with its great jagged rocks and stones ai d boulders, filled with nervous horror. Her vivid it iagination conjured up a picture of her brother tossed by those mighty waves to her feet; perhaps against those cruel sharp-edged rocks, his fair hair beclabbled with blood. Oh God ! She covered her face with her hands, as though to shut out the frightful spectacle. At this moment Jack Breamish came tip; and seeing her in such distress, and still fancying her to be Ailsie, paused, like a soft-hearted fellow as he was, and began to try and encourage her to hope for the best; saying, very truly, what a thoroughly capable seaman her husband Bill was, and that in all probability while they were watch- ing for and anxious about him here, he was snugly sheltered in some quiet harbour further down the coast to southward. Bell had left her cornpanion ere this, and was talking anxiously to a group of people seine little ; distance away. ' "Come, Ailsie, take heart, my dear ! All is not ' lost because we cannot see the land! Depend upon it your goodman is all right." He clapped the sitting figure upon the shoulder encouragingly; when to his surprise his hand was clasped with a despairing clasp, and a pair of blue eyes looked up to him pitifully. "But it is Teddy who is in danger, Cousin Jack. It is Teddy (sob) whom the horrid sea will—(sob)— swallow, and then there will be no one—no—one— left—in the—whole world that—loves me !" . .
At the sound of the poor little voice and the touch of the clinging hand, Jack's heart gave a sudden bound. _ _ _

Amid the noise of the whirling wind and the roaring wave, a voice spoke within him, that stunned and horrified him more than all the danger and hubbub around. A storm raged in his veins and in his miid, before which the material storm of wind and wave lost force and paled. Strange time, indeed, for nature to choose where- in to reveal him to himself ! Yet so it was. He knew now what he had not known before. He loved Silvia Callerley, the wife of another man: And one other thing he knew—that she was un- happy, and left alone in her misery. The one who should have protected and com- forted, left her to bear suspense and terror, with no supporting hand to sustain, no soothing voice to whisper hope. She had a husband, and yet.she declared that the death of her brother would leave her with no one in the whole world to love her. And her hand was clinging to Jack's own, and her pitiful eyes pleaded to his for hope. Poor Jack Breamish ! He was a good, pure- minded man, but nevertheless he was very young, and he had never been in love before. Wisdom is not gained with experience, and twenty-two is certainly not the age for much prudence. A mighty impulse, and a mighty temptation seized hold on him in that critical hour. Oh, what bliss to take those little hands in his, and to whisper that there was one to whom she was dearer than all upon earth, dearer than heaven, perhaps dearer than—ah, not dearer than honour, surely? It was but for a moment that the mad fit held him. He let go her hand, turned away, and ground his heel down, down, into the crunching gravel. Ah, yes! Thank God, he could and would con-: quer self. A few minutes after he turned to Lady Callerley with his old frank smile. "Why, cousin? Cousin Salvia, who would have expected you to be out on such a night as this? It is only stormy petrels such as Bell and I who are used to, and feel quite safe in a gale; but soft - feathered little doves like you ought to be snugly sheltered within their nests !" "How oould I rest without knowing of my brother's safety?' asked Silvia, and Jack felt too sad at heart to keep up his bantering tone. Bell returned with the news that the sloop was now in sight, and the fishermen doubted that she was not in very good trim to weather the storm. They could not imagine 'why she had not kept further away from the land, unless something was desperately amiss, or unless Bill had got scent of the revenue cutter; and so, trying to elude it, had fallen out of the frying pan into the fire. He was evidently quite aware of the danger they were in, and trying now to draw off from the land ; but it would be a tough fight to keep clear of it in the teeth of such a gale. Jack, in his turn, departed to the other end of the bay to reconnoitre. Before he left he whispered to Bell that lie hoped she would look after Lady fjallerley, and see that no harm came to her. • The fisher girl looked at him with a scrutinising She read most plainly the marks of a struggle on his countenance. He was agitated, excited, unnerved. - - _

"Leave her to me," said Bell, with significant emphasis, "it will be a deal better if ye leave her to me. An' see, ponder's Sir Lancelot himsen Hell be the teet 'on to take care Of his wife, aw would say." Jack flushed crimson under Bell's penetrating look. He understood the purport of what she said, exactly as she meant him to do,
"..All rligj and tuank you rhe winspereti, and was a - ,Ov,er the rooks, struggling round to the POW:-

Frenchinanc Day was a place that seemed peculiarly adapted by nature fOr the purposes of free-trading. The sandstone cliffs, higher here than at any other pact of the coast, completely shut out from view a vessel, provided it lay close enough within their shelter. At high tide, the Donny Buss could ride there at anchor, and get rida her cargo in the swiftest and most secret manner; unless any of the coast A J.id's men were on the heights im- mediately above. Then these same cliffs were pierced with a perfect network and labyrinth of eaves and crevices, where kegs and barrels and bales could be stowed away in an incredibly short space of time; and the entrances of these hiding places were exceeding difficult to discover, and were in fact known only to the gang who used them.

FDOM the southerly horn of the bay stretched an ugly jagged ridge of rocks only visible at low water. They bore the significant title of "Death's Ribs." The colour of them varied slightly from the dark sombre tints of the rest of the reels, and upon them little or no seaweed grew; wherefore they showed out greyish white, and not altogether unlike to the skeleton ribs of some gigantic monster. When the wind was from the south, they pro- tected the bay, and reudered the 'ater within their boundaries smooth and pleasant; but when a ner'• easter was blowing, they added instead greatly to the danger of entering the bay. The sea was not yet .completely over them; but the heavy waves dashed into clouds of spray; and hid them from sight, where they lay hall-submer- ged; waiting to give a cruel welcome to any vessel unfortunate enough to be swept upon their sharp and jagged edges. Many a gallant ship had ground herself to powder against those terrible ribs. The little sloop was making a brave fight to save herself froth such a fate.

Skipper Bill knew only too well the sort of greeting lying in store for him. In breathless silence those on shore watched the battle between man and nature; between human skill, courage, and good seamanship; and the in- cessant cannonades kept up by the wrathful elements. The odds were, however, all against the Bonny Bess. Her mainsail had vanished long before, and she was driving in shore with the wind; spite of all her efforts to keep away. She had come within the swirl of the white water, and was plunging and tearing along like a thing possessed; throwing, as she went, the foam high up in the air. A thrill of suspense ran through the watchers when she came to this sea of foam, followed by a deep guttural sound, half sigh, half moan. Old Carr clenched his fists tightly together, and thrust them deep into his breeches pockets. "It's all up," said the man who stood next to him in an excited tone, "they're drivin' reet on te Deeth's ribs."

" Whisht thee! hand thy saw! bide still," re- sponded the old fisherman savagely. The man proved to be right, however. The fated sloop was now tossing helplessly about amongst the breakers; plunging, rearing, tearing, tossing; careering madly, refusing to answer her helm, and at the mercy of the ponderous waves which were throwing her about in such a reckless fashion.

It was now only a question of time. And when a mountain of water reared itself up behind, those on shore were quite prepared for the result that followed. It lifted the little vessel on high, and flung her with terrific force back upon the reef. There was a dreadful crash, and then a grinding, tearing, sound,. as though life were being rent out of her.
Then the waves broke over their work, and throw up triumphantly clouds of white spray, dancing exultant over a dead foe. • _

"There's the last o' ma hunnerd pounds !" said the man who, had spoken before, with rueful em- phasis. OW Carr made no answer. All he possessed in the world, the savings of a hard and penurious life- time, were invested in the Bonny Bess. But dear as money was to him that was not what he thought of, when a lump rose in his throat, and, his keen eyes grew dim.. "Ma poor bit lass—ma canny Ailsie ! Aw'd let the rest gan an' welcome, if aw was sure o' doin' what aw promised ye and bein' able te fetch yer man safe back t,e ye." • This was the substance of Old Carr's meditations. He remembered that Bill had said they were all cursed and for what reason; and wished, for the sake of his dearly-loved child, his own hands had been clean.
CIYAPTER XXXV. A STRONG SWIMMER.

The Bonny Bess had foUght a gallant fight, but alas, there was no manner of doubt that she was thoroughly beaten; and that it was now only a- question of time before those heavy breakers would pound their way through her sides and tear her apart, plank from plank; until, of the trim little sloop nothing would remain but a few floating spars to mark the spot where her death struggle had taken place. But the burning !question among that excited group of men gathered together at the point opposite to the reef where the unfortunate vessel lay, was not how to save the sloop—for that was clearly not within the bounds of possibility—but how to rescue instead those near and dear to them, who were yet on board: those poor fellow creatures who could be seen even through the driving scud ' and the gathering darkness, and whose despairing cries for help were plainly audible, borne inshore upon the wings of the wind. The reef of "Death's Ribs" was divided from the shore by a channel, which, in an ordinary way, it would not have been a difficult task to cross. Indeed, in fine weather,' g good swimmer tt-buld ' have laughed and made light of such a feat as 'that of reaching this exceedingly accessible ridge. But not so at a time like this, and with..such ae"heavy sea on. The tvgter there was heaving and throbbing as though it were boiling in some gigantic Cauldron. It hissed, and roared, and threw aloft great sheets of foam, where the cross* seas met and grappled together in savage conflict. In more recent times nothing would have been easier than to fire a shot and throw a line with the rocket, clean over a ship lying in such a positiosi; but there were no life-saving appliances in those days, no life-boats, no brigade, no rocket apparatus, no anything. What was done then in the way of saving lives from wrecks was done by individual heroism, and at a tremendous risk. But for the most part folks had to stand by and see the poor souls drown; and cultivate as much callousness of heart as possible to save themselves from suffering along with those who could not be helped. High civilisation means highly strung nerves, ana an education into larger capacities for pain. For- tunately these things are only of recent develop- meat; and when violent deaths were more com- mon, they were taken as matters of course; and not agonised over and dwelt on, as we have grown to agonise and dwell upon them in these days of daily newspapers and morbid sensibilities. Ima- gination, unquickened by detail, fails to grasp half the cruelty of destiny. But in a case like this wreck of the Bonny Bess, where every onlooker had some one on board there, related to him or her by the close tie of kinship, no such pleasant indifference was possible. By blood or by marriage all the inhabitants of the village of Breamish were closely united; and one house could not mourn or rejoice, without the neighbouring one participating to some degree in the sorrow or joy.

Therefore the excitement at the point was inten- sified exceedingly by the fact that it was not any mere " furriners," who were in trouble and deadly peril upon "Death's Ribs ;" but "war men," hus- bands, and fathers and brothers, and sons; valuable lives every one of them. All the women-folk had not been so easily assnred as the wife of Bill Widdrington. She was so used to being thought for and taken care of, that she fancied it was sure to be all right when her father told her to "bide at homs and not take on, an' he'd fetch her man back to her, safe and sound eneuf !" There were women in that agonised group of onlookers; and with their continuous urging and pleading, the men were driven well nigh distracted. "Ma two canny lad! Mun aw stand here and see them drooned 1" cried one aged woman ; running hither and thither in blind and. aimless misery, and entreating first one and then another of the men to save her sons, "Oh, canna ye think of owt to do for them? Whatfore was na'aw myed a man, that aw might ha' swam oot yonder to them f‘' " VVho could breist yon wetter 1' said old Carr, sternly, pointing to the seething and roaring cur- rent, "it wad be suicide to try it—forbye we're none of us the best o' swimmers." It was too true that few of the fishermen, living as they did more than half their lives upon the water, were adepts at this useful art. Where was the use of learning to swim, they asked at times scornfully? If the weather was bad enough to -wreck thekboats, It was_ IL.,IN_ to be_ too rough for

them to swim for any length of time, let alofie the fact that their heavy boots were sufficient to draw them down. They have gained more common sense since then ; and when regattas are got up now in fishing villages, swimming races form an important part of the pro- _

granune.- " An' mun we stand here an' see them drooned ?" The wretched mother's plaint was unheeded. A thrill of excitement. ran through the group; and all eyes were glued to the wreck. Was it possible that some one was leaving it? It was becoming too dark to distinguish clearly at that distance, but their vision was keen and clear sighted. Yes. A figure was being lowered over the side, a very difficult proceeding, considering the angle at which the sloop was lying, and also the fact that the waves kept lifting and pounding her incessantly upon the rocks. However, they made out that the figure crawled over the slippery rocks on hands and knees, and then paused a moment before precipitating himself into the charmeL Some of the fishermen declared that they could see it tighten the knot of the rope bound round its waist. The watchers held their breaths, as the figure plunged boldly in, and began to battle with the opposing current. They did not yet recognise who he was, but only that he was evidently young and strong, and an experienced swimmer; for he dived tinder when a volume of water rushed over the place where he was, and managed to dodge & very nasty cross sea in an exceedingly skilful xnanner. "By God, he'll do the trick I" said old Carr, under his breath; then when the aged woman. before mentioned asked again if they could not help him on anyway, he turned to her quickly and answered, "Ay, ye can help him, mebbe ? /e eau pray for him! Ye're a good religious woman, an' there's ne reason why your prayers should na' be heered up aloft 1" It was a splendid sight to see that strong swifs- mer overcoming all obstacles, and nearing the shore. A dozen hands were ready to 'etch hold of him.. The men took each other round the waists and formed a line, to run in and draw him forth, when —a sudden pause, and a sob of suspense- What is that following close upon his heels, ilk ; the waves behind? Quick, quick, or the foe will gain upon you, S'al- lent swimmer, exhausted you are with that long and breathless struggle! Alas poor fellow. fle thinks it is all right now, and relaxes speed, breath.- less and pantino.b. There is a warning shout frora the group op shore. , Too late, too late! The wave overtakes him, sweeps him up, broths over him, and the heavy spar it is carrying slang with it, comes in crashing contact with his Por naked, unprotected, body. The men hear the' sound of a heavy thud, and it sickens them ; they know right well what it means. They set their teeth nevertheless, and themselves for a rush when the wave coulee- Living or dead, they must and will have him now So in another second they meet the mountain ° and water, tear him out of its cruel grasp drag him away from the suck of its back War sok They have drawn the swimmer to shore, kW"' all eyes are bent down to recognise the hero. bride: It is skipper Bill—poor Ailsie's bonnY groom. -He is white and senseless—dead for all that thez can tell at the moment. Worse than this, hi° de has been dared in vain. hody has The rope so carefully fastened about his 4..,‘ in been cut somehow, or given out under the s— and only the jagged end remains to tell iii has been. The rugged face of Bill's father-in-law twitched convulsively as he looked down upon the deadlY work of the storm. "He was the youngest an' therefore the least to blame! It was me that should ha' gone y the penalty for yo , if body had to pa bad deed- n Whatten kind of-fair deulin' is this, avt'd ?" Nobody heeded the words he-nttered with RUC savage energy. His bitter outcry against the ill; sorne- justice of fate passed, most likely, for a lanieutati° over poor Bill's misfortune.

div.head: INQUEST AND rUNERAL.
div.p: INQUEST AND rUNERAL.

On Tuesday Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, Peasley-cross, St. Helens, on the body of James Rennie, aged twenty- one years, of Sutton, whose back was broken by a fall of stone in the Lea Green Colliery, and who died in the Cottage Hospital on Thursday night. Mr. Henry Hall, Government inspector of mines, was present-e-From the evidence, it appeared that deceased was a waggoner, and a quantity of dirt 'having fallen from the roof ho was assisting to clear it away. While packing it, a stone fell from the roof, which seemed secure in that place, and knocked a lamp down. Rennie stooped to pick it up, and while in that position another stone, live feet long and two feet wide, fell and crushed his back against the pack. When the stone was got off him, he was found to ie terribly injured. Mr. Hall said he had examined the place since the accident, and could not see that there had been any omission nu the part of the men. ft would, however, have been better if the foreman had gone in after the first fall, because it was just possible an official might have seen the danger the men could not see.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," end added a presentment in accord- ance with the views expressed by Mr. Hall. Arrangements had been made for the funeral on Tues- day afternoon, and while the inquest was proceeding the mourners were assembling at the house of the de- ceased's father, in Chester-lane. The coffin—which bore the inscription, " James Rennie, died April 14,1892, aged 21 years. Sown in weakness, raised in power. Thy will be done."—was covered with beautiful floral tribu- tes, and was carried by fellow-scholars to the United Methodist Chapel at Marshall's-cross, where a service was conducted by Mr. James Thomson, of Liverpool. In the course of a short address, Mr. Thomson said the eyes of the multitude turned towards that open grave, for not only was deceased looked upon as a good player by the football world, but in his own neighbourhood, and by all who knew him, he was looked upon as a good scholar and a thorough Christian.—The coffin was then placed upon a bier,and carried to the Sutton Churchyard by members of the St. Helens Football Club, with which he was prominently connected. A large number of members of the club were present. One beautiful wreath was from the Committee, and another from the players of the club. The Ravenhead Brass Band which usually attends the home matches, headed the proces- sion, and played" The Dead March "in "Saul." There was a large concourse of spectators in the churchyard, and the sacred edifice, in which a short service was held, • was crowded. The Rev. A. F. Danglish (curate) read , the burial service, and committed the body to the grave. The Ravenhead band then performed a funeral selection, and all that was mortal of "poor young Rennie " was • left to its long sleep.

"RADICALS AND PA;ISTS."-•A BCGOTED PROTEST.

A parishioner present, named Peacocke, called atten- tion to the fact that those schools were used en .the previous Thursday evening for political purposes—(oh oh, and cries of "No politics.") He should like to know by whose authority the use of the schools was granted to Radicals and Papists (" Oh ch," and "Shame.") Ho had a strong objection to their coming in those schools, and it was the first time that Radicals or Papists had had the pleasure of being in them. If he had known as much as he did two days afterwards they (the "Radicals and Papists ") instead of having had a concert should have had a "round robin."—The Rector, who was received with loud applause, said they were always prepared to let the schoolroom to any respectable body. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It was not with them a question of politics at all. (Hear, hear.) The school was paid for and they needed money, and he saw no reason why the school should not have been allowed. (Loud ap- plause.)

div.head: CHURCH FINANCES.
div.p: THE CHURCH FINANCES.

In responding to a vote of thanks, the Rector said there had been an increase of about £2O in the amount of the offertory during the past year over the previous year, but he urged that they should try to raise £7OO by this means. People might think the Rector of Warrington was a very rich man but he could assure them that the amount of the tithe had fallen, and owing to the new Act and change of collector he had received very little indeed, and it had been very hard work for him to do what he had done.
ST. BARNABAS'S.-A FRAC TIMIS MEETING.-COM- PLAINTS AGAINST THE CHURCH OFFICERS.
The annual Easter vestry meeting in connection with St. Barnabas's Church was held on Tuesday morning, the Rev. G. Allton presiding.
PRECAUTIONS AGAINST BOGUS VOTERS.

The Chairman on entering the vestry, the Clerk (Mr. Jenkins) not having arrived, said he had instructions to take the names of those present, for the purpose of for- wardingthem to the chancellor of the diocese with a view to ascertaining who had a right to attend the vestry and vote. Be accordingly took down the names, this being a lengthy procedure, as the room was full, and as he was thus engaged the vestry clerk made his appearance. The Chairman having completed the taking down of the names, said he wished to say a few words before the or- dinary business of the meeting was commenced. He had waited and waited during the past year or two, but this year he had been obliged to place their affairs before the Chancellor of the diocese. Of course this was not an an- cient parish, like the parish of St. Elphin's, St. Paul's, or even like Holy Trinity, which was a chapel of ease. It was a parish only for ecclesiastical pu,poses, and the persons supposed to attend the vestry and vote were those who were members of the Church of England, and supporters of the Church. He did not wish to cause any offence, as those present resided in the parish, but he felt sure that if they knew the right state of things they would do right. He gave them credit for that. They were respectable men, who understood what things should be. Of course, people would not like him to go to Mr. Crosfield's mission room and interfere with affairs there. Still, this was a parish church, and he was the vicar of it, and he always wished to be broad and open with them all, and if they wished to consult him about these matters, he would be most anxious and willing to give advice, because no clergyman had more thoroughly studied the law on Church subjects than he had. He had received a letter from the Chancellor, who had recommended him to get the book of law bearing upon these subjects, and he had done so. Ratepaying was not sufficient to entitle a man to attend or vote at a vestry meeting. That appeared to be quite clear. Lord Coleridge gave judgment on the question in 1889. The letter from the Chancellor of the diocese contained the following :—" It appears from the Diocesan Calen- dar that yours is a new parish now. Consequently, the election of churchwardens must ke, conducted inconfor- mity with the regulations of 8 and 9 Vic., c 70. None but resident householders of the new parish can vote, or even, I think, attend the vestry, and the churchwardens must also be bona-fide residents in the parish. This latter point was emphatically affirmed by a recent decision in the Court of Queen's Bench." There had, the Vicar went on to say, been unpleasantness in the parish since the schoolmaster dispute some years ago. Before that time he was obliged to ask people Co come into the vestry to enable them to transact their business ; it was only since the schoolmaster question had arisen that this ill-feeling had sprung up in the parish. Not one of them had attended the church during the past year, and, there- fore, they had no more right to be present and take part in the proceedings than he had to go and overhaul accounts at Mr. Crosfield'a mission or Mr. Yonge's chapel. But he should put that aside, and leave the matter to their good sense as working-men. They all knew what these things were. Mr, Jenkins knew the law, and it was not necessary for him (the vicar) to enter further into the matter. They would see for themselves the position they had placed themselves in by coming there.

div.head: GENERAL BUSINESS.
div.p: GENERAL BUSINESS.

The Vestry Clerk then read the minutes of the last meeting, and they were adopted.—He then read the notice convening the meeting.—The Chairman nominated Mr. Arthur Byram as vicar's warden for the ensuing year.—Mr, John Thornton proposed that Mr. R. T. Smith be re-appointed people's warden.—Mr. H. Jackson seconded.—Mr. Woolacott proposed an amendment that ' Mr'. William Irairclough be appointed. He said he objected for himself and on behalf of the congregation to Mr. Smith as a warden, as he had utterly neglected his duties and never attended the church, and he thought It was very wrong indeed for a man who took a Position of the kind, never to come near the church or take part in any work connected with it or do en ything to help it in any way.—Mr. Battersby i I should like an explanation from Mr. Smith why -he has not 'attended.—Mr. John Looker seconded the amendment.—Mr. Smith denied the statements of Mr. • Woolacott, and asserted that he had paid pounds where Mr. Woolacott had paid, pence, for the welfare of the church. (Loud cries of " hear, hear.")—Mr. Woola- cott: I am speaking of the last six months.—Mr. Smith : Never mind; you are speaking of my term of office ; illness has prevented me coming for a long time. I fie thought as a churchwarden he had done ,as much as anyone in the parish for the churJ:. Mr. Smith was proceeding to speak of a sum of £lB ss. 6d. collected I last year, when the vestry clerk called him to order, as departing from the subject before the meeting, i the election of a warden.—Mr. Smith : lam just simply vindicating myself by figures against the charge that I have done nothing for the church.—The Chairman said he had kept a record of the attendances of the officers at church, and pointed to the fact he had had continu- ously to make such entries as " No churchwarden," " one churchwarden," " one sideman,"" no sides:flan" and so Leith as showing how the duties had been per- formed.—Mr. W. Fairclough said he had no objection to being proposed, but he had no desire to interfere. He haft I come from a parish where everything was worked very comfortably and smoothly,and he did not want tobe mixed an with any bother, and wanted things to work as com- fortably as where he came from. If there had been any- thing unpleasant let it die away. The church had plenty of room in it, and he thought there were plenty who would do good and be doing themselves good by attend- ing there or somewhere else.—Mr. Unsworth said it was not for Mr. Fairclough to throw slurs upon anyone who was perhaps as good a churchman as him or those lin office.—Mr. Fairclough remarked : "Then let them show it," but disclaimed all desire to cast slurs on anyone.—Another person present observed that he did not think Mr. Fairclough meant to do that.—Mr. Woola cott said with regard to Mr. Smith's statement that he- had raised pounds where he (Mr. Woolacott) bad raised pence, he had raised pounds where Mr. Smith had raised pence.—Mr. Smith: Given pence where you gave shillings—pounds.—Mr. Woolacott: Well, the Vicar knows.—The Vestry Clerk: It is not a matter of how much money has been raised, but how the warden has attended—The Chairman said with all due respect to Mr. Smith and also Mr. Throssel, he could not say they had attended tc their duties pro- perly. Whoever were elected in ' future must do their duty. He should be only too delighted to see those present taking part in all the church entertainments. It was the church of that parish and ought to be supported. He had taken their names down as householders, and in 'future he should call upon them for help since they came there to vote.—The amendment and the original motion for Mr.' Smith's appointment, were out to the , meeting, when the amendment was voted for by three only, the original motiop being carried by an overwhelming majority.—Mr. Arthur Byram nominated Mr. John Looker as his sideman for the year.—Mr. Smith proposed Mr. William Throssel as his for the coming year.—Mr. Williamson See,onded.—Mr. Throssel said as his name had been mentioned in connection with Mr. Smith's as re- garded attendance at church, he should like to explain. He said he was directed also to say that the church in future was never to be without officers at the Sunday morning and evening services and the Wednesday evening services. Therefore a present- ment would have to be made if the church was neg- lected ; and it was thought that more than two sides- men should be elected so that there would always be officers on duty. ELOPEMENT FROM ROCHDALE TO
WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Magistrates' Court, yesterday, John Shaw, aged 38, a travelling optician, wko is a native of Salford, was placed n theadock,and the Chief Constable stated that Ile had been living in Dallam-lane, and was wanted by the police at Rochdale for eloping with another man's wife and stealing property value £.lO. 'lnspector Cox obtained certain information concerning I him, and had telegraphed to the Rochdale police autho- ities, and had a reply that morning that an officer would be sent for the prisoner. He was ordered to be detained and handed over to the constable on his arrival. —We are informed that the woman with whom the prisoner eloped is aged 22 years and is the wife of a Mr. Brooks, of Union-street, Rochdale. Shaw had lodged with them, and eloped with her from Rochdale in the beginning of January. They had been in several places since leaving there, and had only been in Warrington for a fortnight lodging in Dallarn-lane. On Wednesday they went to Manchester, and Shaw returned alone. Meanwhile the Rochdale police and the woman's friends were prosecuting inquiries, and ty the last post on Thursday Mrs. Brooks's mother, who lives in Crewe, heard that the runaways were living together in Dallam- lane, Warrington. and took the first train to this town, but found that they had parted company the night pre- vious. Shaw is stated to be well connected in Salford. ,
MARRIAGE OF MR. J. G. PARKINSON.

lOn Monday, at St. Philip's Church, Dalston, London, by the Rev. F. Cos, vicar of the parish, ;the marriage was solemnized of Mr:John G. Parkinson, youngest son of Mr. George Parkinson, West Brook,Kingsley,Cheshire, to Miss Jeannie Moore, second daughter of Mr. John Moore, Shrubland-road, Dalston. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a charming costume of cream, richly embroidered, and trimmed with orange blossoms. She wore a gold chain, and carried a lovely bouquet, the gifts of the bridegroom. 1 The bridesmaids were—Miss Parkinson (sister of the bridegroom), her costume being of pale green, and hat trimmed with brown and green velvet; Miss A. Watt and Miss C. Minns, who were attired in pink silk, and cream hats with ostrich feathers. They carried baskets of flowers, and wore gold bangles, the gifts of the bride- groom. The church was tastefully decorated, and the 1 service fully choral. The best man was Mr. C. D. Par- ' kinson. The dejeunet was served at Shrubland-road after the ceremony. Later in the afternoon the happy pair left for Dover, en route for Paris and Switzerland. The presents were numerous and valuable.

PADGATE. The vestry meeting in connection with Padgate Church was held on Monday morning. The Rev. J. J. Langham (vicar) presided, and there ws.s a good attend- ance. Mr. W. Royston, vicar's warden, submitted the accounts which showed that there was a balance in hand of over £5. There were, however, still some bills to come in. The Chairman submitted his communicant's alms accounts which showed that there had been a total receipt of £2l 17s. 2d., a balance of £6 11s. Id. being left in hand. The Chairman re-appointed Mr. Royston as Vicar's warden, and Mr. J. W. Fowles was re- appointed people's warden. The following were ap- pointed sidesmen :—Messrs. NV. Houghton, G. Mather, Beavers, and Hodgkinson. Mr. Royston and Mr. W. Houghton were appointed lay representatives. After the close of the ordinary business, Mr. W. Houghton referred to the question of freeing the seats of the church to which he had alluded at former vestries. He was of opinion that in all parish churches the sittings should be free and unappropriated. The Chairmarf said he did not wish to press his views, but he thought the seats should be free, but that was a question that would have to be dealt with at a special meeting, if dealt with at all. Be always felt the need of free seats most on a Sunday evening when the congrega- tion was crowded at the' back, and, he knew, they could not hear.—One of the parishioners present remarked any person would be welcome to go to his seat.—Mr. W. Houghton said people did not care to go into other folks' pews, and Mr. G. Mather mentioned an instance in which a person had been ordered out of a pew at a church at Lowtom—Mr. Fournier remarked that he had had a similar disagreeable experience.—Mr.Royston said one, difficulty in the, way of abolishing pew rents was that the rents were part of the living, and a portion of them went towards the repair of the church. If the seats were made free, the congregation would have to raise the needful money.—The subject then dropped,and the meeting soon afterwards terminated.

div.head: "THAT SLAWTTIN' lIUZZAR !"
div.p: "THAT SLAWTTIN' lIUZZAR !"
A TRUE TALE.
TII-VE—" Wilkins and his Dinah." In the parish o' Lone Yed ther once lived a lad, Wo,.at fourteen yer owd, wur ez big ez his dad; . .

An' his feyther Wild like to ha' see ti him a Tar, But he listed, an' made a greyt SlawCrin' Huzzar ! Ez soon ez he'd jined um, thay order'd that lad To be drilled neet and day in the awkardest squad; But were this to his sojerly sperrits a bar? Eh, nowe! fer he made a fine Slawt'rin' Huzzar !

He wur perfectly matchless i' flight er retreat, Fer wen runnin' away he war soon eawt o' sect; An' he loved, heaw he loved, to smell claimer afar, So it kept miles away fro' this Slawt'rin' Huzzar ! On Review Days he allus war used ez a skeawt,
, To watch thoose Recroots ez kept " gooin' ereawt An' wen the creawds rusht tow'rd the Troopers to far, Noan cud fricken um back like that Slawt'rin

lluzzar ! Once to battle he went, on his owd skyowbald nag, To go in fer glory, er collar some swag; An' to do sitch brave deeds in the coorse o' that war, Ez noan cud cum up to but th' Slawt'rin' Huzzar 1 By Gyow ! he felt quare, when the bullets just , .

miss'd him! It war like " Benbow's Miacher " at wark in his system: lint the truth mun be towd, an' he did get a scar. Just at th' eend o' his spine, fro' another Huzzar ! " 0, mother ! dear mother!" he roar'd i' distress, " Make haste to yore Rootler, his woonds wash an'
, dress; An' no moor shall them sodyeds my eend-quarters

mar, Per aw'll live but i name ez the Slawt'rin' Iluzzar ! Th' Ow i Duke shed a tear when he heerd ez he'd gone, An' the wole o' his regiment wept, to a mon; Wile Boneypart grinn'd, ez he mutter'd "By Gar, I vos glad I should miss him—that Slawt'rin:
When he deed, o'er his grave they made haste to
erect .. _ A meauntain o' pavin' stones eawt o' respect ; An' o'er it, thay rote on a greyt wooden spar— IN MEMORIAM ! " ROOMER," VIE SLAWVRIN' Huzzma ! "

div.p: TUM 0' PEGS. Nyowton God bless o', 23rd April, 1892.
DEA.Tti OF THE REV. DR. ALLON.

The Rev. Henry Alfon, D.D., of the Union Chapel, Is- lington, died on Saturday morning at his residence, St. Mary's-road, Canenbury. Dr. Allan had not been in good health for some time past, but his death was alto- gether unexpected, and he occupied the pulpit only a week ago. He was born on the 13th of October, 1818,at Welton, near Hull, Yorkshire, and educated for the ministry at Cheshunt College, Hertfordshire. In January, 1844, he was appointed minister at Union Chapel, Islington, officiating at first as co-pastor with the Rev. Thomas Lewis, on whose death, in 1852, he be- came sole pastor. He was chairman of the Congrega- tional Union in 1864-65. Although for the space of 46 years he had been actively engaged in the pastoral and public duties of his ministry,he found time to contribute largely to periodical literature. Dr. Allon did much to promote Church music in the Nonconformist churches, and compiled the "Congregational Psalmist," which is very extensively used. Since 1865 he was editor of the "British Quarterly Review." In 1881 he was for the second time Chairman of the Congregational Union in its Jubilee year. The funeral of the late Dr. Allen, took place on Thurs- day afternoon at Union Chapel, Islington, in the presence of an enormous congregation, the mourners including, besides personal friends, numerous representatives of the Congregational connexion and other societies. Dr. Reynolds, of Cheshunt College, conducted the service, assisted by the Rev. T. Guinness Rogers. The weather being beautifully fine,a very large crowd lined the streets in the neighbourhood. The interment subsequently took place at Abney Park Cemetery.
