div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

A. meeting of this Board was held at the Public Hall,. Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon. The Rev. Father Clarke presided, and there were also present, the Rev. Dean Finegan, Major Wareing, and Messrs. It. IL Davies, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: NUMBER OF ABSENTEES.
div.p: THE NUMBER OF ABSENTEES.

The District Education Committee reported as fol- lows: (a)—Tliat during the month of March (five weeks) the numbers of cases summoned before the Committee were the following, viz :—Application for payment of fees 55; for contravention of Education Act 358; total 413. Fees were recommended to be paid in 55 cases; refused 0; number of prosecutions before the magistrates 24; number of convictions 24.—Major Wareing, in mov- ing the adoption of the minutes, reterred with regret to the number of cases that had to be summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, in spite of the fact that the schools were now free.—The Rev. Dean Finegan said that only that morning he found in his own schools that there was a large number of scholars absent.—Mr. Quinn said there had been a lot of sickness in the town.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

The School Management Committee reported as fol lows : (a)—Recommendation, that the resignation of Miss M. A. Ellard be accepted, the engagement to ter- minate April 14th, 1892.—(b)—Recommendation, that Miss A. A. Kirkham be appointed as assistant mistress in the junior department of the Warrington-road Schools (in the place of Miss A. A. Woods transferred to the West Bank Infants' \ , at a salary of £35 per annum. The engagement to date from April 18th, 1892, and to be determinable on either side by one month's notice to expire on the last day of any calender month.—(c)— Recommendation, that Edith Naylor and Kate Wilson be engaged as monitors at salaries according to the scale of the Board, viz: £5 per annum. The engagements to date from May Ist, 1892. Their salaries if engaged as pupil teachers to commence from September Ist, 1892, if they pass the Government examination.—(d)—Re- commendation, that the midsummer holidays this year shall commence at noon on Friday, June 3rd, and end on the morning of Monday, July 4th,lB92.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Committee reported that since their last report, the following sums had been paid into the bank viz : School fees for March : From Simm's Cross school, £l.B 7s. ; Warrington-road scheol, £7 1.83. 7d. ; West Bank school, £l3 2s. 3d. Fee grant : Simm's Cross school, £156 17s. 6d.; Warrington-road school, £69 2s. 6d. ; West Bank school, £lO9. Dire of room, £8 9s. • Overseers on account of precept, £l,OOO ; total, £1,382 16s. 11d.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

A communication was read from the Central Associa- tion for stopping the sale of intoxicating drink on Sunday, asking the Board to petition Parliament in favour of the Sunday Closing Bill.—The Rev. Dean Finegan moved that the Board sign a petition as request- ed, and Mr. Davies seconded this proposal.—Major Wareing objected to the proposal on the ground that it was introducing politics into their business.—The Chair- man concurred with this view of the matter, and Mr. Quinn moved that the communication lie on the table. This amendment was agreed to. and the Rev. Dean Finegan suggested that it would have been better to propose that the communication should lie under the table. (Laughter.)

div.head: CLERK AND TRH COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE CLERK AND TRH COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS.

Mr. Quinn referred to the fact that the Clerk to that Board had acted as a presiding officer at the County Council elections. They had at the time four solicitors in the town, and three of them were engaged as presid- ing officers, the other being left out in the cold. He pointed out that the Clerk was receiving a salary from the rates of the town, and at the very time he was acting as presiding officer, he was being paid by that Board, and therefore, he received two days' pay for one day's work. He (Mr. Quinn) should like the Finance Com- mittee to do something to put a stop to that.—Major Wareing asked that Mr. Quinn might give notice of the question, and this Mr. Quinn said be would do for the next meeting. This concluded the business.

John Bentley was remanded at Stalybridge on Satur- day on the charge of attempting to murder his wife. The woman had refused to live with him because of his dissipated habits, and he shot at her with two revolvers, wounding her so seriously in the side that her condition was considered critical.

At Melksham Police Court, on Wednesday, John Gurd. alias Hamilton, was charged with the wilful mur- der of Henry Richards, at Melksham, on the 9th inst., and of Police-sergeant Molden, near Warminster, on the 12th inst. The prisoner was committed for trial on both charges.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A LADY
div.p: THE MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A LADY

AT SANKEY. THE INQUEST. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on Saturday, at Sankey,* Warrington, on the body of Miss Mary Elizabeth Diaper, Which was found in a pond on Thursday. Mr. Henry Diaper, commission agent, residing at 9, Devonshire-road, Prince's Park, Liver- pool, said deceased was his sister, and was about forty-seven years of age: Deceased had been in a despondent condition since November, when she had been taken suddenly ill and became greatly depressed. She was Hying in Windsor at the time, and as the doctor thought a change would do her good, witness placed her in charge of his sister at Bolton, and subsequently with a sister-in-law at Wavertree. Every care and attention was paid to her, and she seemed to be getting better of her melancholia. She had never threat- ened to take away her life, and she was allow- ed to take walks in the park unaccompanied. Witness had decided after mature consideration to place deceased with his sister in preference to placing her in an institution, as she had a great dread of bricks and mortar.—Mrs. Ann Jane Smith, 10, Kenmare-road, Wavertree, said deceased lived with her for two months. She was not placed under restraint.—Miss Edith Smith said her aunt left the house at 10 o'clock on Monday,the 28th ult. saying she would return to luncheon. She did not do so, and inquiries were at once set on foot, but without result. Deceased was a complete stranger to the locality of Sankey.—Wm. Wilkinson, carter, Great Sankey, said he found the deceased's muff floating on the water on the morning of the 29th ult. He did not think anything of it at the. time. His wife, Helen Wilkinson, found the body on Thursday.—Police Con- stable Slingsby said there were no marks of violence and the body was fully dressed. When the body had been, taken out a boy brought witness a " Liverpool Echo' containing an advertisement regarding the missing lady, which led to her identification—The jury, after a short consultation, returned a verdict of" Found drowned,. but as to how the deceased came to be in the water there was no evidence to show."

div.head: -19.- DEEMING'S MELBOURNE TRIAL
div.p: -19.- DEEMING'S MELBOURNE TRIAL
"A LYING HYPOCRITE."

No reliance is to be placed on Deeming's statements from hour to hour. At one moment he speaks of Miss Rounsevell in the most affectionate terms, and at another he vows vengeance against her for deserting him in his hour of need. The impression which he has produced on the goal officials is most unfavourable, and they re- gard him as a lying hypocrite. The accused man has written to his solicitor, Mr. Lyle, demanding in the most violent language that he shall proceed against Miss Rounsevell, for the recovery of the £2O which he sent her to pay her passage trom Melbourne to Perth. The governor of the gaol is sttongly of opinion that Deeming has destroyed the papers which he accused the warders of having abstracted from his cell. Mr. Haynes, the Perth solicitor, has written to the accused, stating that he has discovered the author of the report that Deeming had confessed himself to have been the perpetrator of the Rainhill and "Jack the Ripper" murders. He entirely denies that Deeming made any such confession to him, and expresses the hope that he may prove his innocence of all the crimes which have been laid to his charge. In reply to Mr. Lyle's interrogatories, the accused states that in the year 1871 he was confined in a London lunatic asylum under the name of Teddy Williams. Mr. Lyle has written to Messrs. Lewis and Lewis, the eminent London solicitors, requesting them to make full inquiry into the incidents of Deeming's early life. At the prisoner's special request he has been examined on behalf of the Crown by Dr. Shields, Dr. Dick (the Inspector-General of Asylums for the Insane), and Drs. Fishborne and Jamieson. These eminent authorities un- animously pronounced him tote perfectly sane. Deem- ing's line cf defence will not involve the ordinary plea of insanity, but his counsel will set up "instinctive criminality " as a bar to a capital sentence.

THE INHABITANTS OF RAINHILL AND DENHAM VILLA. At a public meeting of the parish of Rainhill, held after the vestry meeting on Tuesday night, the Vicar occupying the chair, a reference was made to the recent tragedies at Dinham Villa, and a resolution was submit- ted thanking Mrs. Haves, of Huyton, who owns the property, for her thoughtfulness in not leaving a trace of the villa in which the murders were perpetrated.—Mr. J. Johnson Owen introduced the subject. He said they were indebted to the Chairman for giving them an early opportunity of discharging what many of the inhabit- ants regarded as a public duty—that was to tender to Mrs. Hayes, the owner of Dinham Villa' a public expres- sion of thanks for having demolished the house where the dreadful tragedy took place, which had caused so much painful oxcitement in the neighbourhood. With that object in view he submitted the following resolu- tion :—" That this meeting of inhabitants of Rainhill de- sires to express its sincere thanks to Mrs. Hayes for I promptly demolishing Dinham Villa, the house where the Deeming murders were committed." The Vicar ; thought that the resolution should be in more genial terms, but it was ultimately adopted.

WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVES AND PRIMROSE DAY.

• On Tuesday evening there was a crowded audi- ence, largely consisting of ladies, in the Assembly Room of the Conservative Club, the occasion being meetings in connection with the Warrington Habit- ation of the Primrose League and in celebration of Primrose Day. The annual meeting-of the Habita- tion was first held, Mrs. Reynolds the Ruling Councillor, in the cliair.—Among those present were Aldermen Fraucomb, Sutton, Harrison, and Wright, Councillors Smethurst, John Fairclough, Comaell, Mr. Robert Davies, and Mr. John Hanip- • son, Conservative agent.—Mr. C. H. Wood the secretary, read the annual report. This stated that the Habitation had increased during the year by nearly 200 members; and that Mrs. Reynolds had consented to act as Ruling Councillor for another year.—Alderman Harrison moved a vote of thanks to the lady for her past services and her re-appoint- ment. He congratulated those present as meeting on the anniversary of the death of a great man, a great genius, a great statesman, who had left behind him " a noble name of light and leading on the cliffs of fame." Speaking of the fact that he (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. Pickmere had previously been ruling councillors of the habitation,he said that neither of them had succeeded in intusine any enthusiasm into it. The Primrose League was essentially a ladies' movement; and it was fitting that ladies should succeed in carrying it on well. Under the charming influence of Mrs. Rey- nolds, the habitation had been pre-eminently successful. —Mr. Smith seconded the resolution, which was carried, Mr. Smethurst acknowledging the compliment on behalf of Mrs. Reynolds, who was suffering from a cold.—A vote of thanks wars accorded to the secretary and Mrs. Clare, the honorary treasurer, and the former was re- elected, Mr. L. A. Voisey, jan., being elected in place of Mrs. Clare, who had resigned. —Mr. John Roberts,Coun- enter Smethurst, Mr. Alfred Woods, Messrs. John Coxon and S. Reynolds, Alderman and Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Grounds, Colonel mad Mrs. Bolton, Miss Reynolds, and Mr. John Flampson were constituted the Council, Captain Buckton in proposing these mentioning that Lancashire took the head in the number of members it had on the Grand Council of the League.—Aldermatt Sutton proposed that the following be appointed wardens for the ensuing year, with power to appoint subwardens from members of the League. Town Hall Ward, Mrs. Smethurst ; Whitecross, Miss Praeger ; Bewsey, Miss Atherton; Orford, Mrs. Bolton ; Fairfield, Mrs. W. H. Harrison; Howley, Mrs. Joseph Harrision ; Latchford Ward, Miss Fairhurst. He expressed the opinion that the Conservative formidable and overwhelming forces would soon put to flight the opposing army.—The resolution was adopted. A vote of thanks to Mrs. Reynolds for presiding closed the business meeting. A public meeting was then held of Conservatives and Unionists, under the presidency of Mr. R. Davies. He apologised for the absence of Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. John White, who had had an attack of influenza, and Mr. Robert Pierpoint, who he said would return to War- rington shortly. No doubt many of them had read with more or less interest the speeches made by the Liberal candidate and his friends during the past few weeks in Warrington, and he thought they would all agree with him that they were of the same old tune—(laughter)— all set to the same music, namely, the intense ignerance of the Conservative party and their own particular wisdom in everything. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They all knew that they never hesitated to try to make then responsible for everything that had happened in this kingdom. If they could go back to the reign of William the Conqueror they weted do so. (Laughter.) It re- minded him of Job and his many friends. When he was in his distress they came round him and instead of comforting him everyone had some reason or other for blaming him for something he had done or something he had not done, and at last, in the bitterness of his heart, Job said, "Doubtless ye are the people, and wisdom will die with you." (Laughter.) So they said of the Warrington Radicals. (Applause.) Ile could only say, in seconding what Mr. Hampson had said, that energy and enthusiasm almost always in warlike tactics lay with the attacking party. They were the defending party but if they did not summon up all their enthusiasm-- and enthulasin was catching—then they would be found short.—Alderman Harrison proposed:-"That this meeting expresses its unabated confidence in Lord Salisbury's Government, and hereby tenders its thanks to the mem- bers of the Unionist party in Parliament for the splendid services they have rendered to all classes of the country during the last six years, and further pledges itself to use every legitimate means in its power to secure the return of Mr. Robert Pierpoint as member of Parliament for Warrington at the next election. (Applause.) The Alderman criticised a recent speech of Mr. John Bylands in which the latter satirised the ex-mayor for calling the Conservative Government a constitutional party. Mr. Harrison maintained that it was the most constitutions./ Government that had ever presided over the destinies of the country. He quoted the views of the late Mr. John Bright, Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Henry Jarnes, and the Duke of Argyll as being contrary to those of Mr. John Bylands, and said that if the latter ph med himself upon having madea discovery which they failed to make, l the laugh was rather against Mr. Ryla.nds. (Applause..)—Alderman Sutton seconded the resolution. He thought none of them would support a gentleman from Dublin, about whom they knew nothing except what they were told, in preference to a zentlemaa whom they all knew, and who had done very much for the good of the town. In speaking of Mr. and Mrs. Hous- ton at a recent meeting one speaker said he thought Mrs Houston was the better man of the two. (Laughter.) He did not know that that was much of a compliment, because it implied that they appreciated Mrs. Hous'xe'S songs more than Mr. Houston's speeches. (Laughter and applause.) If we were ever so fortunate as to return ladies to Parliament he bad no doubt her songs would be more appreciated there than the doctor's speeches.—Mr. Thomas Fielding then in aleugthv speech seconded the 'resolution. minutes on the day he was killed I More than thatr he had worked, in 27 days before his death: on 24 days, averaging for these 24 days, 13 hours per day) and working on one of the days for over 23 hours. At the time of the accident, the driver of the train had been on duty over 23 hours ; but, it is said, he had dechned relief. Can we wonder that, under such circumstances, there was an accident? The wonder rather is that, with the excessive hours constantly worked on our railways, disasters are not of more frequent occurrence. It is "not good lenough "to be able to say that a driver or guard working for over 20 hours has declined relief. Even if he is willing,he ought not to be permitted to go beyond the reasonable endurance of his- powers of body and mind, when not only his OWu life but the lives, it may be, of hundreds of pas- sengers, depend upon his being wide-awake and equal to emergencies. One driver has several times been kept at work for over 26 hours at a stretch ; and of another it is said he was " once on duty 38 hours onf; of 41, and twice within one week Wag on duty more than 24 hours." Railway We are glad to see that both Servants' Liberal and Conservative candid- Grievances. ates in the Widnes Division and the Northwich Divisidn have been questioned as to how far they are willing to go in redressing the grievances of railway servants. It is to be hoped a similar course will be taken in every constituency in the country; it is one we have always recom- mended, as we believe it to be calculated to secure in the near future a series of reforms which are greatly needed in the interests alike of the public and of railway servants. It will be seen from our record of the replies to the questions submitted, that the Liberal candidates show themselves much more willing to meet the wishes of the railway servants than are the Conservative candidates; and, as the issues raised are essentially working.. class issues, the masses will not fail to note who are with them and who are against them. There are seven questions, relating in the main to shorter hours and the better protection of life and limb; but Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss has no answer to give as yet to any of them; he simply postpones his reply to that indefinite period when the Railway Servants Committee of the House of Commons reports upon the subject. Mr. H. Wade Deacon, who is expected to replace Mr. Moss in the representation of the Widnes Division, re- plies in the affirmative to five out of the seven questions, and is making inquiries with a view to what will be most likely be a favour- able reply as to the other two. Mr. BRUNNER deals at some length with the issues raised; and railway servants cannot but be pleased with the frank and earnest way in which he champions their cause. As he points out, he has already voted in the House of Commons ", against the "excessive hours of labour imposed on railway servants," and in favour of powers of limitation being conferred on the Board of Trade. His opponent, Mr. George WHITELEY, answers some of the questions in the affirmative; but on the main issue—that of "a maximum working day of ten hours "—he fences in a most unsatisfactory way. He prefers that "such labour questions should be settled,by direct negotiations between employers b.nd employed offers them a stone. div.head: LOCAL NEW.
div.p: LOCAL NEW.

WIDNES CASES AT TES QUARTER SESSIONS. At these Sessions, on Tuesday, Catherine Fleyes was sentenced to six months' and Mary Jane Riley, to three months' imprisonment, for damaging the plate glass windows of John Gerrard and Peter Walker and Co., at Widnes, on the 15th March, to the extent of £5 3s. Bd. and £7 us. fld. respectively. 17041ZPE PIIICKARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- at., and 4, Bridge-at., Runcern.—Adel.

div.head: NEW GENERAL DISTRICT RATH FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: NEW GENERAL DISTRICT RATH FOR RUNCORN.

On Thursday morning a special meeting of Runcorn Board of Commissioners was held at the Town Hall, under the presidency of Mr. H. J. Once. Present : Messrs. Pritchard, Hankinson, Abel, Wass, Coward, Taylor, Bisbrown, Humphreys, Marshall, (sec.), and Lake (law clerk). Mr. Taylor moved and Mr. Abel seconded a resolution to affix the seal of the Board to a general district rate for the present year of 2s. 4d. in the £ estimated to realise £5,811 Hs. 6d. The motion was unanimously carried.
Both PRITCHARD'S Shops are under personal superrislon.and customers may rely upon receiving every attention.—A.
THI3 WIDNES WIFE WO-lINDI-NO CARL

Francis Gaynor, Ellison-street, was again brought up on remand, before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, charged with unlawfully wounding his wife on the 2nd Inst. Superintendent Keighley said he would have to ask for another remand, as the woman was still unable to appear. Dr. Hudson said she was still Tery poorly, and confined to her bed. She would be unable to appear for a month or more. She was not yet out of danger.— Prisoner vrss further remanded for a week.
JOSEPH PEITCIURD. Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- et., and 4. Bridge-at., Runcorn.—.Adval. "THE WRECK OF TUE ARGOSY" AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening next the Tonic Sol-Fa Classes Will commemorate the close of their tenth season by a performance of the above cantata, in the Public Hall. Since their establishment they have been the means of diffusing a large amount of knowledge and experience in the art of singing, and as this will be the largest number of voices ever gathered together for a similar occasion, and the work is favourably known for its exceptional merit, there will doubtless be a crowded attendance on Monday evening. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., has kindly consented to distribute the certificates gained by the pupils during the session just closing. JOSYPH PRITCHARD'S sale shop is 51,High-st., his workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt. RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSE FUND. On Wednesday evening the Football Club, very generously arranged a special match between the past and present, the gate proceeds to be handed over to the treasurer of the District Nurse Fund, which has been the means of doing a great amount of good among the poorer classes of the town. Miss Evans, the popular nurse, who is about leaving the district, started the ball, the present team held the upper hand throughout. Tries were obtained by Crompton (2), May (2), Williams, Gayter. Houghton, Davies and Pendlebury, but from the many tries only two goals were kicked. The past were not beaten pointless, as Woods dropped a goal, and the same player ran in a try. The present team won by 2 goals, 8 tries, to one goal, one try. There was a large attendance and the funds of the institution should largely benefit. After the match the players and a num- ber of friends assembled in front of the Press stand,when Mr.P. Speakman, C.C., expressed his delight at seeing a I large number of people present to assist so worthy a fund. A great amount of good work has been done in connection with it. He sincerely thanked the players for their services.
Wben in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to Parroxatur's, 51, High-Bt.—Advt.

SUSPECTED DROWNING CASE AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday morning, about five o'clock, a man named William Gould, whilst passing along some waste .land near to the Old Quay Works, in close proximity to the river Mersey. came across a hat, a Malacca walking stick, a black American cloth tra- velling bag, containing clothes, linen, and a small box in which was a silver medal engraved " Leith Swimming Club, Cowen rescue medal, won by Thomas Rutherford, 1883." There was also a bundle of clothing. The affair has been reported to the police, who have communicated with the authorities at Leith. So far, the etudes have not been claimed, and a fear is entertained that the man may have walked into the river. PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test for 50 years,and quality and first-elate workmanship are Still plaranteed.—Advt. ROBBERY Ole A WATCH AT RUNCORN. Emma Johnson, a middle-aged woman, was brought before Mr. aL. Davis, at Runcorn Police Court, charged with stealing a watch valued 255., belonging to Samuel Brown, keeper of the beer- house Welsh Harp, Cooper-st. The prosecutor alleged that on Monday night the prisoner and her i little boy entered his house and asked f he could find her a night's lodging. He allowed her to stay because he was sorry for the boy, and he did not i charge anything for the accommodation. At sx o'clock next morning she was apprehended at Mr. Lightfoot's pawnshop, in the act of pawning. the watch.—The prisoner made certain allegations against the prosecutor, which he denied. The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 21 days'imprisonment.

div.p: flflrryt.:l TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1892.
NARROW ESCAPE AT WIDNES STATION.

On Sunday night a woman named Price, who lives at Warrington, and who had been visiting friends at Widnes, attempted to enter a train in motion at the Widnes Central Station. She fell on the lower footboard, and was carried some yards behre the train could be stopped. She was then rescued from a perilous position, having only sus- tained a few bruises. JOSEPH PRITCH•RD keeDS spectacles to suit all sights tram a shilling a pair.—Adet. A CHILD KILLED ON THE CANAL.

Louisa Flack, aged two years and three months, died at the Canal Hospital, Latchford, on Sunday, from the effects of injuries received on the 23rd March. On that date the deceased, whilst playing on the railway at Big Field, Runcorn, had one of her feet run over by a waggon.
JOPH PRITCHARD la prepared to wind and keep in repair private clocks from 108. per annum.—Advt. HOW THE CHURCH BLOCKS THE WAY.

At Conway a singular difficulty has arisen in con- nection with the School Board, which has just been elected. The Church party, who were opposed to the appointment of a School Board, secured a majo- rity on the reprisentation. They,however,declined to attend the meetings,and consequently no quorum can be formed. The deadlock thus caused has been reported to the Education Department. If you want your watch repaired by skilful workmen. take It to PRITCHLRD'S.—Advt.

TRE CREXIICA.T. AND COPPER WORKERS' UNION. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday, a meet- ing of chemical and copper workers was held. Mr. P. J. King, president of the union, gave an address on organisation and the benefits derived from trades unionism, and urged all chemical workers to become affiliated. He confirmed the statement that the union had purchased the block of buildings in Clough:on-street for the purposes of a club.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st. Warrington.—Advt.
A SAD CASE.

Extraordinary evidence as adduced at an in- quest by Mr. Brighouse, at St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, on the body of the illegitimate child of Ellen Chambers, which was born in the yard of the Bridge Hotel on Good Friday morning. The woman was of weak intellect, and, while the jury were inclined to censure her for subjecting her child to exposure, the coroner ruled that the matter of her being taken care of. rested with her father.
Go to PZITCISIRD'S for the beet Ave guinea watch a work- ingman can have —Advt. THE NEW VICAR OF HAYDOCK.

In consequence of the decision of the Archbishop of York remaining unaltered, it became necessary for the Rev. W. J. Melville, the patron of the living of Haydock, to appoint another vicar, and on Thursday morning it was intimated that the Rev. Charles Edward Bowden, M.A., rector of Glencarse, Perth,had been appointed. Mr.Bowden jean M.A. of St. John's College, Cambridge, and was ordained by the Bishop of Exeter. He is highly spoken of as an accomplished and hard-working clergyman.
_ ACE-BRAND SPADES.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge-at., Warrington.

A COLLIER'S DIFFICITLTY AT THE WOOD PIT. A strike on a small scale is in operation at the Wood Pit of Messrs, Richard Evans and Company. It appears that the colliers in the seven foot seam have up to the present been paid Is. 2fd. per ton for getting the coal, with a certain allowance for yardage. It has now been decided by the firm to discontinue the payment for "ribbon," or yard- age. and pay the men Is. 91 per ton for getting the coal. The colliers consider this equal to a reduction of 15 per cent. in their wages, and accordingly re- fuse to work on those terms. The matter has been reported to the Federation, and in the meantime the colliers, about 60, are standing out, pending a settlement. Should the question not be satiefactorily'settled, it is feared that the colliers in the other pits will support those in the Wood Pit, and a general turn-out will be the result.
_ If you want a lucky wedding ring go 10 51, HIGH-sT.,wharsi you will' get a present with it.-4 sot.
ST. HELENS Y.M.C.A., AND DANCING.

For some time past the general committee of the St. Helens Y.M.C.A., have had their minds exercised as to whether they ought to allow dancing in con- nection with any of the social gatherings, such as have been held in the buildings, and the committce recently resumed the consideration of the question. The general secretary (Mr. W. Lightfoot) submitted communications from a large number of secretaries of kindred associations, including Liverpool, Lon- don, Manchester, and Birmingham, who had been asked to say whether dancing was permitted in connection with their Y.M.C.A.'s. The whole of the replies were against the practice, and one secretary stated that, out of 4,500 institutions, he didnot know of one in which it was permitted. The committee decided not to allow dancing on their premises.
Josirx PRITCHARD has the best stock of ladies' silver and gold watehes in the town.—Advt.

THE HOME IRON MAIM Unfortunately, there cannot be recorded any amelioration of the depressed condition of the Eng- lish iron market. Prices show little variation ; but new orders are not for,hcoming, and the continu- ance of the Durham miners' strike prevents business in the Cleveland district, where not a single furnace is working on Cleveland pig, and only five in all are in blast. Manufactured iron is still in limited tequest, and the demand for steel generally is slack. There is, however, some improvement in the enquiry for tinplates. Engineers and ironfounders continue to experience only a moderate enquiry; but ship- building yards are fairly active. The coal trade is tolerably brisk.—lron.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED,—J. and W. DurreN, Sankey-Bt., Warrlngton.—Advt. CANON EYRE AND THE DaaioCRACY.

At St. George's Church, Tiverton, a few days ago, the vicar, Canon Eyre (formerly of tit. Helens), re- plied to an attack made on his recent address on Home Rule by.a section of the ecclesiastical press. Speaking from the chancel, Canon Eyre is stated to have used vehement expressions with respect to certain journslistic re narks and their alleged mis- representation in regard to his political views on a previous occasion. In the defence of his address he had, he continued, addressed himself to the so- called lower classes. These were democratic days, and if the Church of England was to be the Church of the nation she must use means to get hold of the nation; it was his desire that she should come to the front; and laughter in church, instead of be- ing wrong, bespoke a happy religion.
HALTON PARISH.

The annual Easter vestry was held on Tuesday even- ing, in the Girls' Schoolroom. The churchwardens' ac- counts showed a deficit of £35 ss. 5d., this being due to the necessity of putting in a new boi'er for the heating apparatus at the close of the financial year at Fl cost of £4O. The offertories showed an increase of £37 for the year. The Vicar appointed Mr. John Wesley Haddock as his warden for the ensuing year, and Mr. Joseph M. Baguley was appointed people's warden. The following were nominated as sidesmen :—Messrs. Ackerley, Chad- wick, Gough, B. Haddock, J. H. Horton, and Withing- ton. Messrs. J. W. Haddock and H. Thomason were appointed the lay representatives of the parish to at- tend the diocesan and ruridecanal conferences.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The first meeting of the newly elected Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Mclntyre, J. Knowles, S. Taylor, A. R. Norman, J. Weir, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, J. N. C. Williams, H. E. Heywood, J. Baguley, J. Stokes, P. Hall, W. Pickering, J. Smith, J. NI ilkinsoo, C. Mounfield, E. Bretherton, T. Baxter, W. Turner, J. Parr, J. Bate, T. Lea, W. Wilkinson, J. Whitlow and J. Brandreth ; J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk.) APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.

The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner proposed the re-election of Mr. Mclntyre as chairman, remarking that he had given every satisfaction to the members in the past and had get a thorough knowledge of the duties of the position. —Mr. Aaron seconded the motion which was carried unanimously.—ln acknowledging the compliment Mr. Mclntyre expressed his gratification that his past con- duct had met with their approbation and he hoped he should never do anything to forfeit the confidence they had reposed in him. He appealed to the members to support him in the manner they hitherto had done. Mr. W. Wilkinson moved and Mr. Lewis seconded the re-elec- tion of Mr. Joseph Knowles, as vice-chairman and the resolution was carried unanimously. COMMITTEES.

The following Committees were formed. ASSESSMENT Comarrr : Dr. Steele, Messrs. Charles Reynolds, A. Thomas and Henry Neild, ex-officio ; Messrs E. Aaron, P. Hall, J. Mclntyre, Joseph Knowles, Thomas Lewis, S. Taylor, J. Weir, and W. Whitlow, elected guardians. FINANCE COMMITTEE: Messrs. J. Mclntyre, J. Knowles, J. Baguley, T. Baxter, J. Brandreth, J. M. Williams, J. Hall, A. B. Norman, H. E. Heywood, T. Lea, J. Stokes, S. Taylor, J. Weir, J. Whitlow, and J. Wilkinson. The RELIEF SUPERVISION and the VISITING Commirrass were respectively constituted of the members of the whole Board.

The SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE WaS appointed as follows : Messrs. Hervey Talbot, Colonel W. V. Fox, Henry Neild, G. L. Davies, (ex-officio) and Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Baguley, H. E. Heywood, W. Pickering, J. Smith, J. Stokes, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, and John Weir.

div.head: THANKS.
div.p: THANKS.
A vote of thanks was -aCCO;:ded to Mr. Brandreth and Mr. Heywood, for their excellent work on the Finance Committee.

VACCINATION OFFICER. The applicants for the position of vaccination officer for Runcorn district were Mr. William Gittens, jun., Lowland-road ; and R. Moore, Church-st. The latter was selected by a large majority.
In Russia, by a new lavc, anyone communicating to a Foreign Power the contents of a secret State document shall be exiled to the remotest regions of Siberia.

div.head: VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: VESTRY MEETINGS.
(Contiitued from page 3).

FRODSLIAM PARISJI CITURCFI. The annual parish vestry meeting for Frodsham was held in the Kingsley Chapel on Monday morning. The Rev. H. B. Blogg occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. Among those present were the Rev. F. D. Ringrose (curate), Dr. J. liobinson and Mr. C. E. Littaker (vicar's warden), Sm.
A PROTEST.

Mr. Foulkes protested against the meeting' being held in.that consecrated place sat apart for the worship of God in spirit and in truth. To hold in that place a meeting for the discussion of pounds, shillings, and pence, was desecration. The vicar told his "dear people" the Lord's house is a house of prayer, and yet he insisted upon it being desecrated when he had schools in which the meeting might be held.—Vicar's Warden (Mr. C. L Linaker) : Is that all you have got to say ? Mr. Foulkes: It is.—The Vicar called for the minutes of the last meeting to he read, which was done.

THE ACCOUNTS. The Vicar's warden submitted a summary of the re- ceipts and payments for the year ending Easter Day, 1892. The Parish Church offertories were £l4l 3s. 3d., the proceeds of a cantata and sundries, £27 175.; the iron church offertories, £29 Ss. 3d. The charities, special collections, National schools, £lO Bs. 3d.; Church Mis- sionary Society, £ll 18s, 6d.; nurse's fund, £l6 4s. sd. ; Diocesan fund, £8 19s. 10s. ; Chester Infirmary, £2O ; House of Mercy, £5 ss. Id. ; Sunday schools, £6 16s. 2d.; Temperance Society,£6 7s. Bd. ; Missionary Society, £ll I.s. 9d. ;curates' augmentation final, £8 14s. Bd. : Harri- son's Charity,£2 19s. Bd. ; Heatherington's Charity, £10; balance Easter, 1891, £2B 4s, 2d.; ditto 1892, £1 13s. 9d. ; total receipts, £346 17s. 10d. The disbursements were-Salaries: Sexton, £4O ss. ; organ blower, £4 ; the maintenance of divine worship : surplices, £8 7s. 3d.; choir, £l9 3s. Id. ; heating, £ll 9s. Id. ; lighting, £lB is. lid.; and ringing, £26. Alms paid to Vicar, £2l ; insurance, £5 Bs. 9d. ; sundries, £4l 13s. sd, ; iron church expenses, £26 2s. 7d.; charities, see contra, £lO5 16s. 9d. ; Harrison's Charity,£3 ; church furniture, £5 ss. 7d. ; and Heatherington's Charity, £lO.

div.head: _A CONGREGATION OF ONE.
div.p: _A CONGREGATION OF ONE.

In reply to Mr. Foulkes, the Vicar's warden said the gas bill for the quarter ending December was about £6 odd.—Mr. Foulkes said the vicar held early morning celebration and evening services, and there were no con- gregations. He had seen only one person coming from the church at both services, Mr. H. Cr. Linaker : It's the people's own fault. Mr. Heywood moved, and Mr. Watson seconded the adoption of the accounts. Carried.

div.head: STRANGE BEQUEST.
div.p: A STRANGE BEQUEST.

The accounts of the various charities were submitted. The Vicar's warden said help had been given to 70 widows. With regard to the Upton Charity, which was £420 left by Mr. Upton, of Manchester (formerly of Frodsham), for the poor widows, the Vicar's warden said no application had been made to the Charity Commis- sioners. It was a strange bequest, and it had been urged that the churchwardens would have to distribute the whole sum at once, and the opinion of counsel favoured that idea ; but they had declined to follow such a course because they did not believe it was the intention of the testator, and that to give away the capital sum at once would only reduce the rate, as the guardians would stop relief to those parties who happened to get £lO or £2O. The Vicar's warden said it very stupid altogether, and he wished the vestry would take some action.
OFFICIALS.

The Chairman nominated Mr. C. E. Linaker as vicar's warden, and Dr. Robinson was proposed as people's warden.—Mr. Foulkes raised some ebjection but was ruled out of order.—Mr. Linaker nominated his sides- men as follows : Messrs. George Gleave, H. E. Heywood and F. Spencer ; and Dr. Robinson proposed that the pariah sidesmen be Messrs. Bate, R. Watson, and Joseph Gorst. Carried. It was resolved that the lay represen- tatives to the Diocesan Conference be Messrs. Carpenter and Tyler. Messrs, Davies and A. E. Pollard were chosen auditors.

RILA.DSTONII.9. Mr. Heywood moved a resolution, of which he had given notice, that the height of the headstones be Sit. ein., and tite width 21t. 91n., instead of 41 t. 6in. high and 2ft. 6in. wide, as at present. The only argument he could hear in favour of the standing regulation was that the rich might not overshadow toe poor, and yet when it came to a monument any height might be put in.—Mr. Watson seconded the motion.—Mr. Foulkes supported.—Dr. Robinson moved, as an amendment, that the height remain as at present, and Mr. W. Spencer seconded.—On the amendment being put to the meeting only three voted for it, and the original m)tion was car- red by a large majority.

div.head: GRAMMER SCHOOL.
div.p: THE GRAMMER SCHOOL.

,There were five feoffees wanted for the Grammar School te fill up vacancies caused by four deaths and one resignation, and Mr. Riley proposed that Messrs. C. E. Linaker, Ralph Bate, R. Holland, J. Robinson and John Rothwell be appointed.—The gentlemen named were elected.

AN OBJECTION TO FLOWERS. Mt. Heywood proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies who had placed flowers in the church and helped to add to the beauty of the service.--Mr. Dunsford seconded.— Mr. Foulkes : I object to anything of the kind. Flowers are not scriptural.—The Vicar put the potion which was curled.

THE VICAR AND TEE ROMISH LEAFLET. Mr. Foulkes said in the minutes read that mornir4 of the last vestry, the vicar said that he did not know any- thing about the leaflet teaching Mulish practices, which was circulated in the parish about twelve months ago. Now, about a week before that meeting a Chester paper containing a letter describing the leaflet, which was "ringed round," was sent to the vicar by a gentleman present.—Mr. H. G. Linaker : Was that Mr. Foulkes ? Mr. Foulkes: No, it was not Mr. Foulkes. (Laughter.) —Mr. Linaker : All right; go on. (Laughter.)—Mr. Foulkes asked would the vicar tell them that he had not read that letter.—Mr. Linaker : I move that the vicar does not answer the question.—Mr. Tiley : I think the vicar will have more sense than to do so.—Mr. Foulkes: He was written to about a month after it took place, and he has never replied yet.—Mr. Riley: Is there any reso- lution before the meeting F—The Vicar's Warden advised Mr. Foulkes to put himself in order by moving a resolu- tion, but while Mr. Foulkes was standing on his feet, a vote of thanks to the chairman was hurriedly moved and carried, and the vicar vacated the chair.

div.head: FARN WORTH FARIS& CHURCH.
div.p: FARN WORTH FARIS& CHURCH.

On Monday evening. the annual Easter vestry, in con- neetion with the parish of Farnworth, was held in the church, under the presidency of the Rev. J. R. Jones. There were also present—Messrs. P. Longton, T. Baker, J. Glover, J. R. Lea, H. Lea, J. W. Davies, A. Kidd, C. Whitfield, H. Brown, S. Welding, H. Bridge, Knowles, and J. Palmer, sexton. A letter was read from the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright Williams nominating Mr. Longton as his warden and expressing the wish that the other officers would consent to serve another year.

ACCOUNTS. Mr. Longton read a statement of accounts, showing a total receipt of £lO9 17s. Oid. for the past year, and an expenditure of £lO2 Os. Bd.,which left a balance in hand of £7 11s. ; £317 15s. hi. had also been raised dur- ing the past year towards the restoration of the church. The accounts were unanimously passed.
OFFICIALS:

The wardens were unanimously re-elected as follows: —Mr. P. Longton (vicar's warden), Mr. T. Baker (Bold), Mr. M. Taylor (Cuerdley), Mr. .1. Glover (Cronton). The sidesmen were also re-elected : Messrs. J. Brock, C. E. Barlow, T. Carlile, J. W. Davies, T. Fletcher, E. Guest, S. Hoyle, J. L. Bunter, W. Jones, R. Kidd, A. Kidd, .1. IL Lea, 11. Lea, F. S. Lea, G. I. Neill, W. S. Pritchard, T. Shuttleworth, C. Whitfield, J. Moss, J. Warburton, A. Thorpe, and Knowles. Messrs. S. Hoyle and T. Shuttleworth were re-appointed lay representa- tives.

div.head: QUESTION OF LAND TAX.
div.p: A QUESTION OF LAND TAX.

Mr. Langton- said that a certain Mr. Wilcox, of Ditton, has not paid his land tax for the past four years, and he refused to do so. The amount of taxa- tion had been left to the parish of Farnworth a great many years ago.—Mr. Baker thought the landlord ought to pay the tax.—Mr. Longton said he agreed with that remark.—Mr. Brown said the total amount due was £6 145., and Mr. Wilcox refused to pay, be- cause he said he was over-taxed as compared with the other farmers in the district. Mr. Brown added that he had collected the tax for fifteen years, and the amount bad always been the same. After a long discussion, it was decided on the motion of Mr. Whitfield, seconded by Mr. Welding, that legal advice betaken in the matter.
THE REV. YR. JONES.

The Chairman thanked all the workers connected with the church for the warm support he had received from them during the time he had been at Farnworth. The rev gentleman then briefly alluded to his severance with the parish, and thanked them all for their kindness towards him.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH. The annual vestry meeting in connection with the combined churches of St. Mary's and St. Paul's, Widnes, was held on Tuesday evening, at the Waterloo-road Schools. The Rev. G. fl. Garrett, 8.D., presided. Mr. Dwerryhouse read the statement of accounts for St Mary's which showed a total income of £lB2 14s. Bi-d. including £1 31. 30., the balance in hand from last year. The total expenditure, including the amounts given to various societies, was £l9l 4s. 11id., which left a deficiency of £8 9s. 31 Mr. Brookes read a state- ment, showing the total receipt for church expenses at St. Prul'a amounting to £B5 103. Bd.,and the expenditure £B4 11s., , which left a balance in hand of 19s. Bd. Last year the balance was sd. £312 18s. sd. had also been devoted to various objects.

The Chairman nominated Mr. D.J. Brooks as Vicar's warden and Mr. Dwerrybouse was unanimously re- elected people's warden. Messrs. Joynson and F. Neil were elected lay representatives to the ruri-deeanal conference. The following were elected sidesmen for St. 1 Mary's Church :—Messrs. C. Stead, W. Tracey, A. Borth- wick, F. Beattie, P. Tomlinson, A. Tracey, S. Palin, W. Ireland, W. Dixon, H. Hufton, G. Stowe, and T. Ather- ton. Those chosen for St. Paul's were—Messrs. J. Burrows, J. Eastham, Garton, G. Arnell, J. Williams, A. Case, R. Faulkner, S. Deacon, J. Beech, J. Hutchinson, C. Jones, S. Upward, and W. Rowe.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.

Thss annual event took place on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of the Rev. Dr. Preston. lhe accounts submitted showed that the receipts, inclusive of a special gift of £3O, amounted to £144 Os. 20. After the liabilities had been met, there was a balance in hand of £36 10s. 4d., compared with one of 10s. 20. twelve months ago. The Chairman said they were indebted to the firm of Messrs. Timmins for the completion of the ornamentation of the stonework in front of the church. He appointed as his warden for the ensuing year Mr. C. A. Timmins ; and on the motion of Mr. Meadowcroft, seconded by Mr. Salkeld, Mr. Hankinson, sen. was unanimously elected people's warden. The sidesmen chosen were Messrs. Prince, S. Fletcher, Kileross, West- brook, H. A. Hankinson, Pearson, G. Hazlehurst, Harri- son, and Smith. Messrs. Timmins and Flankinson were appointed the lay representativos to the Diocesan Conference. _

RUNCORN PARIS!! CHURCEL This annual vestry meeting was held on Thursday evening, in the National Schools, under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Wood. There was a good attendance. The Vicar nominated Mr. J. r Meredith as inner warden, and Mr. John Littler was elected people's warden by nineteen votes to fourteen received by Mr. Walter Timmins.—Mr. Meredith nominated as his sidesmen, Messrs. W. Timmins, Isaac Speakman, E. Gregory, and R. Abel.—Messrs. W. H. Rogerson, W. Bate, W. Crossley, and T. Nichols were elected people's sidesmen. The following officials were elected. St. Michael's :—Mr. Thomas Speakman, vicar's war- den; with sidesmen—Messrs. Weston, jun., Plant. and Sherlock. Mr. Wm. Cropper was re-chosen people's warden, and the sidesmen elected were—Messrs. Blun- dell, Peacock, and Worrell. Those appointed for Wes- ton were: Vicar's warden, Mr. T. T. Sill; people's war- den, Mr. E. Aaron ; senior sidesmen : Messrs. Joseph Ford, jun., IV. Mitchinson, W. Moores, and Joseph Far- rell. The accounts of the Rigby and Alcock Charities were submitted. Mr. Meredith, the vicar's warden, submitted the accounts. At the Parish Church the re- ceipts had been £413 7s. 7d., and after paying all ex- penses there was a balance of £144 ss. sd. paid to the vicar for Runcorn Curates' Fund. At St. Michael's the receipts reached £153 7s. Bd., and the expenditure was a like amount, while at Weston the receipts and expen- diture alike amounted to £56 Ts. 60. The representa- tives to the ruri-decanal conference were appointed as follows :—Parish Church, Messrs. George Muse and W. Timmins ; St. Michael's: T. W. Speakman and W. Mellor ; Weston ; T. T. Sill and E. Aaron, sen.—The cus- tomary votes of thanks were passed. Mr. James Littler drew attention to the defective heating of the church. Mr. Meredith said the new wardens would see what could be done.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The first meeting of the new Board was held on Thurs- day afternoon, when the following were present :—The Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. James Birchall, Hellas, Middlehurst, Ashby, Graves, G. Davies, J. Randle, Waring, Fitzbrown, Mercer, Goldsworth. E. Burchall, Kenwright, Griffiths, J. Whalley, Burt, Ranson, Lowe, Fisher' . Johnson, P. Longton and A. F. Mann (clerk).o On the motion of Mr. J. Burchall, seconded by Mr. Goldsworth, Mr. P. Longton was unanimously elected chairman of the new Board.

Mr. Longton briefly thanked the Guardians for the honour they had conferred upon him, and hoped the business of the Board would be conducted as well as it had been during the past twelve months. Mr. Daine was elected senior vice-chairman, and Mr. Mercer junior vice-chairman. The Rev. Dean Finegan was re-elected chairman of the Finance Committee and the School Attendance Committee. Mr. W. Middlehurst was re-elected chairman of the Building Committee. Major Wareing was re-elected chairman of the Union Assessment Committee. WOREROTJSE MASTER'S AIRPORT. From the master's report it appeared that there were 548 inmates in the workhouse, against 533 in the cor- responding month of last year; 97 vagrants had been relieved, against 85 in the corresponding week of 1891. Out-door relief had been given to 2,980 'persons, at a cost of £257 is. 9d., this week, against 2,911, at a cost of £249 95., in the corresponding week of last year. Mr. Mercer moved that a revision be made of the out- door relief. Mr. Davies seconded, and also suggested that a re- vision should be made of the inmates. The motion was carried. This was all the business.

div.head: RUNCORN SEAMEN'S _MISSION.
div.p: RUNCORN SEAMEN'S _MISSION.
CONCERTS AND PRESENTATION.

On Tuesday two interesting and enjoyable con- certs were given in the Public Hall, Runcorn, in aid of the local branch of the Mersey Mission to Sea- men. In the afternoon there was a good attendance, and the audience included 41 eh ildren from the Union workhouse, who richly enjoyed the treat placed before them by the band of the training ship Indefatigable. After the entertainment they were taken to the new Institute, Station-road, where they partook of a substantial tea, provided by Mr. and Mrs. Abel. They were waited %mon by the hostess, as well as Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Dykes, and several Sunday school teachers. After they had engaged in a number of games, they were conveyed to Dutton by Mr. S. Taylor, who covered the expense of the waggonettes. In the evening there was a crowded audience. The chair was occupied by Dr. McDougall. The proceedings opened with a descriptive fantasia, "A hunting scene," and the programme con- tained other compositions to which the band did full justice. The members are a credit to their conductor, Mr. A. B. Smith, for they acquitted themselves with remarkable ability. Songs were given by Masters Henry Steen, W. Burgess, Henry Fairclough, F Snape, and Wil- liam Bennett, and the efforts of rairchugh and Steen were especially appreciated. A recitation, " The Yarn of the Nancy Bell," by Mr. R. Tebbs, was enjoyed. Masters F Poulson, W Horn, D May, and WEI Cox greatly delighted the audience with a sailor's hornpipe, which they danced in a clever manner. Masters George Shaw and E Davies sang "The Postillion," Mr W Mitchell, the choirmaster, played the pianoforte accom- paniments. , During the interval, the Chairman said he had been deputed to present a certificate of the Liverpool Ship- wreck and Humane Society and 15s. to William Byfield, who had been the means of rescuing a woman on Feb- ruary 28th, from drowning, at great risk to his own life. The plucky act was performed at the Francis basin. He referred to the dangers of Weston-road, especially on dark rights, and then spoke in complimentary terms upon there being in their midst those who were ready to rescue others from peril. The man to whom he had to make the presentation was on his way from a vessel, when he beard cries from a woman vrtie was in distress. He ran to the spot and rescued her from the water, to her own gratification and the appreciation of her friends. (Applause.) Mr. Bytleld, who resides in Trinity-st., Runcorn, was loudly applauded on the gift being handed to him, and said he would again risk his life under similar circum- stances, if occasion required. (Applause.) The Chairman then made a few remarks about the object for which the concerts were arranged, namely, I the Seamen's Institute. He understood that the aver- age number of sailors, flatmen. and boatmen who had visited it daily was about 50. The place was deserving of all support, as it was a place of refuge for Jack when on land.

Mr. Shaw expressed his obligations to the friend who had been so kind as to give the band food and shelter during their stay in Runcorn, and he was sure they owed a debt of gratitude to the chairman for his services.

div.head: CHARGE OF BIGAMY AT
div.p: CHARGE OF BIGAMY AT
RUNCORN.
RESIDENCE IN WARRINGTON. EXTRAORDINARY EVIDENCE.

On Wednesday at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. John Brundrit, Joseph Partington Ankers was charged that on the Bth April, 1888, he feloniously married and took to wife one Ann Edwards his former wife Priscella Ankers being then alive. Mr. R. D. Maddock appeared for the defendant. Ann Hughes, single woman, residing with her parents at Burwardsley, Cheshire, said she was pre- sent at Burwardsley Chapel on the oth June, 1884, and witnessed the marriage between the prisoner and Priscella Pritchard. She signed her name in the register as a witness. The certificate of the , marriage was produced and gave the ages of the couple as 21 and 17 respectively. The witnesses were deponent and Daniel Ankers, father of the prisoner. s•-- Cornelia Pritchard, mother of the first wife, said she was a widow, and resided in Brymbo, Denbigh- shire. She deposed to the marriage taking place, and stated that soon afterwards the prisoner de- serted his wife, but he returned, and then again deserted her. Examination elicited that witness only knew from hearsay that the marriage had taken place, but they lived together at her house at Brymbo. The following letter was produced : "January 11th, 1892. Dear Son,—l write these few lines, hoping to End you well, as it leaves me at present. Dear son, I hope yo d will get a good wife, and people have no need to talk about you being married for ' your wife Priscilla is dead since Fbruary 15th, 1890. Give my respects to all, and take the same yourself. Your father is dead since you was there. So no more at present from your mother and sisters, Cornelia Pritch- ard." Witness said she did not write that letter, nor cause it to be written,—Cross-examined by Mr. Maddock: She did not know who had written the letter. It was first shown to her about two months ago by the parson at Brymbo. Ann Haynes, who of David Haynes, said she lived in Halton-rd. She remembered going through the form of marriage with the prisoner in Greenway-road Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn. She could not remember the date, but it would be about 4 years since. The pri- soner courted her about five months. He told her he had been married, but he was a widower. He lived with her for about a month at the house of the prisoners mother, in Church-st., and then they removed to War- rington, where he had got work, and where she lived with him for about two months. Her mother then fetched her to Runcorn, and she had not lived with the prisoner since.—Cross-examined by Mr. Maddock : Her name before she was married to prisoner was Ann Edwards. She did not remember the date when she was married to Haynes.—By Mr. Brundrit : Her mother fetched her home because she was uneasy at being away from her mother, never having been out of Run- corn before. She had a very poor memory and could not remember much except that the prisoner married her.

_ Mary Emily Faulkner,wife of Joseph Faulkner,Alcock- st., Runcorn, and sister to the last witness, deposed to wttnessing the marriage of her sister to the prisoner at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, on the Bth April, 1888. _

_ . Eliza Clare, said she was a single woman, ind.lived in Wilson Patten-st., Warrington. She had known the prisoner pince June of last rear, and he had kept com- pany with her since that time.—Mr. Maddock ob- jected to any evidence of this description being placed upon the depositions because it had nothing to do with the charge of bigamy.—Supt. Atherton said he should like the evidence taken because it showed the felonious intent and villany of the prisoner.—k note was taken of Mr. Maddock's objection, aid the witness was then ex- amined with regard to the letter. The prisoner lodged with her mother for a number of months, and he wrote te Mrs. Pritckard and that letter was supposed to be a reply. The envelope bore the Wrexham post mark.— Mr. Maddock again objected, and no further evidence was elicited.

Inspector Cooper deposed to receiving the prisoner into custody from the Wrexham police on April 7th. He brought him to Runcorn and read over the warrant charging him with bigamy and he made no reply. He produced the certificates of the first and second marri- ages, which he had compared with the registers and found correct. In the latter certificate the pris3ner was decribod as a widower.

Mr. Maddock instructed the prisoner to say "I reserve my defence," and he was then committed to the Assizes for trial. Mr. Maddock pointed out that the Assizes were not held until August, and he applied for bail, but his application was refused.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Wynne
Ffoulkes.

A DrsrtrrEDLOan.—James Griffin, living at the Crown and Sceptre, Buttermarket-st., Warrington, sued James Shaw of 9, Howley-lane, for 25., money alleged to have been lent.—His Honour : Are you suing for 2s. P—Plain- tiff : Yes, sir.—His Honour : You are incurring an ex- pense of another shilling.—Plaintiff said that some months ago he was watching a bowling match on the ground at the Horse and Jockey Inn, when defendant won a bet of £1 18s. The amount was paid him in two sovereigns, and lie borrowed from plaintiff 2g. to give the change. Afterwards defendant denied that he had ever borrowed any money, and refused to give plaintiff the 2s. he claimed.—Defendant now denied having had the loan, and his Honour said he could not credit the case of the plaintiff, and therefore gave a verdict for the defendant.

CLAIN FOlt Damien/a,— William Broadhurst, green- grocer, Winwick-road, Warrington, brought a claim against Peers Brimelow, landlord of the Horse and Jockey Inn, Winwick-road, for £lO in respect of the sale of a quantity of potatoes. Mr. W. J. Forshaw (of the firm of Messrs. F. Davies and Forshaw) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Browne defended. Mr. Forshaw said the plaintiff sued for damages for a breach of warranty with respect to the quality of 32} loads of potatoes which he bolaght from defendant on the 9th March. On the day in question defendant met plaintiff's father and told him that he had some potatoes to sell, and asked him if he wanted any. Mr. Broadhurst said he did not, but subsequently told his son, the plaintiff, that Mr. Brimelow had potatoes to sell. Plaintiff went to defendant's yard, and there saw defendant, the latter telling him that he had several bags of potatoes to sell. Mr. Brimelow added, in answer to a question, that they were "good, sound, and wholesome potatoes. They were Champions, and came from Lancashire. and were splendid users." He offered them at ss. 3d. per load. He (Mr. Forshaw) should prove however, that the defendant had purchased the potatoes as a damaged lot from the London and North-Western Railway Company, and that he had paid £5 for them, selling them for k 9 14s. After plaintiff had sold the potatoes to his customers he had many complaints as to their quality. He had to replace them with good pota- toes,and in some cases to return the money that had been paid for them.—The plaintiff corroborated the above statement, and added that Mr. Brimelow had absolutely declined to give him any compensation.—Several wit- nesses were called on behalf of the plaintiff, after which the case was adjourned for a fortnight. CLAIM AGAINST AN EXECUTOR.—Thomas Bellis, a moulder, 32, Laira-at., was sued as executor of Robert Bellis, deceased, by Mary Senior, 90, Battersby-lane, provision dealer, widow, for a sum of £lO 12s. 3d. for provisions supplied.--Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Forshaw for the defendant. —Evidence was given by the plaintiff to the effect that the wife of Robert Bellis, deceased, was in the habit of ordering the goods in question. It was admitted that the husband told the plaintiff at the time of an interview demanding the payment of the money that he had given 10s. to his wife to pay the plaintiff, and that she would have to pay the debt. It was further stated that a debt which was contracted in 1886 was paid off by the wife of the de- ceased in 1889, with a legacy which she received. The debt at issue was commenced in 1839, and ran up to April, 1891. The husband died January 2nd, 1892. R was also admitted that the wife had offered to pay a shilling • week, in the lifetime of the deceased husband, until the debt was liquidated.—For the defence it was submitted that the husband issued an advertisement in the newspapers about 1885, refusing to hold him- self responsible for any debts which might be contracted by his wife. The wife was given a sum ranging from £2 to £2 ss. per week to provide household necessiar4s, whilst the deceased paid the house rent, coals, and taxes. It was argued, therefore, that the estate of the deceased should not be chargeable for the non-payment of debts for which the wife had been given money to pay. —The Judge, in summing up. said that it was often arged that the fact of a woman getting in goods was prima facie evidence that she had got the authority of her husband to pledge his credit. He was rather scepti- cal that there was permission in this case. He agreed that the most likely person for a husband to employ as his agent was his wife, but in the present case he thought that there must be the same proof as in the case I between principal and agent, and all the more so as the claim was against the executor of the estate. It had been admitted that the wife had cleared off a former debt with a legacy which she had received, and further that she had agreed to pay is. a week to clear off the debt. He ruled, under those circumstances, that there had been no authority to pledge her husband's credit. Judgment accordingly for the defendant..
FATAL ACCIDENT 170 AN4ASTRONOMER.

Mr. Ilartnup, astronomer for the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, on Thursday fell from the top to the bottom of the Bidston Observatory Tower, receiving such terrible injuries that death must have been instan- taneous. An inquest was held in the course of the daV, when a verdict was returned in accordance with the facts, and a presentment added that the wall was too low.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

The Conservatives of Warrington bare been stirred into an appearance of renewed life by the advent of Primrose Day. On Tuesday evening there was an imposing array of Primrose "knights and dames" at the Conservative Club, at the annual meeting of the local habitation of the Primrose League, and at the subsequent meeting in celebration of the occasion.

But there were two things which the Conservatives had to deplore,the comparative absence of the prim- I rose and the complete absence of their. candidate,llr. Robert Pierpoint. Nature has not been propitious to the Conservatives in 1892 in the way of multipli- cation of primroses. As they are very scarce—may we accept this as an omen that the primrose will not be in the ascendant this year in the great elec- toral determination of our imperial policy which it will probably witness ?

Despite the absence of primroses and of their candidate, the local Tories indulged in the usual primroseate dreams of triumph which was to be the result of his candidature. According to some of the Conservatives they have been confining themselves pretty much to these dreams, for Mr. Ilampson, their agent, said on Tuesday night that certain of the Tories had been reproaching them for not "waking up," and bestirring themselves like the Liberals; and he, on the other band, accused those who complained of being themselves in a sleepy condition. After the powerful dose compounded of the concentrated essence of primrose administered to them on Tuesday night, they will, I suppose, be- gin to look very much better—or very much worse.

Mr. Fielding in his speech at the Conservative meeting, I see, claimed support for the Tories on the ground that they deserved their country's gratitude for the passing of Disraeli's Reform Bill, as it finally stood. Tais is as egregious a piece of claptrap as any public speaker could attempt to impose on a meeting of electors. The Bill was so prepared by Mr. Disraeli that if it had become law the working classes would have been worse off in point of political power than before. There would have been 237,000 enfranchised by it, but 486,000 of the artisans and labouring classes of the boroughs would have been excluded from voting! The Bill, moreover, was so clogged with fancy franchises, with privileges conferred upon the wealthy classes, that Mr. Disraeli himself absolutely calculated that if it were passed one-fourth of the voting power of the country would be monopolised by the aristoc- racy, one-half by the middle classes, and the re- mainder by small shopkeepers, clerks, and artisans. The great bulk of the labouring men in town and country would have been left entirely out of the pale of the constitution!

The bill, so far as it became of real service to the working classss was really passed by the very man as an argument against whom Mr. Fieldirl points to it; for it was only through the uncompromising contest Mr. Gladstone carried on with its suppor- ters that one surrender after another was wrung from the Conservatives and it assumed the form it ultimately acquired.

Mr. Fielding also made the astounding assertion that the Conservatives deserved the support of the agricultural labourer because they had given him the Allotments Act, and the Liberals ever since he could recollect anything about politics had done nothing for him. The memories of Tories are elastic. Does the County Franchise Act, passed by the Liberals in 1884,which conferred on the agricul- tural labourer the power of voting, count for nothing? This alone is worth all the other measures that Liberals and Tories together have passed in his favour since it has placed the lever in his hands by which he could obtain all other reforms.

Alderman Sutton, who, I suppose, in common with the rest of the Warrington Tories, looks upon Mrs. Houston as a dangerous syren whose seduc- tive vocal powers are exercised in decoying the community from political righteousness, chose to indulge in a little pleasantry at her expense, and in doing so let drop an observation which I do not think was very complimentary to the ladies of whom his audience was very largely composed. He said he had no doubt that when the country was for- tunate enough to have representatives of their sex sent up to Parliament, Mrs. Houston's songs would be appreciated there a great deal more than Dr.llous- ton's speeches. That remark might be construed to mean either that the lady M.P.'s would be mostly Con- servatives, and therefore too antagonistic to Dr. Houston's sentiments to like them ; or that the ladies generally are too light- minded and unintelligent to appreciate speeches su well as songs. Well, if he thinks the latter, there is this to be said on the point, that, while the ladies who have so numerously attended the Liberal meet- ings have had Mrs. Houston almost exclusively to sing to them, the Tortes, to draw the ladies of their political complexion to their meeting,had to have a whole array of musical charmers. One thing Alder- man Sutton's joke about singing in the House of Commons reminds me of—that is that after the next election the Conservatives throughout the country will have to "sing small." MERLIN.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD

The annual meeting was held yesterday after- noon. Present Messrs. F. H. Gossage, D. Wright. B. Brown, J. Midwood, R. Cook, H. S. Timmis, S. Owens, J. Beech, J. Tilley, F. lleyes, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, S. Sadler, H. S. Oppenheim (clerk), and J. Craik (deputy clerk). On the motion of Mr. B. Brown, seconded bf Mr. D. Wright, Mr. F. H. Gossage was unanimously re-elected chairman. div.head: BOATING FATALITY AT WIDNES.
div.p: BOATING FATALITY AT WIDNES.

Mr. Brighouse, on Tuesday, held. an inquest, at the Britannia Arms, West Bank, Widnes, touch- .ing the death of John Shaw, a Waterman, who resided at St 2, Terrace-road, Widnes:, The evidence adduced was to the effect that about a quarter-past three on Sunday afternoon deceased, in company with two mPn named Thomas Tomlinson and Charles Ashley, went for a sail in a small boat. They were proceeding up the river on the Runcorn side, the deceased being in charge of the tiller. There was a very strong wind blowing at the time, and deceased asked Tomlinson to take charge of the boat. At that moment the sail was blown over, and Tomlinson shouted to Shaw to loosen the ropes which held the sail. Deceased,how- ever, failed to do this in time, and the boat cap- sized. The three occupants were thrown into the water, and Shaw, being unable to swim, sank im- me,liately, and was seen no more. Tomlinson clung to one of the oars, and Ashley caught hold of the boat, both being subsequently rescued.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidentally drowned."
MARRIAGE AT HALTON CHURCH.

On Wednesday Morning, the marriage of Mr. Walter Collier, a Churoh-et„ . Runcorn youngest son of the late Mr. !Samuel Collier, and Miss Amv SophiaJcihnstone, of The Mount, Halton, was cele- brated at the Halton Pariah Church. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. G. D. Wray. The bride,who was °Aired in a grey travelling die is, was at- tended by her sister as bridesmaid. Mr. Wm. John- stbne acted as best man. On leaving the church, the newly-united pair were driven to Sutton Weaver Station, where they joined the Scotch express, en route for Luse, on the banks of Loch Lomond, where the honeymoon is to be spent. The happy couple were the receipients of a large number of valuable presents. These included a handsome marble clock, bearing a plate, containing the fol- lom lug inscription :—" Presented to Mr. and Mrs. Collier, on the occasion of their marriage, with best wishes from their employes. April 20, 1892." The various business establishments of Mr. Collier were closed throughout Wednesday, and those engaged by him had a thoroughly enjoyable outing to Chester, in honour of the joyous event.

div.head: SHOCFING ACCIDENT AT COWES.
div.p: SHOCFING ACCIDENT AT COWES.

At Cowes, on Thursday, . a dyer, named Noyes. and his son William, were engaged cleaning clothes whEn the flue of the copper became out of order. The son there- upon threw in some gunpowder to clear it; an explosion followed, igniting five gallons of benzoline. Noyee was blown out of an open door,:and the son was burnt tg death.

div.p: rAVININE BITTERS-NOTHING MORE. Q Onee upon a midnight dreary, ill in bed quite weak and

weary With sleeplessness, lone spirits, and indigestion sore ; While I strove in vain at napping, suddenly there came a tapping, ita af some one gently rapping—rapping at my chamber door "It's Doctor Draughts," I muttered, " tapping at my chain ber door."

'Twas the Doctor, nothing more. Oh t distinatly I remember ; it was in the bleak December, And in every single member of my body pains I bore. eagerly I wished the morrow, vainly had I sought to borrow From drugs surcease of sorrow—sorrow for my pains. galore ; And I asked if I should ever be as healthy as before. Quoth the Doctor. " Nevermore "Tour chest is bad, that's certain; your neuralgia's always
hurting, And your liver is so sluggish that, life's to you a bore; And your heart's so bad at beating that in vain you're sleep entreating. While from weakness even now you perspire from every
pore " But, Doetor, when shall I be fit to pass the threskold of my door?"
