div.head: BEFORE THE MA.CT'ISTB,ATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MA.CT'ISTB,ATES.

A CONFECTIONEE'§ SHOP ROBBED BY BOYS. At the Warrington borough court on Monday, Joseph Frangleton, aged 12, of 17, Crossley-street, and Ernest Aspinall, an older boy, of 5 Crossley-street, were charged with stealing on Good Friday afternoon, a quantity of currant bread and buns, value 4s. in all, the property of Harriet Bennett. confectioner, 33, School Brow. The Chief Constable said about 4 p.m. on Good Friday, the prosecutrix left the shop and went to see her parents. The windows had no shutters, and were exposed, and the currant loaves were in the window. The prisoners and others during the afternoon were playing about when one of the prisoners knocked a lad's head through the window, and both the lads accused took the bread and buns. The prosecntrix came back at 9 p.m. and found them missing. A lad named Lomax said Aspinall knocked his head through the windovr,but touched nothing inside, and Frangieton took a loaf out. The lads afterwards pelted the passengers with fragments of the cakes.—The prosecutrix having given evidence, D.S. Monaghan deposed to apprehending the youths on Saturday morn- ing. Frangleton admitted the theft, but Aspinall denied being on the spot until the other lad incriminated him. Asi to Frangleton the sergeant said the lad was "lost," and his stepfather did not behave to him as he ought to do; indeed the boy said he committed the theft through bunger.—The boy's mother stated that the lad was well looked after.—Aspinall seemed very penitent, and cried bitterly throughout.—Frangleton, who made his third appearance for theft, seemed at first quite indifferent,but a last joined his fellow prisoner in sobbing. Both lads were ordered to be kept in the bridewell till 6 o'clock on Tuesday evening, Frangleton to have six strokes of the birch rod.

div.head: THIIFT OF BOOTS.
div.p: THIIFT OF BOOTS.

Mary O'Reilly was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednesday, with stealing a pair of boots, &Auld time between eight and nine o'clock on Saturday night, from the shop of Felix Summers, boot and shoe dealer, Bridge Foot. She had taken them about nine o'clock to Mr. Horton's, pawnbroker's Win- wick-st., to pledge, and had represented they belonged to her son, aged 14, but they would only fit a boy aged eight or nine years. On being.questioned on this point, she said she had got them from two navvies. They were afterwards identified by Mr. Summers as Ms.—She denied her guilt, but was sent to jail for 14 days' hard labour. THEFT ItY AN EARLESTOWN BOY.

Henry Conroy, aged 13, was charged at the Warring- ton County Sessions on Wednesday morning, with steal- ing, about half-past 11 o'clock on the 10th inst., a silver lever watch, value £.5 55., the property of Elizabeth Price, 9, Sankey-street, Earlestown. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the prisoner, and said he was the son of poor but respectable parents, and his father had Meen employed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. for 36 years, and his character was without blemish. The parents were very much grieved at their son's misconduct, and had given him a sound thrashing. He was now going to Sunday school, and said lie was very sorry indeed for what he had done, and that if their worships would deal leniently with him he would be a good boy in future.— It appeared while prosecutrix was upstairs prisoner came to her shop and asked for some sweets, and while a girl in the shop was up telling her she was wanted, he stole the watch from a nail in the kitchen. He had subsequently buried it in a field, but a little boy that was with him told his sister, and thus it was discovered. —The prisoner was sentenced to receive six strokes of the birch rod.

div.head: THIEVISH OLD_WOMAII,
div.p: A THIEVISH OLD_WOMAII,

Before the WarringtonboroTlgh Magistrates on Thurs- day, Catherine Rush, an elderly woman, who now made her seventh appearance at court, was charged with stealing' about three o'clock the previ«us afternoon, from the stall of Benjamin Alexander, in the market, four reels of cotton and three of worsted, value 4d.—D. S. Monaghan deposed that he saw the prisoner buy a penny- worth of wool, at the stall, then remain about 20 minutes, and steal the reels, put them in ker bass, and walk away. She also stole some biscuits and an orange from other stalls. He took her into custody, and she said she had paid for the articles.—The prisoner : I was going to pay for them, but I had a sup of drink.—Julius Alexander, a boy, the son of the prosecutor, deposed to the disappearance of the stolen articles.—The prisoner was nomrnitted to jail for 14 days.—Her daughter pleaded hard that she might ho sent to the workhouse instead, Saying that he bad just been very ill, and her conduct was all through drink.—The magistrates, however, thought it would be hater for her to go to prison, as they could not compel her to stop in the workhouse, and she would bave medical attendance in jail and be kept from drink.
CHARGE OF BURGLARY.

At the Warrington borough police court, yesterday, William Beasley, labourer, living at the Model lodging- home, Friar's Green, was charged with burglariously entering the house ot Thomas Ilesketh, 3, Wilson Patten- street, on Tuesday night or early on Wednesday morning and stealing therefrom a magnifying glass, a plane, a foot rule, a screwbat, a dust-brush, an oil painting. 'The Chief Constable said the prisoner was a native of Leicester, and had been in Warrington only about four months. Mr. Hesketh had fixed up in a cellar at his residence a bench for cabinet making and had left there overnight the articles stolen, missing them in the morn- ing. The chain had been removed from the cellar grate, and it was clear that the thief had made an entry through it. The police were informed and it was ascer- tained that the articles had been pledged at Mr. Leslie's in Mersey-street. On Thursday morning Detective- Sergeant Monaghan apprehended the prisoner in Friar's Green, who answered to the description of the man who had pawned the things. The prisoner asserted that Ile bought them from a man in the street for 4d. A pocket knife was found upon him which Mr. Hesketh had been using the night beiore.—The prisoner now repeated his former statement.—On the application of the Chief-Con- table he was remanded for a week.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), and Messrs. John Geddes and L. Voisey. A DINERTER.—John Lucas was charged with having deserted from the 13th Battalion of the East India Regi- ment in July last year. P.C. Hollingworth proved the ease, and the defendant was remanded to Strangeways Gaol to await an escort. MONDAY.—Eefore Alderman Frane.omb (Deputy Mayor),

and Aldermen Holmes, Harrison. and Sutton. DRUNK AND DISORDSRLY.—Martin Curley, drunk and disorderly in Stanley-st., was bound over in the sum of R. 5 to keep the peace for six months.—Mary Evans, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horse- •market-st., was dismissed. TURSDAY.—Before R. Garnett. DESERTERS.—Two men named Watson and Whitehead, were charged with being deserters, and they were re- manded to Strangeways Gaol to await an escort. WILDNEBDAY.—Before Mr. Councillor Fairclough (chair- - _ . .

man), and Mr. Alderthan Wright. ARMY DESERTION.—WiIIiam Turner for desertion, on the Bth inst., of Her Majesty's 12th Lancers, stationed at Manchester, was committed to Strangeways jail to await an escort.
- - - DRUNK IN CHARGE OT A FlorsE.—William Lomax, drunk in charge of a horse and lurry in Buttermarket- strEet, on Tuesday afternoon, 'a as fined 55. and costs.
DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Peers, in Winwick- street, on Tuesday night ss. and costs. TRURSDAV.—Before Alderman Olandley (chairman), and

Mr. W. Owen. ARMY DESERTION.—Patrick Butler was charged with deserting, in August last, from the East Surrey regiment of H.M. 17th Lancers stationed in India.—The con- stable, who had arrested him stated that he admitted having deserted the regiment in Calcutta.Lr-The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and said he was in the reserve, and had his discharge at home.—The Chief Constable asked him why he had not acted straightforwardly with the policeman.—The prisoner : I had a drop of drink.—He was remanded till Saturday. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Wright and Chandley and Dr. Gornall. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Patrick Foy, in Fennell-st., the previous night, ss. and costs. NON-MAINTENANCE.—GiIbert Eloult was summoned by Mr. Shearer on behalf ot the Guardians for non-mainten- ance. The case was further adjourned for four weeks. A WOMENS QUARREL.—Kate Bush, of Morris Court, was charged with assaulting Ann Delonze, on the 18th inst. The complainant said the defendant chased her all through Church-st. and compelled hr to take refuge in a house and when she came out, assaulted her; also her daughter.—The defendant said that there had been a wedding and " they all got drunk." and the complainant came out and said she did not care for anybody in the neighbourhood and her husband got witness by the throat. Corroborative evidence was given on both sides and the magistrates dismissed the case. WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. T. Comber (chairman) _

and John White. RIDING ON THE FOOTPATH.—AIfred Lewis, for riding a bicycle on the footpath, on the sth inst, at Great Sankey, was fined is. and costs. ASLEEP ON His CART. Thomas Cooper, for being asleep on his cart, at Penketh, on the 13th inst, was fined 55., including Costs. VAGRANCY.—WiIIiam Davies found sleeping in a stack of straw that morning, at Winwick, having no visible means of subsistence, was discharged with a caution.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office. Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. BRIGHOUSE RANGERS.

The return match was played at Warrington on Satur- day. Holiday-seekers turned up in large numbers, and the gate numbered nearly 5,000. The Rangers, it may be stated, have held the reputation of being one of the best teams in Yorkshire, their forwards being described as the most complete combination which competed for the Yorkshire Cup. Luckily for Warrington, the Rang- ers met more than a match in Hunslet, or the probabil- ity is that we should have had to wait another season before having a glimpse of the " incuntain boys." An- other feature of the match was the appearance of Nicholl, the international forward ; but judging from Saturday's form be did nothing to justify the big name which he has created. The visitors arrived late, and it was 4.10 before a kick-off was effected. At that time a snow- storm prevailed, and, accompanied with a varying wind, matters were anything but agreeable. Wood kicked off towards the railway goal, and so vigorous was the play of the Rangers' front rank that Heesom, the Bates, and Boscow fell back on their lines, and tbe hornestets had all their work cut out to prevent disaster. Boscow was tackled under the posts by Wood, and although James Bate partially relieved,Nicholl and Croft forced the game once more to the Warrington goal i ne,Hcesom saving well A rush by Jagger and Wood found a minor being con- ceded. Exchanges between Boscow and Waddington ended with credit to the former ; but smart play by Thorniley, Jolley, John Bate, and Knowles reached the Tykes' quarter. The effect was quickly neturalised by Senior, A. L. Brooke, and Gilton, the latter being forced into touch at half way, Another minor eventually fell, and still from the drop out no impression could be made, for the Brighouse forwards were accurate in the loose, and the tackling was especially safe. A kick by Evans was well followed up by Turner, but Brooke punted finely to Boscow, whose exchange found half-way. The ' Brat bout of passing in the match was now witnessed, for the Bates and Heesom showed up well, and when the latter was on his running, the whistle ruled the effort void, a decision which did not meet with the approba- tion of the excited crowd. A free kick to Brighouse aided them immensely, but a penalty kick to Warring- ton on the line was well taken up by Holmes, vrho dribbled through his opponents, being eventually joined by Jolley, who accounted for Abbey. The Rangers passed well without making headway, and then Nevins struggled away from a twist of opponents, and once more placed his side on the aggressive. A miss by Potts let in the Tykes again, but an over-eagerness penalized the visitors, and Turner's kick being well followed up by nearly the whole body of forwards, the Rangers narrowly missed having a score recorded against them. Another rush, this time headed by Nichol!, sent the third minor, but from this point the visitors were never really dangerous this half. James Bate received from his com- panion half, and managed to foil his hitherto attentive opponents. The quarter flag was reached, and Turner made his mark from a kick by Brooke. Abbey proved the saviour of his side, and some fine passing by the Warringtonians saw Bate throwing across to Potts. The latter punted to Abbey, who was not at fault, but the Warringtonians next time tested Brooke' and the latter making a sorry mess of the return, the home forwards swept in a body over the line, Thorniley scoring a try, which proved to be the winning point of the match, Hee- sons failing at the easy place. This seemed to give cour- age to the homesters, for their passing was fine on the drop out, and Boscow and Evans kicking and tackling well, the Rangers were kept defending. Donohue re- sponded to a dribble by Nicholl and Jaggar, and Brooke making his mark half-time was then called with the score—Warrington, 0-1-0; Brighouse, 0-0-3. Turner re- started, and Nevins supplemented the kick-off with another kick to the Rangers' quarter-flag. From this Earnshaw dribbled splendidly right to the home quarter, an effort which was applauded to the echo. Smack Bate got smartly away from A scrimmage, and Jolley next being foremost in some loose play at half-way, Warrington again gct the advantage. John Bate tackled Gilton, and his companion the next minute floored Wad- dington, and the game was in dangerous proximity to the Yorkshire goal. Ashton, Turner, Donohue, and Knowles were the leaders in a fine swoop of the oppos- ing forces. Waddington partially relieved,but a dribble by, Turner again landed Warrington on the aggressive. Some fine passing by the Bates, Evans, Fleesom, and Potts saw the latter making the finest run of the day, be- ing forced into touch near the line. Turner and Ashton were prominent, but their efforts only culminated in a minor. Bandies met the drop out accurately, whilst Boscow met Abbey's reply in fine style. Another rush of the visitors was well saved by Boscow, and on the homesters returning to the attack, both Evans and Smack Bate had hard luck, getting over the border line, but being forced into touch-in-goal. The game was chiefly a forward one, end at the call of time the scores read—Warrington, 0-1-3 ; Brighouse Rangers, 0-0-4. Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back; C. Potts, J. W. Evans, and F. Heesom, three-quarter backs; Jas. Bate and John Bate, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair. Tur- ner, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, .1. Knowles, J. Holmes, T. Donohue, J. T. Thorniley, and W. Nevins, forwards. Brighouse Bangere Abbey, back ; Gilton, A. L.Brooke, and Waddington, three-quarter backs; Senior and J. Brooke, half backs; Nichol, Wood, Croft, Jagger, Artni tage, Clarke, Earnshaw, Taylor, and Hopton, forwards

div.head: WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENT'S.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENT'S.
This return match as played at Wilderspool on Bank Holiday. The weather was Unfavourable, and rain falling nearly the whole of the first half, the game was

uninteresting; indeed, it was with difficulty that the players obtained a, proper footing, whilst the slippery state of the oval made the game more of a farce than anything else. Waugh kicked off, and a spell of desultory play marked the initial half. Some clever play by the two Bates gave Warrington a position in the Saints' 25. but as superiar as were Warrington in the back division, so were Rochdale in the forward ranks, the dribbling being at times very effective. Fine kicking by Boscow saw Rochdale defending their lines admirably and, aided by no small amount of luck, Warrington were kept at bay. Near the close of the half Ashworth dribbl- ed well for the Saints, but lloscow and Heesom spoiled the manceuvre, and a free kick by Turner landed the game once more on the Rochdale line. Holmes headed the Warringtonians in one combined rush, but beyond a minor, no point was scored during this half. During the second half, the homesters claimed a monopoly of the play. A free kick, taken by Turner, was seconded by Ashton, and from some loose play Bandies passed to John Bate, who scored. This was followed by Ashton scoring a try from a scrimmage on the line, Turner making a good bid for the major point. Near the close, the passing by Warringten was indeed brilliant, and John Bate again augmented the score from a pass by James Bate. Minors followed, a splendid run by James Bate being loudly applauded. Final score: Warrington, 0-3-5; Roch- dale. nil.

WARRINGTON v. LEEDS PARISH CHURCH.

As ordered by the Yorkshire Rugby Union, Leeds Parish Church paid their visit to Warrington on Wednes- day evening. The Tykes ought to have visited Warringt6n on January 9th, but for some unaccountable reason, failed to put in an appearance. Although our local club had gone to the expense of having the ground covered for the occasion, little or no heed was made to the appeals for an explanation of the breach of contract. Stronger Lands prevailed, and although there was a good gate for a week-day match, the proceeds will in no way recompense Warrington for their previous outlay, and thesurmise is that their engagement with the Yorkshire-

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup
skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: TH

men must have well nigh cost them £5O. Referring to Wednesday's match, Leeds had a capital team in the field, a like remark applying to the fifteen who did duty for Warrington. Oddy kicked off,and Heesom replying, a good run by Watson at once took the oval into War- rington 'quarters. Passing by the Bates saw James running well, and another sprint by the county man landed the oval at the Leeds quarters. Wadding- ton and Ambler kicked well, but Potts with a fine run from a pass by Heesom reached the visitors' quarters again. Some sterling play by Thorniley, Handles, and Jolley was succeeded by a forward rush, headed by Ashton and Turner, Sadderby saving well. The attack was maintained, and the handling code was displayed to a nicety when the Bates and Evans passed well, but Jolley, the final receiver, knocked on the opposite posts. By degrees Leeds worked the oval out of danger, but Turner, Molyneaux, Nevins, and Donohue soon had it on the Tykes's lines again. A penalty kick was here granted against a home half back, but instead of proving relief to the Leeds men,it ended disastrously,for Askten,charg- ing it down, scored near the corner amidst ringing cheers. Turner failed at the difficult place. The latter met the drop out, and Warrington assumed the aggressive direct. A bout of passing on the reserved side by James Bate, Heesom, Evans, and Thorniley was duly appreciated, but Plows luckily saved his side. Jolley and Holmes were conspicuous in tackling Waddington near the line, but the visitors' centre got the oval away with a tremendous punt, Boscow finding touch at centre. Potts was hurt seriously at this juncture, it being found that his shoulder blade had been fractured. Nevins went back to threequarters, and his opening essays were performed admirably. A couple of kicks by the substi- tute found Wright at his best, whilst a moment later the visitors were penalized for a too strict attention to Boscow. Turner's kick was well followed up by Ashton, who made no mistake with his man, and from the scrimmage James Bate got away from a pass by his companion, and, passing to Nevins,the latterwas thrown into touch a yard from the line. Donohue dribbled well, but the Farish men again got the oval away. A sueprise packet was in store for the locals, for Jolley and Turner passing well, the latter threw to Evans. This player attempted to drop at goal, but his kick was charged, and Waddington snapping up the oval from some loose play, scored between the posts, Oddy's successful kick at goal bringing half time, with the score as Leeds, 1-0-0 ; War- rington, 0-1-0. Being five points to two to the bad, the Warrington men went about their work with renewed vigour, and after Jolley had missed an excellent opportunity, Heesom charged down a kick of Wright's, and Thorniley scored near the posts. Heesom, although he was allowed a free place, failed to augment. Warrington were still in a minority, and although still aggressive, no tangible score could be got. The visitors at length got the oval away, but Hee- som's cleverness forced them back. Another glorious chance was missed opposite the posts, but amends were made the next minute, when Holmes passed to John Bate and the winning point was gained, Turner failing to im- prove on this. Handles next got away from a line out, but unluckily the oval was knocked from his grasp when he was passing to a companion. The game became , vigorous near the finish, and although Lends got danger- ously close near the close, Warrington kept them at bay, and in the end the final score was—Warrington, 0-3-0 (six points) ; Leeds Parish Church, 1-0-0 (five points). Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back ; Evans, Heesom, and Potts, three-quarters ; James Bate and John Bate, half-backs : Ashton, Turner, Jolley, Handles, Nevins, Donohue, Holmes, Thorniley, and Molyneaux. Leeds: Wright, back ; Ambler, Waddington, and Plows, three- quarters; Watson and Sudderby, half-backs ; Oddy, Haggas, Robson, C. and J. Richardson, Walker, Farrar, Stephenson, and Kaye.

WARRINGTON "A " v. ROCHDALEI Sr. CLEMENTS "A." —Played at Roc hdale. Warrington losing the toss started the leather, a fine punt by Lawless being the first item of note. While the game was waging near midfield, Lally stole round a pack, running to the line, the home team clearing with a dribble until Mason saved in neut- ral territory. Then Daniels put in a rattling piece of play, and again securing possession ran clear in, but the veracity of the home touch judge was proof against it and the ball was brought back. Ashurst afterwards saved a rush in fine style, and when Lally, Mason, and Lawless got away with some pretty passes, the final pass was mulled and the chance lost. A vigorous rush by the Saints transferred the leather to the visitors' 25, Ashurst again saving, and enabling Bailey, Westall, Higham,and Warburton to dribble back. A smart run by Rowlands was followed by Molyneux and Glover invad- ing the Saints' quarters, where several tight packs were witnessed. Eventually Rochdale got away to midfield, Hampson, Forster, Warburton, and 'Westall retaliating in a similar fashion. Daniels was very conspicuous, and from a free kick Warburton almost placed a goal, the ensuing rush forcing a minor. Although Warrington had to face a snowstorm they continued to have all the best of it, Hampson, Bailey, Molyneux, and Glover get- ting away to the home lines, nothing being scored up to half time. Rochdale resumed, and the oval was at once taken by Bailey, Higham, Forster, and Hampson to the goal. Barton relieved the pressure, forcing the ball past half way where Daniels by a grand screw kick returned the leather, Lally flooring Butterworth on the line. Directly afterwards Warrington had a glorious chance and missed it, and then for a time the forwards mono- polized the game, which was of poor description, the home backs playing continually offside. Warrington continued to press severely, Lawless on one occasion being pulled up on the line, but at last Lally, Mason,and Lawless passed neatly, the last named running over. The Saints then invaded their opponents' half, and while the battle was waging here Lally dodged two or three, and running splendidly down the ground was only floored a yard from the line. Nothing further was ob- tained, and Warrington won by 1-0-3 to nil.

WARRINGTON "A" T. TRANMERE WANDERERS.—This match was played on Monday, at Birkenhead. Davies kicked off, and no return being made, play at once rested in the home 25. Warrington having a free kick, Sampson only just missed the goal. Deaden came to Tranmere's relief, with a good run and kick. Sampson was in fine form, and taking the ball well cleared his lines. Lally now got the oval away, but spoiled a good chance by kicking too hard. Tranmere now had a turn, and reached the visitors' half, but a rush by the visitors took the oval back to the 25 flag. The homesters again got to the Warrington line, but Sampson with a good kick got to the half-way flag. Warrington now did all the pressing, compelling them to touch down to avert disaster. The game now became of a rough nature, Warrington getting a free kick for offside play. Give- and-take play was the order, till half-time was called, with the score reading—Warrington, 1 minor; Tran- mere, nil. Starting the second half, Warrington charged the kick off, play being at once taken to the other end. Tranmere, however, got the oval away, Hancock having a shot at goal, a minor resulting. From the drop out, the play was taken to the Warrington lines, Deaden scoring, the place kick failing. Rowe had a grand chance of scoring, but lost the ball over the line, a very uninteresting game ending with the score—Warrington, 0-0-2 ; Tranmere, 0-1-1. RUNCORN "A " V. WIDNES " A."—This match was played at Runcorn,on Satuday,before a poor attendance of spectators, and in miserable weather, snow falling at intervals during the progress of the game. Neither teams had their full strength, owing to the calls made by the first teams of the respective clubs. Runcorn commenced to attack, bat good tackling on the part of the visitors prevented any scoring for a long time. The play was very uninteresting till Warder ran in for Run- cr‘rn. Snow now fell very heavily, but the play was still continued, and in the end Runcorn won by two goals, five tries, to Widnes one try. Massey scored for Widnes, and Warder, Speakman, Faulkner, Jones, Lang- ley, and Webb for Runcorn, Dumbavand kicking the goals.

div.head: FRODSTIAM FOOTBALL CLUBS.
div.p: FRODSTIAM FOOTBALL CLUBS.

The first fifteen of this club have had a very busy Eastertide, and also a highly successful one. On Good Friday they received a visit from Salford District team, and put paid to their account by 1 goal 3 tries to nil. The scorers were Thomas Darlington and Fred Darling- ton, who each crossed the Salford lines on two occasions, and Rogers converted the last try into the major point. The game was a grand one, and was witnessed by a large number 3f spectators. On Saturday, Frodsham went to St. Helens, and de- feated St. Helens Recreation "A" by a goal to nil. As the Recreation team have not lost a match since Novem- ber this was no mean performance. The try was scored by T. Darlington, and Rogers converted. On Eatter Monday Frodsham received a visit from Runcorn" A," and a large crowd was attracted. Rogers kicked off for Frodsham, against the sun and wind, and the home team at once pressed and the pressure was maintained for some time. Then Rogers ran half the length of the field and then spoiled a brilliatit effort by a pass forward. Hayes got over, but the ball was ruled back on a plea of thrown forward. At half time the score was nil. In the second half Runcorn turned the tables on their opponents, and pressed the whole time, Frodsham only breaking away on three occasions. An unrecognised forward scored a try which was not con- verted, and then Dunbavand completed a magnificent effort by planting the ball over the line, taking three men with him. Final : Runcorn "A " two tries, Frod- sham nil. The game was mostly forward and was of an uninteresting description

div.head: WIDNES V. LEIGH.
div.p: WIDNES V. LEIGH.

The return match between these teams was played at Widnes on Monday. Although the kick-off was fixed for 3.30, Leigh did not arrive in Widnes until after five o'clock, and it was 5.45 when the homesters started, in the presence of only 500 spectators. The game was only three minutes old when Craig finely took a pass from Brennan, and scored a try. Drury failed at the place. After a series of scrimmages in Leigh territory, Hewitt obtained possession, and rushed over, taking Coop with him. Drury again failed at goal. Half-dine arrived with the score :—Widnes 2 tries, Leigh nil. In the second half, a snowstorm swept over the ground, and the wet state of the bail made good play impossible. Leigh after several fine eWorts, scored an unconverted try, and Coupe almcst dropped a goal. Final result : Widnes 2 tries, Leigh 1 try.

div.head: IE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1892.
div.p: IE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1892.
WIDNES v. ST. CLEMENT'S.

The return match between the above teams was played on Saturday, on the Widnes ground, before about 1,200 spectators. The home team started off, and followed well up, a scrimmage ensued near the line, which made play look dangerous. Wright then picked up at three- quarters, and ran the whole length of the field, and safely landed over, but Gordon failed to improve. After the kick-out, some splendid passing was. witnessed amongst the visitors. The leather was then picked up by Drury, who passed to Drummond, and ha again for- warded to Wright, who ran nicely for midfield and scored again, Drury failing to convert. Immediately on a fresh start being made the ball was rushed up by the home team, and a scrimmage ensued, when Drummond picked the oval up and planted it safely over the line. The kick was given to Drury, who failed to land it over. Play had scarcely resumed when Drummond ran over again, Drury's kick being again unsuccessful. Half-time score—Widnes 4 tries, St. Clement's nil. The first quar- ter of an hour of the second half was very evenly con- tested. The visitors then ran the leather up the field, but by smart play it was soon returned again, when Drury collared and reached home safely, his kick at goal also being successful. Drummond picked up about midfield, and handed to Drury, who rushed through and landed over again, amidst tremendous cheers. He took the kick himself, and sent the leather safely over the bar Final result :—Widnes, 2 goals, 4 tries ; St. Clement's, nil.

RUNCORN v. MOSELEY. On Saturday, . Moseley played with Runcorn at the Reddirts, and were defeated, as when :they visited the North earlier in the season. The interest in the match was evidently small and the spectators were few, while the game was at no time exciting. The Runcorn team did not arrive on the field until an hour after the match should have begun, and the game was not started until half-past four. For some minutes Moseley played with considerable dash, and carried everything before them. At length, however, May got away at a good pace, and Runcorn, for the first time crossed the half-way line. , May failed for the moment to gain much ground, but shortly afterwards made a splendid drop at goal, which, however, missed the mark. Moseley then took the ball again, and Stone made a clever run. J. H. Rogers and Rowlands also made a combined run, and the latter gained a long stretch of ground, but was stopped by the Runcorn back. From a kick by the latter, L. J. t yrne made his mark, but J. H. Rogers failed at the kick. Smith again gained a free kick, and Byrne made a fine try for goal, but the ball passed outside the post. Run- core then worked the ball towards the Moseley end of the field, where the game hung for the rest of the half, Moseley being occupied in resisting the visitors, who forced from them a minor point. No major point was scored when half-time was called. After play was resumed, Moseley made continued efforts to score, but were unable to get through the Runcorn backs. A. Rogers and Rowlands played well together, but on several occasions passed very poorly. Runcorn then came away with a clever kick into touch, and Davies with a clean and dashing run got through the Moseley backs and scored. The kick was taken by Hughes, who made a very near shot at goal. Moseley made a final dash up the field, and, although doing their best, were unsuccess- ful. Runcorn again took the ball, and from a try by 1 Davies, Hughes gained a goal. The visitors were still close in goal when time was called, the score being— Runcorn 1 goal 1 try, Moseley 0. RUNCORN v. CARDIFF. _ .

After playing at Birmingham, the Runcorn men tra- velled to Cardiff. Runcorn were without Crompton, Riley, and Dolan, and played the four three-quarters game. Faulkner started for Runcorn before a large crowd. Coslett returned, play being carried on in the centre. Pearson, receiving the ball, got away with a grand run, Houghton bringing up. The play was now in the visitors' 25, Abrams transferring to the home quarters. Riley, following up well, got away, Coslett just bringing him up in time, the home three-quarters passing splendidly, almost resulting in Pearson scoring. Davies transferred to the centre. Coslett got away with a grand run, but Houghton was equal to the occasion, and brought him down in grand style. Both teams were playing splendidly together. Archer got away, and transferred to Pearson, who put on top speed and scored a grand try. Hollingsworth. Abrams, and Davies now put in a bit of neat play, and were the means of the game being carried on near the hoe* lines. Play was removed to the centre. The visitors put in some splen- did play, and were hovering round the home lines, May getting over after some grand passing, making the score equal. Half-time was then called, the game standing 1 try each. After reversing ends, the Cheshire contingent played strongly, and tried hard to score again, and taxed the home defence severely. The Runcorn half backs played grandly, their passing causing great ad- miration. For a long time Runcorn penned their op- ponents, Davies being held on the line. Bobo afterward the whistle went, terminating a brilliant game, which resulted in a draw-1 goal 1 try each.

in the fifth place, whilst in 1890 they were bracketted equal with Aston Villa for the Bth and 9th " holes." One strange feature of the wanderers' position is the fact that although they rank third, they have scored no more goals than any of the first ten, whereas West Bromwich Albion, who are down in the last four, have five more goals to their credit. The defence has been the backbone of the Wanderers' team.

MISCELLA NEO US. At the usual Easter athletic sports of the Liverpool Athletic Grounds Company, held at Stanley Park, Liver- pool, on Monday, T. It. Allen, of Warrington won the third prize in the 120 yards flat race handicap, J. Bar- low carried off the third prize in the one mile handicap. and J. Massey was second in the 220 yards handicap, Warrington runners are therefore making a very suc- cessful start this season, and we hope to record many similar occurrences.

div.head: NOTES ON -GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON -GAMES AND
ATHLETICS. ,
FOOTBALL-RUGBY _ .

The victory of Leeds over Wakefield Trinity in the Yorkshire Cup was very popular, and there is no doubt that after what happened last week a large number of Yorkshiremen would have been sorry to see Trinity win, plucky though their Cup efforts have been in the pre- sent and past seasons.

• -- A try to nil is net a big margin, but it serves for Leeds, especially as it was a try worth recording. On the play itself, Wakefield were superior, and with more scoring power, and perhaps a little more luck, they must have won. Three-parts of the game were really in Trinity's favour, but Leeds were scorers and they were not, which made all the difference in the result. When the play got out to the three-quarters there was only one team in the hunt, and that was not Wakefield.

The Yorkshire Cup will certainly go to Leeds town for the first time in 15 years over which the competition has extended. But it is by no means certain that it will go to the Leeds Club. The Plumslet forwards are as good as Wakefield, who were better than Leeds, and if the Goldthorpes get any chances Hunslet will win.

A rather peculiar case came before the Chester County Court judge the other day, when the secretary of the Chester St. Oswald's was summoned by a photographer for the cost of certain photographs of the team. The judge would not decide the case against the secretary alone, but told the plaintiff to add the names of all the persons appearing on the photo, and he would make them all pay. It is apparently rather dangerous to be with a team when it is photographed.

Lancaster are laying the unction to their souls that they are now the champions of North Lancashire. Every club in that district with any claim to distinction has been successfully encountered, and never during this season has a defeat been recorded against them by their loving neighbours. Knowing what powerful organisa- tions exist in the northern end of the Palatine, this return stamps the Lancaster club as a most formidable body.

Sunderland have now won the League trophy, and that is something to be proud of. • And they have not won by a flake either, for they have done much more travelling than any other team, and have left all behind, with two matches stilt to play. div.head: REMARKABLE INCIDENT.
div.p: A REMARKABLE INCIDENT.

It is a scene in the lecture room of a medical college in New Orleans. The professor is lecturing before an intelli- gent class of medical students. He is describing the human body, its defects, and the danger by which it is surrounded. In order to illustrate it he has fluids from the human body, which he is subjecting to chemical tests.

"Gentlemen," he said, " I have described to you the appearance ot the human fluid in a diseased state ; I will now show yon how the same fluid appears in a healthy state," and he subjected his own to the test. As he held it up to the light for a moment, his hand trembled, he caught his breath, he paled, and exclaimed :1 " Gentlemen, I have just made a most horrible dis- covery : I myself have Bright's disease of the kidneys." Well might he be stirred to his inmost depths. Ho knew that his profession held out no hopes for any person in that condition. The 'pat hies and the 'ologies were powerless to save. He was a doomed man according to them, and, like many a great and valuable life, he was sacrificed to the tenets of the medical profession. In less than one year he was dead. The above dramatic and strictly true incident shows the terrible danger and mysterious nature of this modern disease, which may well be called th demon )f the present century. It steals into the system like a thief, manifests its presence 12y the commonest symptoms, and fastens itself upon the system before the victim is aware. It is nearly as hereditary as consumption, quite as common and fully as fatal. Entire families, inheriting it from their ancestors, have died, yet none of the num- ber knew or realised the mysterious power which was removing them. Hundreds of people die daily of/what is called heart disease, apoplexy, paralysis, rheumatism, pneumonia, and other common diseases, when in reality it is Bright's disease of the kidneys. These are solemn facts, but all the more serious because of their solemnity. There has never been but one remedy known for the cure of Bright's disease, or even for its relief, and that, remedy has become the most popular of all preparations known to the world. It is Warner's SetrZ " Cure. It has taken men, and women, too, who were in the lowest stages, and restored them to perfect health and strength. It will invariably check the first stages of this terrible disease, if taken in time It is endorsed by physicians, approved by scientists, and used by the best people in the land. It is a scientific preparation, and owes its popularity wholly to its power. It can be procured of any reliable dealer.

div.head: WARRINGTON SAILING MATCH.
div.p: WARRINGTON SAILING MATCH.

The twenty-third anniversary of this match took place on Saturday, the course being from Runcorn Bridge to Six Acre, round a flag-boat moored there and thence down to the west end of ThewNis wall, in line with which is the winning post. The com- peting boats having to lie at their stations all night on the Widnes side was the proximate cause of daraage to two of them. The Maggie was run into by a passing steamer and somewhat damaged, and the Tom Bowling had its centre-board bent so as to inter- fere very materially with its working. Nevertheless, both boats started, as indeed did the whole of the competing craft, viz.:— No. Boats' Names. Captains. Length. 1 Pink W. Warburton 14 9 2 May Fiy T. Sherritt 15 10 3 Primrose S. Leigh l7 2 4 Florence H. Warburton, jun ..... ....20 0 5 Rose John Leigh 20 0 6 Bessie James Green 20 0 7 Thin Bowling F. Howard • 20 0 3 Woodcock John Peers 21 0 _ _ _.
9 Maggie John Burthim 2L 2k 10 Gipsy James Davison 26 51

The weather at time of starting was very changeable, alternating between cold squalls with snow and bright sun and very light airs. All the boats got well away, and the course was run with,4ut material accident. The start was made a few minutes to one. All went on swimmingly, with the tide flowing, to the rounding of the buoy, and the boats had to strive against a head-wind and a contrary tide. At Crosfield's Wharf the real tug- of-war occurred, as is usual. It is essentially the awkward corner of the race, and often gives the most exciting incidents of the contest, for here the boats, however far separated in the running, often get into ' close—sometimes too close—proximity with eachoother. The first boat to round the buoy and the one which had hitherto led the running, was the first starter—the "Pink." She was followed by the Woodcock, which, havingover-hauled the Pink, kept the leading place, beat- ing against a very light head-wind and a tide still run- ning the wrong way. This state of matters lasted until the wind died away altogether and the turning tide took the best drifters and those most favourably placed for drifting, past the winning post, in the following order, viz :
SAME. PRIZE. £ S. D. 1 Gipsy 3 8 6 2 Maggie 3 Woodcock 1 10 0 4 Florence 5 Rose

_ 6 Primrose 7 Mayflower 8 Pink 9 Bessie 9 6 10 Torn Bowling 8 6 There was as usual a large number of spectators. In the evening the crews partook of a substantial dinner at the" Royal Exchange," after which business was gone into, under the presidency of the commodore, Mr. H. Warburton, jun. No objection was raised to any of the boats, and the prize money was handed over as above. The meeting was brought harmoniously to a close by the introductioa of a piano and a pianist, and contributions of songs, &c., by the members.

div.head: SPANISH ANARCHISTS.
div.p: THE SPANISH ANARCHISTS.
ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL THE KING.

In the course of his furthet examination before the magistrate, Munoz, the alleged instigator of the recent attempt to blow up the Chamber of Deputies, has made a statement which has caused a great sensation. He declared that an Anarchist meeting was recently held at which lots were cast to decide which of those present should kill the young King of Spain.

div.head: MR. JIRATIN MTA.RTHY AND THE IRISH
div.p: MR. JIRATIN MTA.RTHY AND THE IRISH

PARTY. Mr. Justin M'Carthy, addressing, his constituents in Londonderry on Tuesday night, said no English party was of any account whatever to the Irish party that helped them to fight the Irish battle. He pledged him- self that that party would never pledge itself to any measure of Home Hula till the whole Irish people had had an opportunity giving their assent to it. He denied that separation was their aim. All they wanted was government like that which Canada enjoyed.

div.head: EXECUTION AT WEXFORD.
div.p: EXECUTION AT WEXFORD.

Daniel Hanley was executed at Wexford Gaol, on Tuesday, for murdering the old woman Mary Ann Lyons, at Bandarig, two years ago. The condemned man has been visited daily by the gaol chaplain and the nuns of Mercy Convent. The culprit's younger brother James was convicted and sentenced for com- plicity in the critne, but subsequently reprieved. Scott was the executioner.

div.head: MINERS' STRIKE, &c.
div.p: MINERS' STRIKE, &c.

At a special meeting of the North Wales Miners' Feder- ation at Wrexham, on Saturday, it was resolved that nct more than five days a week should be worked at any pit, but that the masters and men at each colliery should fix upon a day most convenient to themselves. The Durham miners have decided by ballot to continue the struggle. Sir George Elliott, M.P., writing to a Newcastle owner, says that if not a ton of coal were drawn in the county for twenty years it would make very littlo difference to'the world's supply. He is con- vinced that the great majority of the men disapprove of the line that is being taken, and that their good sense will soon enable them to see that it is impossible to pay the wages demanded when the selling price of coal has been lowered.

Two young men named George Masters and John Slade,and a young woman named Alice Welsh,of Church Knowle, Corfe Castle, were drowned off Swanage, on Monday, by the capsizing of a pleasure boat. A married woman named Elizabeth Armstrong was on Monday morning remanded at Manchester on a charge of murdering her daughter, aged twelve months, by drowning it in a dolly tub.

div.head: ST. JACOBS 0
div.p: ST. JACOBS 0
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The first meeting of the new Board was,held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse. Present Rev. J. W. A. Tanner, Messrs. J. Stokes, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, J. M. Williams, H. E. Heywood, J. Baguley, J. Knowles John Whitlow, W. Turner, J. Brandreth, J. Bate, C. Mounfleld, E. Bretherton, J. Weir, T. Baxter, W. Wilkinson, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: ME CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ME CHAIRMAN.

The Rev. J. W. A. Tanner moved the reappointment of Mr. J. Mclntyre as &airman stating that they could not do better.—Mr. „Aaron seconded the motion with pleasure, and it as carried unanimousiy.—Mr. Mclntyre then took the 't flair, and thanked the members for their renewed confidence.

FINANCE. The following gentlemen were appointed a finance committee, on the motion of Mr, Aaron seconded by Mr. Tanner.—Messrs. Mclntyre, Brandreth, John Hall, J. Stokes, John Weir, Wm. Whitlow, John Whitlow,Joseph Knowles, Thomas Baxter, J. M. Williams, H. E. Hey- wood,and John Bagaley.

FRODSHAM PAROCIII4 COMMITTEE. On the proposition of Mr. Thomas Lewis, seconded by Mr. Heywood, a Parochial Committee for Frodsham and Frodsbam Lordship was appointed consisting of the Guardians of the two townelaips, the ex-officio Guardians and the following ratepayers : Messrs. Thomas Davies, John Robinson, H. Tiley, Ralph Bate, Mr. Percival and Mr. Collinson.

div.head: ALLOTMENTS,
div.p: ALLOTMENTS,

The Clerk said he had received a letter from the Local Government Board stating OA they had been called upon in pursuance of the order of the House of Commons ito prepare a return giving particulars of the cases in which land had been acquired for allotment by Rural Sanitary Authority's under the provisions of the Allotment Act of 1887, and where authorities had not acquired land for that purpose the reasons must be given for not doing so.—The Chairman : None have been asked for—that is sufficient reason.—The, Clerk said he had replied that the Authority had not acquired any allotments in consequence of their deeming it unneces- sary to do So.—The Clerk's answer was approved.

div.head: 'SEWAGE OF STOCiTON HEATH.
div.p: THE 'SEWAGE OF STOCiTON HEATH.

A letter was read from Mr. Robert Davies, of Warring- ton, calling the attention of the Authority, as a rate- payer of Stockton Heath-within-Appleton. to the build- ing which was going on on the north side of the Bridge- water Canal and along the new road from Twenty Step Bridge to Tom Painees Bridge. He heard that wee person intended to put up 30 houses with two w.c.'s in each along the new road, • and that extensive building Operations were going oh on the north side of the Bridgewater Canal, and he thought that a special inspector ought to be appointed, for it was fins possible for Mr. Farrington to look after everything.. Od the south side of the Bridgewater canal they feared that they would have no water during the next summer, owing to the excessive demand on the present means of supply, for, as it was, they were often without water many hours of the day, and the Slop Canal having drainektheir wells, they were altogether in an unpleas- ant position. By baying no ashpits, and he was told that many housesevere about to be built with insufficient space at the back for ashpits, a great burden would be thrown upon the sewers, and that the strictest ear. would be required to keep Stockton Heath in a sanitafy condition, and if so, it was certainly the duty of some one to speak, and to call the attention of the Board to what was going on, for it was evident that Stockton Heath was about to become a populous place. There was a general impression that in Stockton Heath 1 there were no building bye-laws whereas he had a copy at home of some sent isy the late Mr. Li naker about two years ago, and he thought that these bye-laws ought to be published nevi, and strictly enforced for the public health. Water closets were very awkward things dur- ing frost, but he felt sure that he need say no more to engage the attention of the Board.—The Clerk said bye- laws were in force and no house was erected at Stockton Heath without a plan being submitted and approved.— The Medical Officer said Mr. Davies's remarks with re- gard to the sewerage of Appleton deserved attention.— The Clerk said there wiS a scheme for the *tension of the sewerage of Appleton, and the subject was in the hands of a local committee.—Mr. J. Whitlow: And Mr. Davies is a member of that committee and not attended yet.—The Clerk : I think if Mr. Davies is so anxious about it he should attend the committee meetings.—The Clerk was instructed to communicate with Mr. Silcock, the engineer, who had propounded the scheme, and as- certain his costs up to the present time, and his charges for superintending the work should it be carried out. He was also instructed to reply to Mr. Davies informing him that he was a member of the Committee and that there were bye-laws in force.—ln reply to the Chairman, the Inspector said if the new buildings did not increase more rapidly than at present he could manage Stockton Heath or any other place. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The Medical Officer reported an outbreak of typhoid fever at the chapel house, Hill Cliffe, in Appleton, and the disease was of considerable severity. The drainage and sewerage, both to the chapel house, and the chapel outbuildings were untrapped, and the interior of the house was in direct communication with the sewer. This was in his opinion the cause of the outbreak and required immediate attention. The improvements and alterations recommended last year in connection with the extensive outbreak of typhoid fever on premises just ' below this chapel had not been carried out. A nuisance now existed dangerous to health. The report was approved.

A FILTHY HABITATION. The Inspector reported that he had inspected a cottage situate in Church-street, Frodsham, and found the same in a most wretched and filthy condition. Liquid filth was percolating through the flooring of a bedroom into the pantry of the adjoining house. The bedrooms were in a most shocking condition and appeared to be the playground for three or four children, whom he was given to understand, were not allowed to go out of doors, consequently they could not get to the closets and the bedrooms contained vessels filled with excrementitious matter and urine. There were no bedsteads in theplace but an id mattress or two on the floor, and the whole appearance and the atmosphere of the place was disgust- ing. Notice had been served to have the whole oi the interior of the premises thoroughly limewashed and cleansed and purified, and this notice had expired and had not been complied with, and he was unable to gain admission. The Inspector now applied for power to obtain a justices order for forcibly entry if required.—Mr. Williams said he had become acquainted with this case through lending the woman money to pay a magistrates fine and he could corroborate the inspector's statement. The house was in the most filthy abominable condition imaginable. He was passing the place late one night and through a small window he saw a child fas- tened to a mangle by its clothes and its mother was beat- ing it most unmercifully with an implement she held in , her hand.—Mr. Heywood said the children had not been to school for nearly twelve months and the Attendance Committee were powerless because if they got judgment there was nothing in the house on which to distrain.— The order asked for was granted.
BUTTON WATER SIIPPI Y.

A discussion took place upon the Sutton Water ques- tion. £62 had been spent and no water obtained, and that the estimate was that £54 would be required to bring the engineering operations to a successful.conclu- sion. An opinion was expressed that the landowner and 14ndiords ought to bear the finalcost, and a Committee. was appointed to thoroughly deal with the question The Committee appointed consists of Messrs. Bate, liaguley, Rigby, Baxter, Wilkinson, Heywood, Lowe, Acton, Aaron, Stokes, E. Wallington, and Wade. awn AUDITOR'S CERTIVICATR as to the correctness of the accounts for the past half year was produced. There was no surcharge.

div.p: Ettters to tin (Stator.
TORY NOTIONS OF FAIRNESS.

Sir,—l am very much pleased to see that the Rev. F. W. Willis, the rector of Warrington, has shown that he is willing to treat both parties alike in letting the National Schoolrooms in Church-street. It is notorious that for years the Conservatives have never had any difficulty about obtaining, the National School in Church street, when they wanted a meeting ; but it is some- thing new for the Liberals to have such a gathering in it as resulted from the reception held there by Dr. and Mrs. Houston ? This did not of course suit the Tories who have peculiar notions of fairness ; and I see that one of them raised an objection at the vestry meeting on Thursday night. Us said he did not think that the room should be let to " Radicals and Papists." The Rector's answer was that they were always prepared to let the room to any respectable body, as it was not with them a question of politics. This shows that the Rector has a sense of justice ; but what about the Tory objector ? Is he so stupid as not to know that there are Radical Churchmen ? And what about the people he calls Papists? Is he so densely ignorant as not to know that there are Catholics who support the Tory party? Perhaps these Catholics,when they see how they are regarded, and how they are stigmatised by the rank and file of the Tory party, will begin to ask themselves if they have not got in the wrong box. Hitherto they have got more kicks than half-pence.— Yours truly, Warrington, April 22nd, 1892.
A RADICAL ELECTOR.
THE " OBSERVER " AND DR. HOUSTON.

Sir,-1 have set myself no congenial task, but yet one that a sense of duty and a hatred of petty meanness de- mands. I am about to instruct the "Warrington Observer" pere et file. In the absence of the night school which it is said is about to be opened in Academy- at., instruction for the time present seems necessary, and, indeed, is asked for, though I doubt much whether the most powerful dynamite bomb yet perfeoted would cause a rent in the Tory skull sufficient to admit of even the smallest of intellectual rays. The vulgarity and tap- room slang of the many-eyed-one—who, by the way, might requisition the ordinary house-duster to fleck the smuts from his party-glasses—l now pass over with only the one remark, that. where Dr. Houston has deigned to notice him, he has done so in his own kindly, cultured way, and his treatment is in striking contrast with what Tories are led to believe has been ever the "high tone" of their "leading lights," but what Liberals know to be the very bathos of all political prostitution. The "infant 3' in a "nonsensical twaddle" leaderette says that:—" Dr. Houston forgot to point out what were the unjust laws under which the people of Ireland suffered," and could not if he would do so. He did not forget ; but he knew he was speaking to a room full of intelli- gent men who could, and did, read and understand. For the help of the deluded " dull " outsiders, I place before your readers briefly what the unjust laws are. An Irish landlord is allowed to raise his tenants' rents at pleasure, and thereby confiscate for his own use the whole of the improvements made. Land that has been won from the mire of barren bogs, or made arable amongst heath and rocks by years of patient toil, that has been fenced, drained, built npon, improved in every way requisite for its successful working, has been cruelly wrested from its (in all equity) rightful owner, when he was unable to pay an admittedly exorbitant rack rent. Nor does the Land Act of 1891 atop this. For by the strangling of the " Healy clause," which was meant to guarantee compensation for all improvements made, the landlords can still, and have, evicted then- sands of people from the land that their own industry alone has made valuable. The working of the Act, where it applied, was put into the hands of Commis- sioners of the landlord and land agent class, who were naturally antagonistic to the tenants. Reductions have only reached an average of 19 per cent., whereas in Eng- land many farms have been reduced voluntarily 50 per cent, in ten years, and this as an adequate result of the fall in prices. All improvements, such as house-build- ing, draining, making of roads, gates, &c., are in Eng- land done by the landlords, in Ireland by the tenants. As a consequence, rents habitually raised for this cause are nothing if not legalised robbery. Is the law that nermits this just? No man, whether Catholic or Protestant, can have or carry arms of any sort, if there is a suspicion, however slight, of Irish National feeling. Orangemen can have, and do use arms on their defenceless neighbours without hindrance or punishment. The system of education is almost purely secular, all religious teaching being by law strictly forbidden during !school hours in every village. It is administered by a Protestant Board, although three-fourths of the children are Catholics. In the higher schools, colleges, and Dublin University religious teaching at any time is not allowed. All this occurs in a Catholic country, and is supported by rates levied on a Catholic people. , The smallest pettiest Act of Parliament for local pur- poses,has to be passed at Westminister at incredible cost. For instance—in the case of the Central Ireland Railway 7i miles long, opened in 1885, the Parliamentary and Law costs came to £4,322 or 8 per cent, on total cost Of line, , which was £52,460, and 72 per cent. on £6,025, the cost ,1 of land. Many improvements are never attempted owing' to this unjust, uncalled for expenditure. The 'Municipal Franchise can only be exercised by male occupants of houses of from £25 to £3O rental,with the result that the main bulk of the poorer people are not represented on the Town Councils, and in the poorer neighbourhood all their wants are disregarded. A very different state of things exists in this country. Whether a Tory or a Liberal Government is in power, the Castle officials, who are all Tory and Protestant,— entirely out of sympathy with the feelings of the people —remain fixed ; all facts supplied to the Chief Secretary are filtered through this polluted source. The entire mass of officialdom necessary to work prisons, education, poor-law, and in fact all and every- thing pertaining to the requirements of a nation is composed of Tories and Protestants, many of them Eng- lish and Scotch army officers and others. To realize this, fancy England ruled and governed by Irish Catholics,and some idea will be gained of the feelings of the Irish people. Nearly five-sixths of the Irish M.P.'s are declared Nationalists, and yet they are allowed no voice in the making or abolition of laws concerning their constituents. It is 92 years since the legislative Union was imposed on Ireland by fraud, force, and bribery never equalled in modern history. While the population ef all European nations has increased considerably, Ireland alone, has, with all her fertility and resources, decreased one-half.

If this occurred in any other part of the world,-English- men would not be slow to discover, proclaim, and de- stroy the cause. Is it any wonder, then, that Irishmen should be determined to gain, at any sacrifice, the man- agement of their own local affairs? Rather would the wonder be if they were not. Men of all shades of religious opinion, outside the Orange clique, are work- ing and striving for this, knowing as they do that there is no country in the world more free from religious in- tolerance than Ireland.—Yours LE A.
THE LOCK-OUT IN THE COTTON TRADE.

The Council of the Amalgamated Association of Opera- tive Cotton Spinners met on Thursday in Manchester, and appointed four delegates to meet the masters' repre- sentatives with reference to the proposed arbitration. Some misapprehension exists as to the number of spindles in the Oldham district affected by the lock-out. The following figut es have been officially supplied .--Number of spindles stopped represented by members of the Masters' Association. 9,477,326 ; number represented by non-members, 362,300—t0tal number stopped, 9,626,839

div.head: FATAL FIRE IN RUSSIA.
div.p: FATAL FIRE IN RUSSIA.
NINE BODIES FOUND. FIFTEEN PERSONS MISSING. Si. PETERSBURG, THURSDAY.—A fatal fire occurred

here yesterday morning in a three-story house let out in tenements. The flames spread so rapidly that the occupants of the upper floors had not time to escape by the staircase, and some of them were only saved by jumping from the windows. Many, however, ware unable to avail themselves of even this means of exit, and when the fire was extinguished nine bodies were found in the ruins. Fifteen persons are still missing.

div.head: EXAMINER,' SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER,' SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1892.

BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRA.YCLE. (MIXED.) BI TUN 0' DICK 0' BOB'S. Abeawt Sunday tradin' neaw, an' moore specially Bacca. ' Aw'm ageean id, fro' th' creawn o' ml heyd to th' sole o' ml foot; but for o' thad wod aw say'll nobbut end i' smook ; yo' meet wi' varra few foak willin' to bacca a skeeam for stoppin' this evil—but keep this remark a cigarette. Aw ne'er wor i' favour o' ony Boort o' Sunda' tradin' whether it's beer, bibles, or chipt pratoes ; aw'm nod a teetotaller, an' aw wod'nd mek onybody sooa hi Act o' Perlyment ; an' though aw'm nod a Baccanalian aw like to see a chap enjoy his pipe Sunda' or werWay—it's moore respectable nor Sunda' cricket—but aw like him to ged his bacca o'th' Setterda' neet. Yo' see it's this way : AS long as shops oppen o'th' Sunda' mornin' just so long will fooak put off buyin' till then ; they'll ceawr i'th' pubs up to tornin' eawt time o' th' Setterda' neet, when they know as they want surnmat to eyt forth' next day—ay, an' summat to sup too—but they know th' shop'll be oppen o'th' Sunda'. Id used to be alleawable for tooathri shops to oppen a bit o'th' Sanaa' mornin' for th' sale o' perishable:goods, but they stertid' orderin' accordinly, an' neaw it's a case o' hevin' to oppen o'th' day to clear eawt. We sometimes criticise th' Irish, but aw've bin i' th' Emerald Isle, an' aw think aw'm reight sayin' as there's nobbut but five cities i' o' Ireland where jerry-shops are alleawed to oppen ov' a Sunda' an' then nobbut fro' two o'clock to seven; an varra few pubs tek eawt a license for thad. Aw dudn'd see one shop o' ony other soort oppen as far as Belfast were concerned. .

Wod bi this ? Well, aw think stiaws olez show which way th' wind blows; Ireland's sowberer nor England, Scotland, an' Wales. An' a lot moore moral, accordin' to a book justpublished on" Illegi- timacy"—or some sich title—deealin' wi' th' number o' bastards born every year i' th' British Isles. An' then, there's thad little affair at Accrington t'other week, yo' know. Wod abeawt that? • *

Do yo' know whooa's birthday id is to-day ? Will Shakespeare's ! He'd ha' bin three hunderd an' twenty-eight iv he'd lived. Lived ! Wey, he isn'd deead, an' ne'er will dee this side o'th' Millen- nium. Now yo' know Shakespeare were a doctor's bottle-wesher, iv we're to believe o' as we're towd, an' that's why we quote him, an' honour hm! An he were a sowjer, accordin' to another mon ; that's why we co' him immortal, an' drink to him at din- ners every April 23rd ! An' he werkt for a butcher an' kilt pigs, says another; an' a fourth tells us he were a lawyer's clerk, an' a fifth says he were a grammer-skoo' teycher. Well, o' as aw con tell yo'is as he were a Poet, an' a good un at th' job, whether Bacon helpt him or nod ; an' aw believe he were born at Stratford-on- Avon, an' deed theere at th' age o' fifty-two, i' Anno Domino 1616. Between bein' born an' deein' aw believe he went to skoo' ; naarlockt abeawt,coourted an' varra strong, fer he were wed afoore he were eawt ov his teens, to a woman seven year owder nor hissel' ; med a good husband an' fayther, are wrooat some plays as is to be bowt for a bob—th, price o' four flat pints, an' yet there's hunderds o' heawses beawt a copy, Shakespeare hed een in his heyd, an' he used 'em. He tells us abeawt " the poet's eye in a fine frenzy rolling," an' id " glancin' fro' earth to heaven, fro' heaven to earth ;" his een were sich as no other chap ever hed. One must ha' bin a rapid rectilinear lens an' t' other a microscope as lengthened eawt into a tallyscope ;th' foot seemed tobe olez focussin' every- thing on instantaneous plates. an' a grand bit o' werk id wor to judge bi' th' prints fro' th' negatives Ihe geet. Iv yo' want to know sumtnat abeawt love buy Shakespeare an' read Romeo an Juliet, Othello, an I in fact welly every one ov his plays: th' same iv yo' 11 want wit, humour, an' broad farce. Shakespeare con tell yo' moore abeawt th' country nor ayther Gilbert White or Jefferies con ; fro' th' lark at Hea- ven's gate singin' to daisies pied, an' banks whereon the wild thyme grows. An' yo' con be accommoda- ted wi' plots as'll nick yo'r hair stan' on end, or laugh till yo'er split ; an' yo'll bind things in his book—this shillin' vollum—as'll ease yo'r trouble or soothe yo' affliction. There's thowts in id as'll act as guides through life, an' to death, tco—in fact there's nobbut one moore book i'o' th' world as con- tains as mich experience, an' consolation, an' sich beauties, an' ov coourse thad is—th' Bible ! Ne'er bother yo'r heyds abeawt Shakespeare writin, a satire on his skoo'-mayster ; iv he dud do th' skhoo'-mayster deserved id, depend on 't. Nor whether he went pooachin' deer at Charlecote ; deserted his wife an' served her a shabby trick i' nobbut leeavin' her his second best bed in his will; nor iv he deed ov a fayver after a stiff beawt o' boozin'. Aw dorn'd believe ony o' these buzzes, nor thad Yankee bunkum aheawt Lord Bacon writin' Shakespeare's playes. Lord Bacon ! Him write The Merry Wives of Windsor, or The Tempest ! Bacon! Well, they couldn'd ha' med a maize guess. Chaps! Deny yo'rsel's o' hofe a gallon, an' buy a copy o' Shakespeare, an' see heaw mony shadows hes bin t'en for substance ; see wod true monlimass is—yigh, an' womanliness, too. Then, when yo' read th' noospappers next April abeawt o' these Shakespeare commemoration dinners tekkin' place, yo'll nod be as puzzled ta yo' are (happen) this year; nay, yo'll wonder heaw id is as there isn'd moore fuss med nor there is—iv it's possible, but certainly why moore fooak doesn'd attend 'em. Iv ony other nation hed sich a poet as Shakespeare to booast on, they'd hey a public halladay on his birth- day—to judge bi th' way they pilgrim fro' every corner o' th' world to Stratford-on-Avon.
AN EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENT AT

RUNCORN. 1 In December of last year, a body rtrgs discovered 'in a basin, off the canal in the vicinity of Ashridge- stristit, Runcorn. /t was mutilated to a Very great eStent,aud so far decomposed that it had evidently been in the water for sometime. A man named Joseph flopley, of Penketh-lane, had been away from home several weeks, and the wife and daugh- ter identified the remains as those of husband and father respectively,and theiropinion was confirmed by others, to whom the man was well known. The chief means by which they arrived at this conclu- sion was by a peculiar mark on the head. At the inquest, held on December 2nd, a verdict was re- corded that the said Joseph Hopley was found dead' The body was duly interred under that name, and the family mourned as those for one dead. . . . .

So far ihe circumstances are of a straightforward character; and it still remains for the extraordinary part of the story to be recorded. On Good Friday evening who should return to Runcorn but the man who was considered to be dead and in his grave. His appearance among his friends and relations con- siderably startled them, and it was some time before they could realise that he was in reality the man whose remains they believed they had committed to the grave in all solemnity more than four months ago. An officer of the local police force, who knew Hoyley, met him the other evening in the vicinity of the cemetety, and his first impression was that it was an apparition. He vas not satistlea that the man was in reality the one supposed to be buried until he had spoken to him and received an assur- ance that he was the same, and in the flesh. His identity was fully established and an explanation showed that after leaving home lie had gone into Lancashire, and had travelled about that county, as well as Yorkshire, for some months. Ile stated that he had written a letter which was returned, to him with the statement that it was impossible for him to be alive, as he had been duly interred. He, how- ever, determined to come home to confirm what he had stated. This is an instance in which the saying exemplified that " truth is stranger than fiction."
THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE MEDICAL OFFICER.

The report of Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer of Health for Warrington, on the health and mortality of the borough together with an account of the sanitary work accomplished during 1891, has just been printed- It is exhaustive and admirably pre- pared, and we quote from it the following particulars.

POPULATION, &c. EJtitnated population at midsummer, 1891, 53,000. Area, 2,004 acres; density of population, 26 per acre; number of inhabited houses, census 1891, 10,190. Births : Males, 1,119 ; females, 1,121 ; total, 2.240; birth- rate, 41.46. Deaths: Males, 746; females, 609 ; total, 1,355 ; death-rate, 24.63. The following table shows the populatiou and rateable value of the municipal borough since 1851 :

A HIGH BIRTH RATE. The birth rate for the year was 41.46, one of the high- est in the kingdom ; Warrington, therefore, in this respect, has not followed the general rule, in a very reduced birth-rate. The birth rate of England and Wales during UK was 31.4 per 1,000. In London it was 31.6, whilst in the 27 large provincial towns it aver- aged 33.2, ranging from 24-4 in Huddersfiold, 26.2 in Halifax, 263 in Brighton, and 28-7 in Bradford, to 36 4 in Salford, 36.5 in Cardiff, 36.6 in Sheffield, and 37.8 in Sunderland.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL* ACCIDENT IN LONDON.
div.p: FRIGHTFUL* ACCIDENT IN LONDON.
• LOSS OF gionT LIVES.

Shortly bef - ore six o'clock. orr -Monday. evening, a terrible accident happened .at_the Hampstead•Fle.ath Station orthe London and lihrth-Western .Railway, by which at least eight persons have lost their lives, while several others were removed to the nearest hospital, suffering from various and severe injuries. Theday, having been fine, an immense number of holiday makers had visited Hampstead Heath. According to a rough computation, it is believed that over 3:00,000 people visited this favourite spot. At the time mentioned above a thausand of these were returning homewards, and their anxiety to secure seats in the trains, which were running at frequent intervals, was quickened by the appearance of dark heavy clouds, which threatened a storm. Vie railway station was besieged by a dense solid moss of people of all ages, all eager to get first on, the various platforms. The regulation of such a confused crowd was little short of impossible. To reach either of the platforms a flight of steps has to be descended, one being provided for each platform. The crush on the stairs leading to the platform on the up line was terrific, and in this crush men, women, and children, all fared alike. Many were injured, and it is feared- that two women and six children were suffocated'. Immediately upon the police hearing of the catastrophe,. they had the railway station doors closed for a time,. while they pro- ceeded with the work of rescue. Dr. Evershed was sum- moned to the station, and the police' ambulance and stretchers were called into requisition to convey some of the injured to Hampstead Police Station, where Dr. Payne and Dr. H. Cooper Rose were quickly in atten- dance; while others of the injured were taken to the house of Dr. Cook. Some revived after treatment, while others were despatched in cabs to the hospitals ; but as before stated, two women and six. children succumbed to the injuries they had received, and their bodies were removed to the Hampstead Moruary. Some were there identified by relatives or companions.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

The inquest on the the disaster at Hamp- stead Death Station, on Monday, was opened at Hamp- stead Provident Dispensary on Thursday. Stephen Heaton said he was in the crush with his wife, who fell and was killed. The people could have got through had the gates been open. After other evidence of identifica- tion, medical evidence was given that the victims died of suffocation. Ely Mills, stationmaster, said the staff at the station on Monday was sufficient. After other evidence of identification, Mr. William Payne said he examined the bodies of the victims at the station. They died from suffocation. Ely Mills sai,4 he had been station master at Hampson Heath Station twenty-four ' years. The ordinary staff was six men, but on Monday there were seven additional men and two traffic inspec- tors. Thirty thousand passengers, independent of juveniles, passed the station, but that number had been exceeded. He considered the staff sufficient. The gates at the foot of the staircase were open. The collector's box was tittle obstruction, but the crush would not have occurred had a boy not fallen. William Exton, ticket collector, corroborated. Mr. Scott, medical student, who was in the crush, de- scribed the scene on the staircase. There was a great

crowd, and much horse-play. He saw four boys behind the box blue in the bite. Four were killed. The gate was open because it was against the wall, and he was pressed on it. No officials were regulating the traffic.— Robert Tusk said he was one of the boys behind the box, and ascertained that the gates were closed.—James Hewetson, member of the Hampstead vestry, gave evi- dence of the unsafe approaches to the station, and the inadequacy of the staff.—Police-superintendent Pearce said he had never had complaints of any difficulties at the station.
The inquest waskadjourned till Tuesday neat.
