div.head: EDUCATION AT ST. HELENS,
div.p: EDUCATION AT ST. HELENS,
UNSATISFACTORY ATTENDANCE.
PROPOSED RECONSTRUCTION OF THE DEPARTMENTS.

The School Attendance Committee of the St. Helens Corporation recently appointed a sub-com- mittee to visit every elementary school in the borough and inquire into the attendance of the scholars and other matters, with a view to making the department more efficient, and rendering more assistance to managers and masters. The following report has been prepared:— We have visited all the schools within the borough in order to obtain some idea of the working of the present arrangements of the Committee. We find one universal complaint of the total average obtained, which is attri- buted generally to the following special causes :- 1. Recurring absence of children on Mondays or Fri- days, or on both days. 2. Number of officers inadequate for work to be done. 3. The fitfulness and irregularity with which sum- monses are ordered, the fewness of their number, and the length of time which elapses between the report on whiAti a summons is ordered and the time of ordering. We are of opinion that these causes of complaint are substantially true, and that the work of the committee requires to be re-arranged and better organised, and particularly is this so in view of the assisted education which—while it makes the income of the schools depen- dent largely on attendance—has the effect, we have been frequently told, of decreasing the average attendance, although it increases the total number of scholars on the books. ,f We would therefore suoest— o„ _ . . _

1. That there should boa superintendent officer whose duty it should be to supervise the work of the other officers, to undertake, as far as possible, all offile work, and a1:3(1.a small district near at hand, and the following scale of pay be adopted—viz., £lOO per annum on appointment, rising to £l2O per annum by five equal instalments of £4 per annum, upon the work being done each year to the satisfaction of the commit- tee, and uniform to be provided by the committee. 2. That in addition to such superintendent officer there shoold he at least three attendance officers, and 1 that for these officers the following scale of pay be I adopted for all appointments :-253. per week on ap- pointment, rising annually by is. per week to 355. per week, upon the work being done each year to the satis- faction of the committee, and uniform to be provided by the committee.

3. That, for the purpose of receiving officers' reports upon the,visitation and the examinations of parents, a meeting should be held weekly—or certainly not less than fortnightly—at which the result of such visitations ' should be reported, and, if necessary, summonses ordered; and for that purpose a small sub-committee should be appointed, so that there may be a continuity, and regularity of policy in the matter of summonses on some such principle as (subject to exceptional circum- stances) first meeting, parent warned ; second meeting summoned if attendance still bad; third and each suc- ceeding meeting, summoned until attendance better; instead of, as now, when a parent, prior to being sum- moned, is sometimes warned at intervals of one month three or four tines, and then perhaps summoned and warned again, with the result that parents become cal- lous and give much more trouble than if promptly dealt with.

4. That reconamendations 1,2, and 3 being carried out, the schoolmasters and schoolmistresses should be asked to send regularly every Friday afternoon a list of irregular scholars during the week, specially marking those constantly absent on Monday and Friday, and that visitation upon such lines be commenced first thing the Monday following, and that the officers' reports thereon be submitted at the meeting of the sub-commit- tee on (say) the following Thursday, at which Sny parents the officers think ought to be required to ex- plain the absence of their children from school should be notified to attend; and that immediately after such meeting the lists be returned to the teachers with the result of the cfficers' inquiries and the decision of the sub-committee entered thereon. 5. That all summonses so ordered shall ise made returnable as far as possible on Friday in the following week. .

6. That all details he arranged with a view to the officers being in the office as short a time as possible, and particularly so at the commencement of the week, when it is most important their work should be promptly done. 7. That in future a census of the children in the borough be taken by the officers during the summer holidays in every alternate year. We are of opinion that the existing offic:xs, Thomas Dutton and Ezra S. Wood, have done their work well and satisfactorily, but we regret to say we have received many complaints throughout the district in charge of a third officer, and it did appear to us that his work had been anythina but satisfactorily done. We therefore recommend :—(I) The appointment of the senior officer, Thomas Dutton, to be superintendent at the maximum salary of £l2O per annum. (2) The retention of Ezra S. Wood, the second officer, at his present salary of £2 per week. (3) That the third officer be requested to tender his resignation. (4) The appointment of two new officers—one in place of the third officer and an additional one. (5) The rearrange- ment of the visiting district to fit in with our other recommendations.
T. C. Wit.com, Members JOHN' P. MEARNS, of the JAMES BURCHALL, SU/b-committee. ALFRED J. FOOTE, WM. JOHN JEEVES, Town-elerk. THE COMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATION:

At the monthly meeting of the St. Helens School Atten- dance Committee on Wednesday evening, Alderman T. Wilcock presiding, the Town-clerk complained about the publication in a newspaper on Tuesday of a private and confidential report drawn up by a sub-committee for con- sideration at that meeting. The matter was one of a serious nature' and until the recommendations of the sub-committee had been confirmed by that committee the document was of no weight whatever.—The Chair- man said he had not disclosed any information.—Coun- cillor Foote expressed himself" as thoroughly disgusted" at the publication of a private and confidential docu- ment.—Councillor Brook said he thought he was the person who gave the report to a reporter, but it was obtained from him under false pretences. Ile had not the slightest idea that the report was intended to be private, but apart from that fact the reporter tola him that he could have obtained a copy at the Town Clerk's office,but the office was closed. He siniply handed the re- port to him to look at,and not to copyor publish.--Coun- cillor Mearns said he thought Mr. Brook womid have known that reporters would publish any information they could obtain. The report was then considered in private. and the following recommendations, bearing on the reconstruc- firm of the department, were confirmed :—The appoint- ment of the senior officer, Thomas Dutton, to be super- intendent, at the maximum salary of £l2O per annum. the retention of Ezra S. Wood, the second officer, at his, present salary of £2 per week. That the third officer be requested to tender his resignation. The appointment of two new offleers—one in the place of thelthird officer— and an additional one. The rearrangement of the visit- ing dintricts to fit in with other recommendations,

div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE BY A

CLERGYMAN. At Dublin on Thursday, Miss Mary McKenzie Lappin , a schoolmistress, residing at Cookstown. North. of Ire- land, was awarded- £375 damages against the Rev. Andrew John Tilson, rector of Kilglass, county Longford for breach of prOtnise tc marry, The defendant, who kdid not call any witnesses, was represented to have borrowed various sums of money from the plaintiff while pursuing his studies. He was at one time curate at West Houghton, Lancashire.

div.head: RAVAGES OF AN ASOAPED WOLF.
div.p: RAVAGES OF AN ASOAPED WOLF.

/Early on Thursday morning the large wolf which blade its escape from a travelling menagerie in Sussex, and which caused much alarm owing to having torn to pieces, on different farms, a large number of sheep, was shot dead by gamekeepers on the farm belonging to Mr. Wm. Barris, of the Central Meat Market. The wolf, observing the keepers, made for them, and they would I have been doubtless killed by it had they not been I properly armed.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AND THE FEMALE FRANCHISE.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AND THE FEMALE FRANCHISE.

A. pamphlet by Mr. Gladstone was published on Wed-1 nesday, setting forth his reasons for hoping that the House of Commons will not consent to the second reading of the Bill for extending the parliamentary franchise to women. The Bill, he urges, is a narrow one, excluding the entire body of married women, who must be superior in one element of fitness—the lifelong habit of responsi- ble action. Moreover, the subject has never been taken into view by the public mind at large, and in the face of the coming election the promoters of so profound a change should be content with a continuance and exten- sion of the discussion.

div.head: RREST OF LONDoN ANARCHISTS.
div.p: A RREST OF LONDoN ANARCHISTS.

At Bow-street Police Court, London, on Wednesday, David John Nicholl and Charle3 Wilfrid Mowbray, the former described as the editor and the latter as the pub- lisher of the Anarchist newspaper," Commonweal," were charged with inciting and encouraging certain wrsons to murder certain other persons, to wit the Home Secre- tary, Sir Henry Hawkins, and Inspector Melville. An article which appeared in the issue of the paper of the 9th of April was the cause of the prosecution. Formal police evidence as to the arrest of the prisoners and the seizure of various documents was given. Mr. Vaughan, the magistrate, remanded the prisoners. MGmbray stated that as soon as he saw the article in question he disapproved of it, and he severed his connection with , the paper.

div.head: TRR DEATH RATE.
div.p: TRR DEATH RATE.

If allowance is made for the year containing 53 weeks, and the increase of population, the death rate for the year was 24'63 per 1,000 a very unsatisfactory one when compared with recent years, and especially so when our zymotic death rate (3.1), including influenza is the lowest since 1886 (2.3) •, the death rate alone of influenza being about 1 per 1,000, and that from lung diseases 5.7 per 1,000. It is nearly 2 per 1,000 higher than in 1890 (22. 68), 3.09 higher than the average (21 52) of the 10 years (1981-1890). The death rates in the several wards of the borough were as follows :—Town Hall, 242 ; Whitecross 32.; Bewsey, 27.5 ; St. John's, 25 ; Fairfield, 23.6 ; Orford, 21.8 • Howley, 282; St. Austins 16.3 ; Latch- ford. 223. in this table, the deaths are all apportioned to the wards to which they severally belong, but still it is imperfect in reference to Whitecross Ward, which contains the Workhouse, and out of the 150 deaths that occurred at that institution during 1891, I have been unable, in consequence of lack of information, to appor- tion 51 of them, consequently, the death rate of this ward is an abnormal one, and will remain so until some more accurate method of recording the street from which the person has been removed has been adopted by the Work- house authorities. INFANTA'S MORTALITY. Of the 595 deaths rqistered last year in children under five years of age, no less than 350 were infants under 1 year. In 1890 the number was 351, out of 583, 1889, 318 out of 570, and in 1888 277 out of 495. Calcu- lated by the proportion of deaths under 1 year of age to the births, registered the infant mortality in Warrington for the year 1891 was equal to 155 per 1,000, a consider- able reduction from last year,when it was 171 per 1,000, and nearly the same as the average of the 5 years (1886- 1890) which was 156. Infant mortality in England and Wales was 149, and in the 25 towns was 167.

ZYMOTIC DEATH RATS. The death rate from this cause was 31 per 1,000 of the population, against 3.88 in 1890, and 3 6 the average of the ten years (1881,90). The zytrsotic death rate in England and Wales was 183, and in the 28 large towns was 2.42 per 1,000. The lowest rates were 1.1 in Brigh- ton,l.4 in Derby, 11 in Birkenhead,and 1.8 in Norwich; while they ranged upwards in the other towns to 3.2 in Sunderland, 3.4 in Blackburn, 3-5 in Leicester and in Salford, and 3.8 in Preston..

DIPITIIERIA IN UNMADE STREETS. This insidious disease, though, not accountable for so many deaths as in 1890,.was endemic in two new dis- tricts of the town. In the early part of the year nine cases were reported in the White Cross Ward, eight cases in Lloyd-street, and one in Wellfield-street. These streets are unmade, and in wet weather are frequently covered with stagnant water, the effluvia from which is frequently complained of by the inhabitants. The sewers in the neighbourhood also emit sewer-gas to which I have referred in previous reports as being the cause of several cases of enteric fever and diphtheria. In the majority of these new houses the rain water pipes pass directly into the sewers, a system of sewer ventilation fraught with great danger, as the joints of the water pipes are never perfect, consequently sewer-gas is con- stantly escaping, and where the joints are near windows or doors there is a frequent pollution of the air of the dwelling. The other dietrict where several cases of diphtheria occurred was the neighbourhood of St. Mary's street, Latchford—new houses, apparently without any sanitary defect, except that the street is unmade, the district is low, and frequently flooded ia wet weather. In connection with these cases I must point out that about the same time several deaths from croup were re- corded in the adjoining neighbourhood of Old-road, which I am inclined to. believe were pure diphtheria. Here also in 1889-90;,1 have directed your attention to the condition of the sewers as a likely cause of disease

risrLININZA. During the past year we had a return of the epiaemic malady, which had during the latter months of 1889 and the beginning of IVO worked such ravages throughout the country. In Warrington the disease was very pre- valent, though the truth of this can only be asserted in general terms, and its real extent at the times cannot be gauged by any available statistics. For on the one hand, as Influenza is not one of the diseases included in the regulations for compulsory notification, no inform- ation was In this way obtainable, and on the other, a large proportion If the cases were probably of so mild a character as never to come under the cognizance of a medical practitioner. Some idea of the relative severity of the outbreak at different periods may, however, be gleaned from a study of the numbers of deaths returned as resulting from it. It will be seen that in the week ending May 2nd the first mortality (3) attributed to Inffuenza occurs, and that this increases some- what irregularly till, in the week ending June 6th, the maximum (13) is reached ; after this we get a decline in the number of weekly deaths and during the latter part of the outbreak, extend- ing on into August, single ones only occur. But at the same time, it may be observed that the fatality of lung disease at this period was, on the whole, greater ' than at other times. Many of these deaths were doubt- less due to pulmonary complications of influenza, and so in a just esbimate should really be included in the sum of those due to epidemics. Their number at any rate affords evidence of its disastrous results. The nature of this mysterious disease it is not part of my province here to discuss, but I may as well mention the view as to its character which, at the present moment, receives most general support, viz., that it is a disease capable of being transmitted from man to man, and that this is the chief manner in which it is spread, though the poison may alao undoubtedly be diffused by the air. THR CHIEF SANITARY REQUIREDIHNTS TER BOROUGH. 1. The occuirence from time to time of Enteric Fever points to the importance of making the sewerage of the town as perfect as possible, and, until that is done, a thorough and systematic flushing and disinfection of the sewers should bacarried out.

2. The appointment of a "Special Sub-Committee" to carry out the " Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1890," would, in my opinion, give a valuable impetus to the measures necessary for the improvement of the dwellings of the working classes. 3. div.head: DEATH OF A WARRIN9TONIAN OCTOGENARIAN IN AMERICA.,
div.p: DEATH OF A WARRIN9TONIAN OCTO- GENARIAN IN AMERICA.,

A REPUTED CENTENARIAN, AND THE FATHER OF 22 CHILDREN. We have received a cutting fromthe " Pittsburgh (U.S.) Despatch," of the following article which has appeared in that paper, recording the death at Pittsburgh, in January last, of an aged man who was formerly an ironworker in Warrington. The , article is accompanied with what stated by his relatives in Warrington to be an excellent portrait of the deceased, and is as follows : " Three score years and ten is, the allotted age of: man ; few attain it, and still fewer live beyond it. Edward Sefton, formerly of Warrington, Lancashire county, England, was an exception, He died on Saturday last, at the home of his son, Wm. Sefton, at the advanced age of 101 years and 2 months, having been born in the latter part of 1790. In many respects Edward Seften was a remarkable man. He followed the business of a labourer in the iron mills at Warrington, and although he was addicted to the use of tobacco from early boyhood, to the day of his death it had no ill-effects, and he could recall no serious illness throughout his long life. His fondness for smoking (he did not chew,few English- men do) was illustrated during his last illness, which only lasted a couple of days, by his insisting on being propped up in bed to enjoy the solace and luxury of his pipe. He had passed his 40th year before he married, but he was blessed with 22 children, four of whom survive him, his wife having died in February, 1867. These four include his oldest and youlugest. The oldest is Ellen, wife of Benjamin Monis of Pittsburgh, who is 65‘years of age, and the young- est, Samuel Sefton, aged 35. The other two are William and John Sefton, who also reside in Pitts- burgh. The deceased CaMO to Pittsburgh. about 10 yeats ago. Previous to that time his four surviv- ing children had come to this country, and the old man was left alone in Warrington, still working in an iron mill as a labourer, though he was then 91 years of age. His children, however, were anxious to have him with them, and sent for him. So the , old man made the journey alone, mod arrived in Pittsburgh without mishap. He 'never again, en- gaged in any active employment, altho,ugh he fre- quently asked his s6ns to secure him work, and was especially active in performing various small jobs about the.: house. His health continued excel- lent, his apposite was good, and he never wore glasses or used a stick. His step was light and active, and he-.Vas bright and cheerful up to the day of his death„ which resulted from old age. In ad- dition to his children there are also a number of grandchildren and several great-grandchildren."

We are sorry, however, to have to discount con- siderably the interest of the article by stating that our Pittsburgh contemporary has somehow fallen into an extraordinary error as to the deceased's age. A representative of the " Examiner " has had an interview with his brotber,Dlr. George Setton,cotton worker, and the deceased's niece, with whom he formerly resided in Back Stamford-at., and learns that his age at the time of his death was only 83 years. He was employed many years ago at Hallam Forge.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. • CONTAGICUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 aim 1886. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that as the Board of Agriculture have by Order taking effect from and itnmediately after the Thirteenth day of April, 1892, revoked the Cheshire (Foot-and-Mouth Disease) Move- ment Order of 1892, and the Cheshire Markets and Fairs (Foot-and-Mouth Disease) Order of 1892, and by Orders which also take effect from and immediately after the Thirteenth day of April, 1892, declared the following .Areas. viz "A District or Area in the County of Chester, com- prising all the parishes of the Poor Law Union of• Altrincham, that is to say the parishes of Agden, Altrinchatn, Ashley, Ashton-upon-MerseY, -Aston-by. Budwortb, Baguley, Bexton, Bollin Fee, Bollington, Bowden, Carrington, Dunham Massey, Etchells, Ful- sham, Hale, High Legh, Lymm, Martha!! with Little Watford, Mere, Millington, Mobberley, Nether Knutsford, Northern 011erton, Over Knutsford, Part- , ington, Peover Inferior,-Peover Superior, Pickmere, Plumbley, PownaU Fee, Rostherne, 'Sale, Tabley Inferior, Tabley Superior, Totten, Timperley, Toft, •and Warburton, and "A District or Area, comprising the Boroughs of Birkenhead and Chester, and such part of the County of Chester as is comprised within the Poor-LaW Unions of Birkenhead, Chester, Tarvin, and Wirral. TO BE FOOT AND-MOU 111-DISEASE INFECTED ZONES. Such Areas or Districts are suhject to the pro- visions of the Foot-and-Mouth Disease Order of 1892, No. 2, which provides (1.) That no Public or Private Sale of Cattle, Sheep. or Swine, fat or store, shall be held in' an Infected Zone, otherwise than in accordance with the regul- ations set out in such Order. (2.) That Public Sales of Fat 'Cattle, Sheep, or Swine may be held in an Infected Zone with a Licence of • the Local Authority on the conditions named in the order, or such further conditions as the Local Authority think expedient. (3.) That every Market, Fair-ground, and Sale-yard, in which a Licensed Public Sale of fat Cattle, Sheep, *or Swine is held, shall, as soon as practicable after the Sale, and in any case before it is again used for Animals is cleansed and disinfected in the manner prescribed in the Order. (4.) That Cattle, Sheep, or Swine shall not be moved into an Infected Zone otherwise than in accordance with the Regulations mentioned therein, which Re- gulations provide that Cattle, Sheep, Or Swine may be moved into an Infected Zone' with a Movement License of the Local Authority Zone, District with- in the Zone into which they are to be moved, which License shall be obtained before the • animals are so moved. • (5.) That Cattle, Sheep, or Swine shall not be moved ' - out of ah Infested Zone, except in the manner spe- cially authorised by the Order, and subject to the Regulations mentioned therein. Forma of applications for Licenses for holding Public Sales within Infected Zones may be obtained from the Local Inspector of the Distict in which the proposed sale is int3nded to be held, and must be delivered to him not later than 5 p.m. on the Wednesday in the week previous to that in which the dale is proposed to be held. All particulars respecting movement Licenses can also be obtained from the Local Inspectors of Police ap- pointed under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Acts. Dated this 19th day of April, 1892. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Cheshire County Council.
